    Room area is the exam weight (the guide's approximate share of scored items). Open a room for its objectives. Each small square is one objective sheet: outlined means unread, filled means you have read it.

    What you get from each sheet

    • You know what each objective asks. Every sheet opens with the objective in the guide's own words, so nothing is paraphrased.
    • You recognise the tempting wrong answer. Each sheet ends with how the exam tests the objective, and names the trap family behind every wrong option.
    • You spend time where the points are. The floor plan sizes each domain by its exam weight, from 7% for Developer productivity to 14% for Governance and safety.
    • You finish before the deadline. The month plan fills your days from a start date to your exam date, then keeps the last days for five practice papers.
    • You keep your place. A sheet is marked read when you scroll to its end, and the page offers to continue where you stopped.

    How it works

    1. 1Read the sheet. A worked example, then the decision rules the exam relies on, then how the exam tests them.
    2. 2Recall it. The Remember box holds what you should be able to say in two minutes. Say it back at the end is an optional one minute check.
    3. 3Follow the plan. Sheets in the first phase, a review of the Remember boxes in the second, practice papers in the third.

    Learn every objective in the order the guide lists it. Meet every trap before the exam sets it.

    Where chapters connect

    The doors on the floor plan mark four links between domains.

    • D1 and D3: wrong citations after a refresh start as a feedback signal in §1.9 and are diagnosed in §3.10.
    • D3 and D4: the same refresh failure is the diagnosis-order case in §4.10.
    • D3 and D5: least privilege means removal in §3.2 and is scoped in §5.2.
    • D1 and D5: redacting before the model call in §1.10 is the boundary rule §5.3 applies to regulated data.

    Questions before you start

    Is this an official Anthropic course?

    No. It is independent preparation built from Anthropic's Exam Guide v1.0 and a set of study notes written for this project. The Sources page says what each kind of claim rests on.

    Which exam does it cover?

    Claude Certified Architect – Professional (CCAR-P): 63 items, 120 minutes, closed book, with a pass mark of 720 on a scale of 100 to 1,000. Every objective heading in the course is copied from the guide.

    What if I sit the exam after 7 December?

    Anthropic has announced that exam content changes on 7 December 2026, and that updated guides publish on 17 November. This course is pinned to guide v1.0. A sitting on or after 7 December is governed by the updated guide, and every sheet would need rechecking against it.

    How long does it take?

    You choose the dates. The month plan sizes each day by how many study note sections a sheet covers, so a six section sheet gets a day to itself. The default exam date, 3 December 2026, is a placeholder until you enter your booking.

    Where is my progress saved?

    In this browser only. Nothing is sent anywhere, and you can untick any sheet.

    Do the sheets replace practice papers?

    No. The sheets teach the objectives. The five practice papers come in the last phase of the plan, sat in Practice Mode.

    How was each chapter checked?

    By script against the guide and the study notes, then read once by an independent auditor and an independent cold reader. Facts taken from Anthropic's live documentation carry the date they were read. The Sources page lists them.

    Nothing to sign up for

    There is no account, no email and no payment. The whole course is this one file, and it works offline.

    The three published samples

    The guide prints three sample questions, one each from Domains 3, 2 and 4, and says they are illustrative and not drawn from the live item bank. They are paraphrased here. Decide on your answer, then open the reveal.

    Sample 1, Domain 3: Integration

    A support agent can read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds and delete accounts. Staff only ever read tickets and draft replies. Applying least privilege, which change reduces risk most?

    1. Add logging to the refund and delete tools so misuse can be audited.
    2. Remove the refund and delete tools from the agent's configuration.
    3. Keep all the tools and add a confirmation prompt before refunds and deletions.
    4. Replace the agent with a larger model that follows instructions more reliably.
    AnswerOpen once you have chosen.

    B. Least privilege means removing capabilities the role does not need, which shrinks the attack surface instead of watching it. Logging and confirmation prompts are detective or compensating controls, and model size has nothing to do with authorization scope. This project tags options A and C DETECTIVE-FOR-PREVENTIVE. The idea is taught in O3.2.

    Sample 2, Domain 2: Models, Prompting and Context

    An application sends the same 8,000-token system prompt and policy document on every request, followed by a short, varying user message. Latency and cost both matter. Which optimization addresses both most directly?

    1. Truncate the policy document to its first 1,000 tokens.
    2. Switch to the smallest available model regardless of fit.
    3. Put the static system prompt and policy before the dynamic content, and enable prompt caching.
    4. Move the policy document into a few-shot example block.
    AnswerOpen once you have chosen.

    C. Stable content first, with caching on, lets the repeated prefix be reused, which cuts both time to first token and cost without discarding required context. Truncating loses needed policy, a blindly smaller model risks quality, and a few-shot block does not create a reusable prefix. This project tags the truncation option DISCARD, because it throws away policy the answer needs. The idea is taught in O2.5.

    Sample 3, Domain 4: Evaluation and Optimization

    A RAG system suddenly returns confident but incorrect answers after a document refresh, while latency and model version are unchanged. Where do you look first?

    1. The model weights have silently changed.
    2. The retrieval and indexing step is returning irrelevant or stale chunks.
    3. The temperature setting is too low.
    4. The context window has shrunk.
    AnswerOpen once you have chosen.

    B. Confident wrong answers right after a refresh, with the model and latency unchanged, point at retrieval feeding the model poor context, for example a broken re-index or mismatched embeddings. The other causes would not be triggered by a refresh, and the stem says the model version is unchanged.

    This project tags A, C and D EVIDENCE-MISMATCH, because the stem's evidence does not support them. A wrong option can fit more than one family, and the project's own scenario for the same failure tags the temperature option WRONG-AXIS. The mechanism is taught in O3.5 and the diagnosis order in O4.4.

    Read together, the three rationales reward three habits: remove what the role does not need, put stable content first so it can be reused, and look first at the layer that changed.

    On the day

    You need a valid, unexpired government photo ID whose name matches your registration exactly (guide §11). Closed book means no notes, phones, smart watches or second monitors, and an online candidate must stay in view of the webcam for the whole session (guide §12).

    Month plan

    The 38 sheets spread over the days you have, with a review pass and the five practice papers at the end.

    Pick a start date and your exam date. The plan fills the days in three phases.

    In the first you learn the sheets in guide order and sit the section drill for each. Days are sized by how many corpus sections a sheet covers, so a six-section sheet gets a day to itself.

    In the second you re-read the Remember boxes domain by domain, heaviest first. In the third you sit Papers 1 to 5 in Practice Mode, one a day, and the day before the exam is rest.

    Book before 7 December 2026, when exam content changes. Cancelling or rescheduling closes 48 hours before the appointment.

    The default exam date, 3 December 2026, is a placeholder that leaves a few spare days before the content change. Change it to your booking. Your two dates are stored in this browser only.

    Solution Design & Architecture

    Domain
    D1
    Exam weight
    17%
    Objectives
    6
    Scored items
    about 11
    Guide
    v1.0, section 6

    Seventeen percent of the exam is Domain 1, about 11 of the 63 items. Its six objectives form one chain, and each step takes the output of the one before.

    1. TranslateA business states an outcome. Find the decision inside the workflow that a model can own.
    2. DesignWire that decision into input, processing, output and feedback.
    3. SelectPick the simplest pattern that meets the stated requirements.
    4. OrchestrateAdd agents only where one agent cannot do the job.
    5. DecomposeSplit whatever is still too big to evaluate as one unit.
    6. AlignExpress the whole design in the unit the business measures.

    Every step constrains the next. A wrong answer in this domain is usually a design that works in isolation and has no justification in the requirement the scenario states.

    One idea sits at the centre. The patterns form a ladder: a plain model call, an augmented LLM (the model plus retrieval, tools or memory), a workflow (fixed steps in your code), an agent (the model decides the path) and multi-agent (a coordinator plus specialists). Move right only when the rung to your left demonstrably cannot meet a stated requirement. Each step right buys adaptivity and costs predictability, tokens, latency variance and debugging effort.

    Foundations tested whether a design is correct. Professional tests whether it survives production and whether you can defend it to the person holding the budget. Carry four questions into every scenario: what does it cost at volume, what breaks first under real traffic, how would you explain it to a non-engineer, and what does a regulated sector add.

    Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions

    Sheet
    D1-1
    Exam weight
    17%
    Domain
    Solution Design & Architecture
    Corpus sections
    1.1 1.2
    Reading time
    ≈ 10 min
    Position
    1 of 6 in D1

    The sales director of a commercial insurance broker asks, "Can Claude write our quotes?" The broker issues 400 quotes a week, and each one takes an underwriter 22 minutes on average. An underwriter is a person who decides whether to accept an insurance risk and at what price. The week holds 8,800 minutes of quote work, about 147 hours.

    Three underwriters have about 35 productive hours a week each, 105 hours between them, so the team is about 42 hours a week short and quotes wait. Turnaround, the time from a request arriving to the quote going out, averages 3.2 business days, and the broker loses business on any quote that takes longer than 2 days.

    Before anyone picks a design, each step of the work needs scoring for what a model can own (§1.1), and today's cost needs writing down in a unit the business already uses (§1.2).

    Score every step on its own§1.1

    What you automate inside a workflow, the chain of steps from a request to a result, is a decision: a recurring point where someone reads inputs and forms a judgment. An outcome such as "quote faster" is too broad to build, and a task such as copying a field into another system involves no judgment.

    Four fit signals favour automating a step. More cases arrive than people can handle. The same kind of judgment recurs, and someone eventually sees whether it was right. That result is the feedback. The inputs are in a form a machine can read. The volume is high enough to repay the cost of building.

    Five wrong-stance signals show that handing the decision itself to the model is the wrong stance. The decision is irreversible and rare. A regulation requires a human decision-maker. The output is novel and creative, with low repeatability. The human relationship is the product. A human must gate every iteration, which means approving each pass before the next begins.

    Apply the signals to one step at a time, never to the whole workflow. A workflow almost never scores the same all the way through, and the split that results is the design. The broker's process has five steps, and the figure scores each one.

    Classifying the risk tier, which places a risk in a band, is the slow-feedback case. The loss ratio, claims paid against premiums earned, shows whether a tier was right only after 12 months. A slow result does not rule a step out. It needs a proxy signal, a fast measure that stands in for the slow one. How often underwriters override the model's tier is one, because it shows the day someone disagrees.

    Pricing and signing is the regulated step. The quote needs a licensed underwriter's signature, so the model prepares a complete draft and the underwriter decides. That step holds 4 of the 22 minutes. The three automated steps hold 16, or 73% of the total, and a verdict of "not a fit" for the whole workflow would give those up.

    Where the human relationship is the product, as in relationship-managed sales, the model prepares the conversation and a person holds it.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A step is high-volume and machine-readable, and its correctness is visible immediatelyAutomate the step.All four fit signals are present.
    • A step's outcome feedback arrives 12 months later, for example a loss ratioAutomate it, with a proxy signal such as the override rate or the reopen rate (the share of resolved tickets that come back).Long feedback latency needs a fast surrogate, not disqualification.
    • A step requires a decision that a licence or the law assigns to a personThe human decides, and the model prepares the draft.Regulation is a boundary, not a constraint to engineer around.
    • A whole workflow is judged "not a fit" because one step is regulatedReject that judgment. Decompose first: split the workflow into steps and score each.Per-step scoring is the technique. Whole-workflow scoring loses the automatable majority.
    • The human relationship is the product being soldAutomate the preparation, not the interaction.Removing the relationship removes the value.
    Go deeper: the broker's week in numbers

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule. The design automates the three steps worth 9 + 3 + 4 = 16 minutes a quote. That leaves 22 minus 16 = 6 minutes, made up of 4 for pricing and signing and 2 for formatting and sending.

    Across 400 quotes a week, the automated steps remove 400 × 16 = 6,400 minutes of human work, about 107 hours. The underwriters' remaining work is 400 × 6 = 2,400 minutes, or 40 hours, against the 105 they have.

    The 6 minutes is a projection. Whether turnaround falls below 2 days is a separate question, and only a measurement against the baseline in §1.2 can answer it.

    Fix the baseline and the unit before you design§1.2

    A request names a mechanism, and the pain behind it names the requirement. The director asks for quotes written by Claude, while the pain is a turnaround of 3.2 days with business lost beyond 2 days. The target is turnaround. Quality of prose is not the binding constraint, the factor that actually limits the result.

    Before designing, state what the process costs today in a value unit, a unit the business already uses: minutes per item, FTE-hours (hours of full-time-equivalent staff time) per 1,000 items, dollars per transaction, or days of turnaround. That statement is the baseline. For the broker it reads 22 minutes and 3.2 business days per quote, and the business case is written in that sentence.

    Without a baseline no design can be compared with another and no value can be reported. The system ships and works, and nobody can show it helped. An improvement that was never measured cannot be defended to the person who funded it.

    If no baseline exists, measure the current process before committing to a design. A plan to "measure the improvement after launch" produces a number with nothing before it to compare with.

    One case has no baseline to find: a capability that never existed. A per-unit comparison needs a per-unit figure from before, and a new capability has none, so there is no efficiency baseline. The value is argued as transformation, one of the five value pillars, the kinds of business value that objective 1.6 lists.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • The request is "can Claude write our quotes", and the stated pain is a 3.2-day turnaround that loses business above 2 daysTarget the turnaround. Quality of prose is not the binding constraint.The requirement is the metric named in the pain, not the mechanism named in the request.
    • No baseline is available for the current processMeasure it before committing to a design.A design chosen without a baseline cannot be defended or compared.
    • The proposal is to "measure the improvement after launch"Reject it.Measurement with no before produces a number with nothing to compare it to.
    • The capability did not previously exist at allNo efficiency baseline exists, so argue transformation.A per-unit comparison has no denominator, because there is no earlier cost per unit.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide says its exam items are written against the objectives, and it gives this one a single line. Its three samples cover Domains 3, 2 and 4, so Domain 1 has no official sample. The shapes below come from this project's scenario set, not from Anthropic, and the Trap families page defines each label.

    InferenceExpect options that all automate something and differ in which step they target, with the disqualifying constraint placed in the setup of the stem.

    A broker wants faster quotes. One step in its process requires a licensed underwriter's signature.

    • CorrectAutomate the extraction, the lookup and a risk-tier recommendation. Hand the licensed underwriter a complete draft to sign, and state the value as turnaround time.
    • WrongOVERSPECAutomate the whole quote, sign-off included, with an audit log and a confidence threshold for oversight. The scenario requires a human decision-maker, and no threshold satisfies that requirement. The option puts a monitoring guarantee where the required person should be.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISDeclare the workflow unsuitable for automation because of the regulated step. It applies the wrong-stance test to the whole workflow, when the technique is to decompose it and score each step.

    A stakeholder asks for an AI drafting tool. The stated pain is turnaround time.

    • CorrectBaseline the handling time per item and the turnaround in days, then design against the turnaround requirement.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEBuild the drafting tool as requested and measure satisfaction after launch. It delivers the requested mechanism, leaves the stated requirement untouched, and gives nothing to measure it against.
    • WrongREPAIRInstrument the deployed system with dashboards and derive the baseline afterwards from its own logs. It reconstructs after the fact a measurement that could have been captured cleanly before the project started.
    Say it backA broker's quotes take 3.2 days and it loses business above 2. One step needs a licensed underwriter's signature. What do you measure first, and what do you automate?

    Measure the baseline first: minutes per quote and days of turnaround, because turnaround is the requirement. Then score the steps one by one. Automate extraction, lookup and a risk-tier recommendation, use the override rate as a proxy while the tier waits 12 months for its outcome, and give the underwriter a complete draft to sign.

    Connections

    This is the first objective in the guide, so it leans on no earlier one.

    • O1.2, §1.9: the override rate used here as a proxy is a feedback signal there, and it counts only when it reaches something that changes behaviour.
    • O1.2, §1.10: the draft handed to the underwriter is an output with a human consumer. Inference: §1.10's rule to put the reasoning beside the verdict applies to it.

    • O1.6, §1.12: the baseline is the before that the five value pillars are stated against, and the new-capability rule returns there as transformation.
