No live-document check was needed: the chapter states decision rules and no product facts.

    Remember

    1. The unit of automation is a recurring decision inside a workflow. Score each step, never the whole workflow.
    2. Four fit signals: scale past human capacity, a repeatable pattern with observable feedback, machine-readable context, volume that repays the build. Five wrong-stance signals: irreversible and rare, regulation requiring a human, novel low-repeatability output, the relationship as the product, a human gating every iteration.
    3. Slow feedback, such as a 12-month loss ratio, still means automate. Add a fast proxy: the override rate or the reopen rate.
    4. A licensed or statutory decision stays human, and the model prepares the draft. One regulated step does not make the whole workflow a non-fit. If the relationship is the product, automate the preparation.
    5. A request names a mechanism and the pain names the requirement. Design against the metric the pain names.
    6. Baseline first, in a business unit: minutes per item, FTE-hours per 1,000, dollars per transaction, days of turnaround. Measuring after launch has no before. A capability that never existed has no efficiency baseline, so argue transformation.

    Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)

    Sheet
    D1-2
    Exam weight
    17%
    Domain
    Solution Design & Architecture
    Corpus sections
    1.9 1.10
    Reading time
    ≈ 8 min
    Position
    2 of 6 in D1

    A support team runs an AI triage system on 12,000 tickets a month. Reviewers change the category on about 4% of them, which is 480 corrections a month. What the architecture does with those corrections decides whether the system ever improves. If a fix overwrites the field, the correction is lost. If it is stored as an event and routed somewhere that changes behaviour, the team gains 480 labelled examples a month.

    A system has four stages: input, processing, output and feedback. The corpus's reading is that the fourth is the one omitted when a system ships.

    The chapter's second idea is placement. Each rule goes at the earliest stage that can enforce it, because a filter further downstream only repairs what an earlier stage could have prevented. To place a rule, ask which stage first has what it needs to enforce it, and if two stages can, take the earlier one.

    Feedback is closed only when something changes§1.9

    A loop is closed when a correctness signal reaches something that changes the system's behaviour. Signals come in three kinds. Implicit ones are almost free: a reviewer edits a draft, overrides a category or rejects a suggestion. Explicit ones take effort, such as ratings or a labelling queue.

    Outcome signals are the most decisive and often the slowest. Whether a ticket reopened shows within days, while the loss ratio (claims paid against premiums earned, in insurance) takes a year to settle. A fast signal, such as the override rate or the reopen rate, is added as a proxy alongside the slow one.

    The gap between what the model produced and what the human shipped is labelled data that costs almost nothing to collect. It only counts if the correction is stored as an event beside the original prediction.

    Then it has somewhere to go. Two destinations are the evaluation set (the fixed test cases the system is scored against) and the prompt or its few-shot examples (sample inputs and answers shown to the model). The others are the retrieval and indexing layer, the routing thresholds that decide what goes to a human, and the choice of model.

    Someone has to own that step, and a regular review of the disagreement cases is one way to do it.

    Logs, dashboards and monitoring alerts do not close a loop. They record what happened without saying whether it was right, so they change nothing by themselves.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A deployed system with human reviewers has shown no improvement in six monthsCapture the overrides and route them into the evaluation set and the prompt.The signal exists and is being discarded.
    • The scenario's architecture lists only input, processing and outputThe feedback path is what is missing.There are four stages, and this is the one omitted at ship time.
    • The outcome signal arrives 12 months laterAdd a fast proxy alongside it, such as override rate or reopen rate.A loop that closes annually cannot steer a monthly release cycle.
    • The team proposes a monitoring dashboard as the improvement mechanismIt is insufficient on its own.It shows what happened, carries no correctness label and changes nothing.
    • Citations go wrong after a document refreshRoute the signal to the retrieval and indexing layer.The failure is in retrieval, not in the model.
    Go deeper: three signals wired for the triage system

    The 480 overrides are one of three signals worth wiring (a worked example, not a corpus rule). In practice an override is one stored row: the ticket ID, the model's category, the reviewer's category, the prompt version and a timestamp. Rows where the two categories differ are the disagreement cases, and sampling them into the evaluation set is a single query.

    The triage system also drafts a first reply. The edit distance between that draft and what the agent actually sent is a second signal: heavily edited drafts go into the evaluation set, and lightly edited ones confirm the pattern is working. Both of these are implicit signals.

    The third is the reopen rate at seven days, joined back to the original category and confidence. It is an outcome signal that arrives within days, which is why it works as a fast proxy, and it can catch a failure the other two miss: a confident, plausible triage that resolves the ticket wrongly. Each signal has a named destination, which is what makes it feedback.

    Put each rule at the earliest stage that can enforce it§1.10

    Start at the front. The input boundary does three jobs: it acquires the data from a webhook, a queue or an upload, it validates and normalises it, and it decides what to trust. Content from outside your control is untrusted until the boundary decides otherwise. The boundary also fixes what the rest of the system can never recover, because context that was not captured here does not exist downstream.

    Processing is the model call plus the code around it. The common mistake is giving the model work that code does exactly: arithmetic, lookups, schema validation, threshold checks and required sequencing. Redaction is the same kind of work, and it belongs at the boundary, before the model sees anything.

    Take a support agent that sometimes acts on the wrong account because it skipped identity verification. A firmer prompt makes skipping less likely. A programmatic precondition is a check in code that blocks the account-action tool until the verification call returns a verified identifier, and that rules skipping out.

    The output is a contract, and whoever consumes it sets the terms. A service that routes on the result needs a field it can parse and an explicit confidence value it can compare with a threshold, because routing is code and code cannot act on prose. How the confidence value is produced and calibrated is a separate design question, and routing only needs the field to exist.

    A human reviewer needs the reasoning and the citations beside the verdict.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Unsupported file types reach the model and produce garbageReject them at input validation.Only the boundary can stop them before the model sees them. Later stages can only detect the damage.
    • Personal data must not reach the modelRedact before the model call.Filtering the output afterwards does not undo the exposure.
    • Step A must always come before step BMake it a programmatic precondition that blocks B until A returns.A prompt instruction is probabilistic; a precondition is deterministic.
    • A downstream service routes on the model's outputReturn a JSON contract with an explicit confidence field.Routing is code, so it needs a field and not prose.
    • A human reviewer consumes the outputPut the reasoning and citations beside the verdict.The consumer determines the shape.
    • Customer tier and history would help the modelAttach them at the input boundary.They cost nothing there and cannot be recovered later.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three sample questions cover Domains 3, 2 and 4, so Domain 1 has no official sample. The two shapes below come from this project's own scenario set, not from Anthropic. Each wrong option carries a family label, and the Trap families page defines all eight. InferenceExpect a stem that names an output's consumer, and a stem where personal data must be handled before the model call.

    An accurate system with human reviewers shows no measurable improvement after six months.

    • CorrectCapture reviewer corrections as labelled events and route the disagreement cases into the evaluation set and prompt revisions.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDAdd a monitoring dashboard for accuracy, latency and volume. It sounds like the professional answer, but it only measures the plateau.
    • WrongDISCARDMove to a more capable model. It replaces a working part instead of adding the missing one, and a system with no feedback path cannot improve at any ceiling.

    A support agent occasionally acts on the wrong account because the identity check is skipped.

    • CorrectAdd a programmatic precondition: block the account-action tool until the verification call has returned a verified identifier.
    • WrongREPAIRStrengthen the system prompt to always verify first. It handles at the prompt layer a sequence that must hold every time, so enforcement stays probabilistic.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEAdd few-shot examples that show the correct call order. It raises compliance without guaranteeing it, on a requirement that needs a guarantee.
    Say it backA triage tool shows reviewers its category, and a reviewer fixes a wrong one by editing the field. Six months on, accuracy is flat. Which stage is missing, and what is the first change?

    Feedback is missing. Store each edit as an event next to the original prediction, then route those disagreements to the evaluation set and to prompt revisions. The overwritten field is the discarded signal.

    Connections

    • O1.1, §1.1: the fast proxy (override rate, reopen rate) first appears there, for steps whose outcome arrives 12 months later.
    • O1.3, §1.3: "paths that can be listed in advance belong in code" widens this chapter's deterministic-work rule from one step to a whole workflow.
    • O3.5, §3.10: wrong citations after a refresh are routed to the retrieval and indexing layer here and diagnosed there.
    • O4.2, §4.3: reviewer overrides are real production traces, the first source an evaluation set should draw on. O4.6, §4.12 records the prompt and model version per request so a change can be attributed.
    • O5.4, §5.3: a control that fires after the request is assembled is too late, which is §1.10's redaction rule applied to regulated data.
    • O5.3, §5.8: a reviewer shown a fluent conclusion without its evidence tends to approve it. Inference: §1.10's rule to put reasoning and citations beside the verdict guards against that risk.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 1, second objective. Course corpus §1.9 and §1.10. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states architecture rules and no product facts.

    Remember

    1. Four stages: input, processing, output, feedback. Feedback is closed only when a correctness signal reaches something that changes behaviour.
    2. Logs, dashboards and alerts record what happened and carry no correctness label. They are not feedback.
    3. The cheapest labelled data is the gap between what the model produced and what the human shipped, stored as an event. A slow outcome signal needs a fast proxy.
    4. The input boundary acquires, validates and normalises, and decides what to trust. Context not captured there does not exist downstream.
    5. Arithmetic, lookups, schema checks, redaction and mandatory order belong in code. "Must always" gets a precondition in code, because a prompt cannot guarantee it.
    6. The output contract is set by its consumer: a service needs a parseable field and a confidence value, a reviewer needs reasoning and citations.

    Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)

    Sheet
    D1-3
    Exam weight
    17%
    Domain
    Solution Design & Architecture
    Corpus sections
    1.3 1.4
    Reading time
    ≈ 10 min
    Position
    3 of 6 in D1

    Should 50,000 monthly invoices go through a fixed five-step pipeline or through an agent, a model that picks its own next step? Of the 50,000, 96% (48,000) come from 40 known vendors in stable formats, and 4% (2,000) are one-offs, malformed or new. The pipeline cannot process the 2,000. The agent can process all 50,000, but it spends agent-level cost and response time on the 48,000 that never needed it.

    The corpus lays the options out as a five-rung ladder. First is the plain call: one prompt, one response. Second is an augmented LLM, a large language model (LLM) given retrieval (fetching documents at request time), tools (functions it can call) or memory (information kept between interactions). Third is a workflow, which runs fixed steps in your code. Fourth is the agent, and fifth is a multi-agent system, a coordinator over specialists.

    Move right only when the rung to the left demonstrably cannot meet a requirement the scenario states. Each move right costs more: the same request can take different routes (nondeterminism), and response times spread out (latency variance). Calls multiply, and with them the tokens (words and word parts) you pay for. Results get harder to evaluate, and a wrong action reaches further (a wider blast radius).

    Ask whether the paths can be written down in advance§1.3

    A set of paths is enumerable when you can list every route a request may take before it runs. Enumerable paths belong in code. If the next action depends on a discovery that cannot be listed in advance, the model has to choose it. That requirement alone pays for an agent. Without it, sitting further right earns no credit.

    Branching does not make a path unlistable. Take a request that is classified and sent to one of five specialised handlers. The five branches are written down, so the model chooses from a fixed menu. That is routing, and it is still a workflow.

    Needing data is a different question from choosing the path. When a task needs current or private data and the path is fixed, retrieval solves it. The result is an augmented LLM, and it adds no nondeterminism to the control flow, the order in which steps run.

    Traffic can be mixed. In the opening example, 96% of invoices share a known format and 4% are novel. Give each population, meaning each group of similar requests, the cheapest rung that handles it. A workflow takes the 96%. A validation gate, a check inside the workflow that sends failures down a different route, hands the other 4% to an agent on an exception route.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Five known steps, in the same order, on every requestBuild a workflow.The paths are enumerable, and code is cheaper, faster and testable.
    • Classify the request, then dispatch it to one of five specialised handlersStill a workflow: the routing pattern.Enumerated branches are routing, not agency.
    • The number of steps is unknown, and each action depends on what the last one foundUse an agent.A non-enumerable path is the requirement that funds the move right.
    • The task needs current or private data, but the path is fixedUse an augmented LLM.Retrieval solves it without control-flow nondeterminism.
    • 96% of traffic is one known format and 4% is novelBuild a workflow with an agentic exception route.Match each population to the cheapest rung that handles it.
    Go deeper: what Anthropic's own post says about patterns

    This is not a corpus rule. It comes from Anthropic's post "Building effective agents", published 19 December 2024. The post defines workflows as systems where models and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, and agents as systems where models dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage. Its basic building block is a model enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory, the same combination the ladder's second rung names.

    The post names five workflow patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimiser. Prompt chaining splits a task into a sequence of steps. Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialised follow-up task. Parallelisation runs subtasks at the same time, either as independent sections or as repeated runs that vote.

    In orchestrator-workers a central model breaks the task down, delegates to worker models and synthesises their results. Its subtasks are determined by the orchestrator from the specific input and are not pre-defined, which separates it from parallelisation. In evaluator-optimiser, one call generates a response while another evaluates it, in a loop.

    On when to use agents, the post says they suit open-ended problems where the required number of steps is difficult or impossible to predict and a fixed path cannot be hardcoded. It also recommends the simplest solution possible, and says agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance.

    Read the setup for the sentence that rules a workflow out§1.4

    The opposite error is staying too far left. Three phrases in a setup rule the workflow out: "scope is not known up front", "each step depends on what the previous step discovered" and "the relevant tools are identified at runtime". Any one of them makes the path unlistable, which eliminates the workflow before the options are compared.

    A workflow forced onto an unlistable task silently handles only the enumerated part. Adding tests to a legacy codebase of unknown structure shows why. The code has to be mapped first, and what the map shows decides the next step, so no fixed script can react to it. An agent with dynamic adaptive planning revises its plan as dependencies surface.

    The two designs differ in the shape of their cost. A workflow's cost is a point, because every request makes the same calls. An agent's cost is a distribution, because some requests take many more calls than the average. Budget against the tail (the slowest and costliest few percent of requests) and not against the mean (the average).

    A stated service-level agreement (SLA), a commitment about performance such as response time, filters designs before they are compared. A p95 target means that 95% of requests must finish within the limit, so it measures the tail, and an agent whose mean passes can still fail it.

    Simplicity is the default. A task with a known path, such as the same six-section review for every submission, gets a fixed pipeline (prompt chaining: each step's output feeds the next).

    When the scenario states that the path cannot be known in advance, the simpler rung is wrong and loses the item. A team that wants an agent because the workflow "feels rigid" has stated no requirement, so ask which path cannot be listed.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A request to add thorough tests to a legacy codebase of unknown structureAn agent with dynamic adaptive planning.Scope is discovered by mapping first, so no fixed script can react to it.
    • "Produce the same six-section review for every submission"A fixed pipeline (prompt chaining).It is predictable and reproducible, and agency adds nondeterminism for nothing.
    • An agent is chosen, and a p95 latency SLA is statedRe-check the choice: the agent's tail may fail the SLA even if its mean passes.An SLA filters designs before they are compared.
    • A team proposes an agent "because the workflow feels rigid"Reject it unless a non-enumerable requirement is stated.Rigidity is a feeling, and enumerability is the test.
    Go deeper: the invoice pipeline, costed and timed

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule. Assume $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens; these are round figures for the arithmetic, not a quoted price. The pipeline makes 5 calls per invoice, each with 4,000 tokens in and 500 out. That is 20,000 in and 2,500 out, which costs $0.0975 per invoice and $4,875 a month across 50,000 invoices.

    The agent averages 9 calls per invoice. Because the Messages API is stateless (the model keeps no conversation between calls), each call sends the full history so far, so assume an average of 12,000 tokens in and 400 out per call. That is 108,000 in and 3,600 out: $0.378 per invoice and $18,900 a month, or 3.9 times the pipeline.

    The hybrid sends 48,000 invoices through the pipeline at $0.0975 and 2,000 to the agent at $0.378. That is $4,680 plus $756, or $5,436 a month. The 2,000 also pay for the three pipeline calls made up to the gate, at $0.0195 each, which adds $117 and makes $5,553.

    That is 13.9% above the pure pipeline, against 288% above for the pure agent. It prices every exception invoice at the agent's average, though the exceptions are the hard cases.

    For the timing in the figure, assume each call takes 1.5 seconds. The pipeline always takes 5 calls, or 7.5 seconds. The agent averages 9 calls, or 13.5 seconds, and its 95th-percentile invoice takes 20 calls, or 30 seconds. Against a p95 limit of 15 seconds, the pipeline passes, and the agent's mean passes while its p95 fails.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three sample questions cover Domains 3, 2 and 4, so Domain 1 has no official sample. The two scenarios below come from this project's own set, not from Anthropic. Each wrong option carries a family label, and the Trap families page defines all eight.

    The corpus says both directions appear as separate items. InferenceExpect one stem that sounds sophisticated over enumerable requirements, and one that states a requirement a workflow cannot meet. A third shape may ask which statement justifies a design: the sound one cites a requirement from the scenario, and the weak ones cite a general virtue such as "agents are more flexible".

    A document pipeline is described as intelligent and adaptive. Its stated requirements are five fixed steps.

    • CorrectBuild a fixed workflow with a validation gate, and route gate failures to an agentic exception path.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDBuild it as an agent so the system can adapt to future document types. It sounds more capable and future-proof, but nothing in the stated requirements is non-enumerable, so the agent adds cost and latency variance on 100% of traffic to serve a hypothetical.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEBuild a workflow with no exception route and send anything unhandled to a human queue. It is the right rung for the majority, but it drops the stated requirement to handle novel formats.

    The corpus stem is short, and its explanation of the half-move refers to a requirement to handle novel formats that the stem does not spell out. In a full item, expect that requirement to be stated, as the 4% of novel traffic is in the opening example.

    An open-ended investigation can only be scoped by exploring first, such as adding tests to a legacy codebase of unknown structure.

    • CorrectUse an agent with adaptive planning: map the structure, prioritise high-impact areas and adapt as dependencies surface.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEUse a fixed pipeline with predetermined steps, extended to cover the most likely cases. It covers the enumerable subset and silently drops the requirement that made the task non-enumerable.
    • WrongDISCARDSend one large single-pass prompt covering the entire codebase at once. It replaces staged, adaptive work with a monolith that dilutes attention across everything.
    Say it backOne team wants an agent for a six-section review it produces for every submission, because the workflow "feels rigid". Another wants a fixed script to add tests to a codebase nobody has mapped. How do you rule on each?

    The first is a fixed pipeline. The review has the same six sections every time, so its paths can be listed, and "feels rigid" states no requirement that an agent would meet. The second is an agent with adaptive planning. Scope is discovered by mapping first, so no fixed script can react to what the mapping finds.

    Connections

    • Leans on O1.1, §1.1: the decision found there is what a rung has to carry out. "Workflow" there means the business process whose steps are scored one by one, and here it names a design pattern, fixed steps run by code.
    • Leans on O1.2, §1.10: code takes the work it does exactly, such as arithmetic, lookups and mandatory order, at a single step. Here the same reasoning covers a whole path that can be listed in advance.
    • O1.4, §1.5: the ladder's fifth rung follows the same rule. A coordinator over specialists needs one stated justification from three: parallelism under a latency requirement, context isolation or per-role tool privilege. Otherwise one agent with the right tools is the answer.
    • O1.5, §1.11: plans get the same split, a fixed pipeline for known scope and dynamic adaptive decomposition for discovered scope. Its confidence-tier split, a cheap path for routine cases and an expensive one for hard cases, parallels this chapter's hybrid.
    • O1.6, §1.12: a stated SLA is a filter applied before designs are compared, and the point-versus-distribution cost shape returns there.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 1, third objective. Course corpus §1.3 and §1.4. Live checks, read 2026-10-25: Anthropic, "Building effective agents", published 19 December 2024 (anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents), for the definitions, the five workflow patterns and the guidance on agents in the first fold; Anthropic documentation, "Using the Messages API" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/working-with-messages), for the statement that the API is stateless and the full conversational history is sent each time. The token rates, call counts and call times in the second fold are assumptions chosen for the arithmetic, not prices or measurements.

    Remember

    1. The ladder runs plain call, augmented LLM, workflow, agent, multi-agent. Move right only when the rung to the left demonstrably cannot meet a stated requirement.
    2. Enumerability is the test: can the paths be written down in advance? If so, they belong in code. Choosing from a fixed menu of branches is routing, and it is still a workflow.
    3. Current or private data on a fixed path needs retrieval, an augmented LLM. Mixed traffic gets a workflow with an agentic exception route.
    4. A setup sentence that makes the path unlistable rules the workflow out. A workflow on such a task silently handles only the enumerated part.
    5. Workflow cost is a point and agent cost is a distribution. Budget against the tail, and test a stated p95 SLA against the agent's tail, not its mean.
    6. "Feels rigid" is a feeling. Reject an agent unless the scenario states a non-enumerable requirement.

    Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies

    Sheet
    D1-4
    Exam weight
    17%
    Domain
    Solution Design & Architecture
    Corpus sections
    1.5 1.6 1.7 1.8
    Reading time
    ≈ 14 min
    Position
    4 of 6 in D1

    A research brief splits into four independent threads. One agent that takes them in turn needs 40, 55, 35 and 50 seconds, so the report arrives after 180 seconds. Four agents working at once, one branch each, finish when the slowest branch does, after 55 seconds. The price is tokens (words and word parts): typically four to five times a single agent's spend, because context one agent held once is duplicated across every agent.

    The multi-agent design in the corpus has one coordinator and several subagents. The coordinator divides the task, hands out the parts and brings the results together. Subagents never talk to one another. Every message passes through the coordinator, an arrangement called hub-and-spoke.

    Find the reason the scenario gives for more agents before adding any. After a defect, ask what the coordinator did before asking what a subagent did, because each subagent sees only what the coordinator gave it.

    Add agents only for a reason the scenario states§1.5

    The corpus accepts three reasons for more than one agent, and the scenario must state at least one. The first is parallelism under a latency requirement, which buys wall-clock time. The second is context isolation. The third is privilege separation. If the scenario states none of them, a single agent with the right tools is the answer.

    Suppose each of four research threads adds 30,000 tokens of material. A single agent then holds 120,000 tokens when it begins to synthesise, with thread one's material still in the window while it reasons about thread four. Four isolated agents hold 30,000 each, which keeps every window small even though the total across agents is higher, and a synthesis agent receives four structured summaries, compact records with named fields, instead of four transcripts.

    Privilege separation is set in configuration: the drafting role is built without a write tool, and the verifying role without a search tool. Every split also adds a handoff between the coordinator and a subagent, and each handoff loses information. A direct channel between subagents would dissolve both the isolation and the privilege boundary, and the token cost would remain.

    That makes multi-agent the most expensive rung of the pattern ladder, so only the three reasons justify the climb. A sequential task has no independent branches to run together, and where cost is the named pillar the multiplier works against it. The corpus gives stakeholders one sentence: "We pay more tokens to buy wall-clock time and clean separation of privilege."

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Four independent research threads, and turnaround is a stated commitmentMulti-agent, with parallel fan-out.The latency requirement funds the token multiplier.
    • One agent's context would exceed the window, or threads would contaminate each otherMulti-agent.Context isolation is the justification.
    • A drafting role must not have write access, and a verifier must not have search accessMulti-agent.Privilege separation is the justification.
    • A sequential task with no latency constraint, where one tool set would serveSingle agent.Nothing funds the multiplier.
    • Cost is the stated pillar and the subtasks are sequentialSingle agent.Multi-agent moves the named pillar the wrong way.
    Go deeper: Anthropic's own token figures

    This is not a corpus rule. In Anthropic's post "How we built our multi-agent research system" (13 June 2025), "agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions" and multi-agent systems "use about 15× more tokens than chats".

    Those baselines are chats, and the corpus's 4 to 5× is measured against a single agent. Dividing the two figures gives 3.75. The post does not state that ratio, so this is an inference, and it lands just under the corpus range.

    The post says multi-agent systems "excel at valuable tasks that involve heavy parallelization, information that exceeds single context windows, and interfacing with numerous complex tools". Parallelism and context isolation appear in the corpus list too. It names as poor fits the problem areas that "require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents".

    Its cost condition is that the task's value be "high enough to pay for the increased performance", which is the corpus's rule that the multiplier needs funding.

    Ask what the coordinator did before blaming a subagent§1.6

    The coordinator owns four things. Decomposition is how it splits the task before delegating, for example into distinct subtopics or source types. Context passing is what each subagent receives, and in what form. Error handling is what happens when a subagent fails. Termination criteria say when the work stops. A subagent's context is isolated, so it knows only what the coordinator passed it.

    Because the coordinator owns those four things, an output-level symptom in a multi-agent system usually traces to it and not to a subagent. A subagent that returned correct results on the ground it was assigned, meaning its part of the task, has done its job. A wrong report then points at how the parts were assigned, what was passed, how failure was handled or when the loop stopped.

    Three terms in the rules below need a gloss. A prompt is procedural when it lists steps, and goal-oriented when it states the goal and the quality criteria. With structured error propagation, a failure returns to the coordinator as data it can act on. A recovery policy is the coordinator's rule for what happens next: retry, skip or escalate.

    The Task-equivalent is the capability that lets a coordinator start subagents at all. When it is missing from the coordinator's configuration, there is nothing to delegate with.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • The report misses whole subtopics, and every subagent returned correct resultsThe coordinator's decomposition was too narrow.Rules out: subagent query quality.
    • Two subagents investigated the same groundThe coordinator did not partition the space before delegating.Rules out: missing deduplication after the fact.
    • The final report's citations are wrong or missingContent and metadata were passed as merged free text.Rules out: the synthesis agent failing to "remember to cite".
    • One subagent's failure terminated the whole runThere was no structured error propagation and no coordinator recovery policy.Rules out: the subagent being unreliable.
    • The coordinator attempts everything itself and never delegatesThe Task-equivalent spawning capability is absent from its configuration.Rules out: a system prompt that does not mention delegation.
    • Research output is shallow and checklist-likeThe coordinator prompt is procedural instead of goal-oriented.Rules out: too few subagents.
    Go deeper: how the Agent SDK expresses these controls

    This is not a corpus rule. It comes from the Agent SDK page "Subagents in the SDK", read on 25 October 2026. A coordinator starts a subagent by calling the Agent tool. The page says the tool appears as "Task" in the initial tool list and that tool-use blocks before Claude Code v2.1.63 also named it "Task", which is the "Task-equivalent" of the corpus row.

    A subagent definition takes a description, a prompt and an optional list of tools, among other fields. A tool left out of that list "isn't in the subagent's session at all", with "no permission prompt or error". That is removal by configuration, the form of least privilege that §3.2 requires.

    The page also says that an ordinary subagent starts with a fresh context window. The only content passed down is the Agent tool's prompt string, and only the subagent's final message comes back. A fork, which copies the parent conversation, is the exception. These two narrow channels are where handoff loss happens, which is why §1.7 is about the passing format.

    The runtime does not enforce the corpus's topology. The page says a subagent can spawn subagents of its own, with 3 layers below the main agent allowed by default, and that a subagent given the SendMessage tool is told the names of other agents it can message. Hub-and-spoke is a design choice made in configuration.

    The page's advice for a coordinator that answers directly instead of delegating is to name the subagent in the prompt and write a clear description. Inference: that advice suits a coordinator that has the tool and leaves it unused, while the corpus row covers the case where the tool is absent.

    Pass findings with their sources attached§1.7

    A synthesis agent can cite only what reaches it as a separate field. So the coordinator passes each finding as content plus metadata: its provenance, meaning source URL, document name, page and date. Merge the two into free text during aggregation and attribution, the link from a claim to its source, is lost. An instruction to cite cannot restore it, because the agent cannot cite metadata it never received.

    Conflicts and audits depend on the same separation. When two sources report different values, keep both with their attribution and mark the conflict. The coordinator decides which to use. A regulated audit trail needs the citation, the input and the prompt version, and flattened provenance loses all three.

    The receiver of a handoff can also be a person. A human who receives an escalation does not have the transcript, so the handoff summary must stand alone. It carries the entity ID, an issue summary, the root cause, the actions already taken, the amount or quantity at stake, the recommended action and the reason for escalating.

    A gap in the synthesis goes back to the coordinator, which sends targeted queries and runs the synthesis again. With only 3 of 5 sources returned, failing the run discards three good sources. The coordinator synthesises instead, with coverage annotations that mark what is well supported and what is missing. That is graceful degradation.

    Zero results from a subagent is a finding. Read zero results as a timeout and the coordinator retries for nothing. Read a timeout as zero results and an access failure goes unreported as an empty finding.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • The synthesis subagent must cite sourcesPass findings as {content, metadata} with source URL, document name and page.Citation requires the metadata to survive as metadata.
    • The synthesis output has coverage gapsThe coordinator evaluates, re-delegates targeted queries and re-invokes synthesis.Refinement is the coordinator's job.
    • Human reviewers keep re-asking for information the system already gatheredPass a structured handoff summary that is self-contained.The human has no transcript access.
    • Upstream inputs were partially unavailable (3 of 5 sources returned)Synthesise with coverage annotations marking what is well supported and what is missing.Graceful degradation: do not fail the whole run.
    • A subagent returns "0 results"Accept it as a valid finding.An empty result is information; a timeout is an access failure.
    Go deeper: one finding, before and after

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its figures are invented. Merged into free text, three findings reach the synthesis agent as one sentence: Revenue rose 12%, margins fell 2 points and headcount is flat, per the filings. The agent can write "per the filings" and nothing more exact.

    Passed as records, each finding keeps its own source: {content: "Revenue rose 12% in 2025", metadata: {url, document: "Annual report 2025", page: 14}}. The page number is a field, so it reaches the report intact. If a press release gives a different revenue figure, both records go forward with their attribution and the conflict is marked.

    Fan out what is independent and chain only real dependencies§1.8

    Three shapes cover the choices. In parallel fan-out the coordinator sends independent subtasks out together. In sequential chaining step B needs step A's extracted entity, which is a real data dependency. Iterative refinement repeats a loop when one pass cannot guarantee coverage. Serialise only what depends on an earlier result, and send everything else out in one turn.

    Parallel delegations must be issued in a single coordinator turn. The Agent SDK documentation defines a turn as one round trip: the coordinator produces output that includes tool calls, the tools run, and the results feed back to it.

    The corpus rule is that delegations spread across turns run one after another and raise no error. Issued over four turns, the four research branches take 40 + 55 + 35 + 50 = 180 seconds again.

    The refinement loop runs delegate, synthesise, evaluate for gaps, re-delegate targeted queries and re-synthesise. The coordinator needs sufficiency criteria to know when to stop. An iteration cap is a safety net that limits spend and says nothing about quality, so a loop that never ends is missing criteria, and a tighter cap does not supply them.

    The coordinator's prompt states goals and quality criteria and gives no step-by-step procedure. A prompt that dictates the steps leaves the coordinator nothing to decide, and the research it directs comes out shallow and checklist-shaped, as in the last row of §1.6.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Three independent aspects of one customer issueParallel fan-out in a single turn, then synthesise.Independent work done in series wastes wall clock and repeats context fetches.
    • Step B needs Step A's extracted entitySequential chaining.It is a real dependency.
    • Coverage of the synthesis cannot be guaranteed in one passAn iterative refinement loop with stated sufficiency criteria.Gap evaluation and re-delegation belong to the coordinator.
    • A refinement loop runs indefinitelyAdd explicit quality criteria for the coordinator to evaluate against.Termination is a criteria problem, not a counter problem.
    • The coordinator emits its delegations across successive turnsFix it to one turn.Otherwise the parallel design is sequential in practice.
    Go deeper: a refinement loop, and turns in the Agent SDK

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule. A coordinator researches five subtopics and states two criteria: each subtopic has at least two independent sources, and no two findings conflict without an annotation. After the first pass, subtopics one to three have two sources each, subtopic four has one and subtopic five has none, so 40% of the subtopics fail the first criterion.

    The coordinator sends two targeted queries in one turn, runs the synthesis again and checks again. When every subtopic has two sources and no conflict is unannotated, the loop ends. A cap of five passes stands behind this as a safety net. If the cap ends the run instead, the report may still miss the criteria, and the cap has judged nothing about it.

    The Agent SDK pages read for this chapter (25 October 2026) list safety nets of this kind: a maxTurns limit, a spend cap (maxBudgetUsd) that counts subagent spend, and limits on subagent nesting depth and concurrency. These bound a run and judge nothing about the report.

    The subagent page also says a subagent the main agent spawns runs in the background by default, with its report arriving in a later turn, and that Claude waits when its next action needs the report. Inference: whether delegations issued one per turn run in series therefore depends on the runtime and on whether the coordinator waits. The exam rule stays as the corpus states it: issue independent delegations together.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three sample questions cover Domains 3, 2 and 4, so Domain 1 has no official sample. The shapes below come from this project's own scenario set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a stem that shows a defect in the final report and asks where the fix belongs, and check what the coordinator did before choosing a subagent change.

    A research report omits entire subtopics, although each subagent returned correct results.

    • CorrectWiden the coordinator's decomposition and have it explicitly partition the space before delegating.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISImprove the search subagents' query construction. Right vocabulary, wrong owner: each subagent did its job on the ground it was assigned.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEIncrease the number of subagents to broaden coverage. More agents on the same narrow partition produce more of the same gap.

    A sequential analysis task has no stated latency, context or privilege constraint.

    • CorrectA single agent with the required tool set.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDA coordinator plus three specialist subagents, for separation of concerns. It reads as the more rigorous design, and it adds 4 to 5 times the tokens and a handoff at every boundary to meet no stated requirement.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISTwo agents that pass results directly to each other, with no coordinator. The coordinator boundary is what buys context isolation and per-role privilege. A direct channel removes both and still pays the multi-agent token cost.

    Design shapeHuman agents receiving escalations keep asking customers for details the system already collected. The answer is a structured handoff summary with the entity ID, root cause, actions taken, amount and recommended action. Giving the humans the raw transcript is DISCARD: it replaces a compact designed artifact with the whole history, which they must now read end to end.

    Escalating earlier is WRONG-AXIS, because the context would still not be transferred, and it lowers the autonomous resolution rate.

    A billing dispute with three independent issues is investigated one issue at a time. The answer decomposes it into three issues and dispatches them from a single coordinator turn, with shared customer context, then synthesises one resolution. A faster model is WRONG-AXIS, because it shortens each call and leaves the serial order in place. Dispatching across three successive turns is HALF-MOVE: the decomposition is right and the execution is still sequential.

    Say it backA research report leaves out whole subtopics, yet every subagent's output is correct. One colleague proposes better search queries for the subagents, another proposes more subagents. Where does the fix go, and why do both proposals miss?

    The fix goes in the coordinator: widen its decomposition and have it partition the whole space explicitly before it delegates. The subagents did their job on the ground they were assigned, so better queries cannot reach ground nobody assigned. More subagents on the same narrow partition repeat the same gap.

    Connections

    • O1.3, §1.3: this chapter leans on the ladder. Move right only when the rung to the left cannot meet a stated requirement, and multi-agent is the last rung, so §1.5's justification test is that rule applied once more.
    • O1.2, §1.10: this chapter also leans on it. Context not captured at the input boundary does not exist downstream, which is a subagent's position, and the consumer sets the output contract, here a synthesis agent or a human with no transcript.
    • O1.5, §1.11: the coordinator's first duty continues there, with a stopping rule of one evaluation criterion and one failure mode per unit and structured summaries passed between units.
    • O1.6, §1.12: a stated latency commitment removes serial designs before any are compared, so independent steps fan out as in §1.8, and where cost is the named pillar, §1.5 keeps sequential work on one agent.
    • O3.2, §3.2: least privilege means the capability does not exist, which is how a drafting role ends up with no write tool. O3.1, §3.1 splits an agent that holds 22 tools into role-scoped agents of 4 to 6 tools.
    • O5.4, §5.5: an audit record holds what was sent and which model and prompt version produced the output, which flattened provenance (§1.7) cannot supply.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 1, fourth objective; the guide states the objective in one line and gives no further detail. Course corpus §1.5 to §1.8. The branch times, the 30,000-token threads and the examples in the folds are this chapter's illustrations, not corpus figures. Live checks, read 2026-10-25: Anthropic, "How we built our multi-agent research system", 13 June 2025 (anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system), for the first fold; Anthropic, "Subagents in the SDK" (code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents), for the §1.6 fold and the last two paragraphs of the §1.8 fold; Anthropic, "How the agent loop works" (code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop), for the definition of a turn in §1.8 and the caps in its fold.

    Remember

    1. More than one agent needs a reason the scenario states: parallelism under a latency requirement, context isolation, or privilege separation. With none, use one agent. The price is typically 4 to 5 times the tokens, plus information loss at every handoff.
    2. Hub-and-spoke: subagents never talk to each other. The coordinator owns decomposition, context passing, error handling and termination, so an output defect usually traces to it.
    3. A subagent knows only what the coordinator passed. Pass findings as content plus metadata, because an instruction to cite cannot restore metadata that never arrived.
    4. A human receiving an escalation has no transcript, so the handoff summary stands alone. With partial inputs, synthesise and annotate coverage. Zero results is a finding; a timeout is an access failure.
    5. Independent work fans out in a single coordinator turn. Chain steps only on a real data dependency. Across turns, delegations run in sequence and no error appears.
    6. Refinement ends on stated sufficiency criteria, and the cap is a safety net. The coordinator's prompt states goals and criteria, never steps.

    Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving

    Sheet
    D1-5
    Exam weight
    17%
    Domain
    Solution Design & Architecture
    Corpus sections
    1.11
    Reading time
    ≈ 7 min
    Position
    5 of 6 in D1

    Suppose a pull request touches 14 files and about 800 changed lines, an average of 57 lines per file. One prompt reads the whole diff and returns one verdict. The review comes back shallow, and it approves a pattern in one file that it flagged in another.

    Decomposition is the repair: split the task into units that each get one job. Most of Domain 1 uses it. A workflow splits a task into steps, an architecture splits a system into stages, and a multi-agent system splits it into roles.

    Cut where two criteria meet, and stop when handoffs cost more§1.11

    A task left in one unit fails in four ways. The first is attention dilution: a pass over many inputs goes deep on some and shallow on others, and you cannot predict which. The second is mixed criteria. If one unit is judged on accuracy, tone and completeness together, a failing score does not say which of them failed.

    The third is that a partial failure cannot be recovered, because the single call is redone whole. The fourth is that there is no seam: no boundary where a validation, an approval or a cost control could attach.

    The corpus gives one granularity rule. Split until each unit has one evaluation criterion (the one question its output is judged on) and one failure mode (the one way it can go wrong). Stop when the overhead of the handoffs exceeds the benefit. A unit with one criterion tells you what to fix when quality drops.

    Cut where two criteria meet or where a gate has to go in. A natural-sounding process name is no reason to cut. The review in the figure splits at the one place where two criteria meet: local correctness, judged file by file, and cross-file consistency, judged once over the results by an integration pass.

    There are five ways to cut. A functional split follows the stages of a process, such as extract, validate, enrich and format. An aspectual split sends the same input through different lenses, such as a security pass and a style pass. A data-partition split divides a corpus into chunks, as in a per-file pass followed by a cross-file pass.

    The remaining two cut by the case in front of you. A confidence-tier split sends routine cases down a cheap path and hard cases down an expensive one, and it is the main architectural lever on cost. A risk-tier split follows blast radius, meaning how much damage a wrong action does and whether it can be undone. Reversible actions run on their own, and an irreversible one waits at a gate.

    The two tiers answer different questions. Difficulty sets the confidence seam and is what moves cost. Blast radius sets the risk seam and is what governs autonomy. A scenario that names cost as its pillar calls for the first, and one that mixes routine actions with a single action nobody can undo calls for the second.

    Separately from where to cut, the plan has a shape. A fixed pipeline suits a scope you know in advance, and it is predictable and reproducible. Dynamic adaptive decomposition generates subtasks from what the earlier steps find, which suits an open-ended investigation. A review that always follows the same template gets the fixed pipeline, because adaptivity there adds nondeterminism, meaning results that can differ between runs, for nothing.

    What crosses a seam is a structured summary: issues found, exported symbols changed, dependencies touched. If the integration pass instead receives all 14 raw diffs, it carries the same dilution the split existed to remove. Every handoff also loses context that was implicit in the shared context window. A design split so finely that later steps lack what earlier ones knew should be merged. Over-decomposition is a real defect.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A 14-file pull request is reviewed in one pass and the output is shallow and inconsistentRun a per-file local pass in parallel, then one integration pass over the summaries.Two criteria, local correctness and cross-file consistency, need two units.
    • The integration pass receives all 14 raw diffsPass the structured per-file summaries instead.Raw payloads reintroduce the dilution the split existed to remove.
    • 90% of cases are routine, 10% are hard, and cost is the named pillarSplit by confidence tier: a cheap path for routine cases, an expensive path for hard ones.Routing by difficulty is the primary architectural lever on cost.
    • Most actions are reversible and one is irreversibleSplit by risk tier: reversible actions run on their own, the irreversible one is gated.Blast radius, not confidence, sets this seam.
    • A design is split so finely that later steps lack context that earlier steps hadMerge steps.Over-decomposition is a real defect.
    • A review repeats and always follows the same templateUse a fixed pipeline.It is predictable and reproducible; adaptivity adds nondeterminism for nothing.
    Go deeper: the review and the tiers in numbers

    A worked example with invented figures, not a corpus rule. Suppose each per-file call takes 20 seconds. Fourteen in sequence take 280 seconds. Fanned out in parallel, the wall clock is the longest branch, 20 seconds, and a 25-second integration pass brings the review to 45 seconds. Each call also reads about 57 lines instead of 800.

    A second example, again with invented prices. Take 10,000 cases a month, 90% of them routine, at $0.02 a case on the expensive path and $0.002 on the cheap one. Everything on the expensive path costs $200.

    Split by tier, the9,000 routine cases cost $18 and the 1,000 hard ones cost $20, a total of $38 plus the cost of the triage step. The saving holds only while triage costs less than the $162 it saves.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three sample questions cover Domains 3, 2 and 4, so Domain 1 has no official sample. The shape below comes from this project's own scenario set, not from Anthropic. Each wrong option carries a family label, and the Trap families page defines all eight. InferenceExpect stems that describe a task's scope and ask which plan shape fits, and stems where one large pass produces shallow or inconsistent output.

    A large multi-file code review produces inconsistent verdicts and misses issues that span files.

    • CorrectSplit it into two passes: parallel per-file passes, then one integration pass over the per-file structured summaries and the dependency graph.
    • WrongDISCARDMove to a more capable model with a larger context window. It replaces the model instead of fixing the structure, and attention dilution over a large mixed input persists at any capacity.
    • WrongREPAIRAdd detailed instructions to the single prompt about consistency and cross-file effects. It patches with prose a defect caused by asking one unit to serve two evaluation criteria.
    Say it backA review pipeline sends 40 changed files through one prompt, and its verdicts vary from file to file. Where do you cut, and what does the second unit receive?

    Cut where two criteria meet. Run one pass per file for local correctness, in parallel, then one integration pass for cross-file consistency. The integration pass receives each file's structured summary and the dependency graph, not the raw diffs.

    Connections

    • O1.3, §1.3: paths that can be listed in advance belong in code. This chapter leans on that test. The fixed-pipeline rule applies it to the plan, and dynamic decomposition is for scope that cannot be listed in advance.
    • O1.2, §1.10: a rule goes at the earliest stage that can enforce it. A gate in a risk-tier split is one such rule, and it needs a seam to sit in.
    • O1.4, §1.7: content and metadata pass as separate fields. Inference: this chapter's structured summaries follow the same idea, compact records instead of raw payloads.
    • O1.4, §1.8: independent work fans out in parallel and the wall clock is the longest branch, so the per-file passes run together and the dependent integration pass runs after them. A coordinator issues parallel delegations in a single turn.
    • O1.6, §1.12: when cost is the named pillar, confidence-tier routing plus the smallest model that clears the bar for each tier is the lever that moves it.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 1, fifth objective. Course corpus §1.11. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states design rules and no product facts. The time and price figures in the deeper block are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Split until each unit has one evaluation criterion and one failure mode. Stop when the overhead of the handoffs exceeds the benefit.
    2. Cut where two criteria meet or where a gate must go in. A natural-sounding process name is no reason to cut.
    3. Five cuts: functional, aspectual, data-partition, confidence-tier (moves cost) and risk-tier (governs autonomy by blast radius).
    4. Fixed pipeline for a known scope, dynamic adaptive for a discovered one. A repeating template gets the pipeline.
    5. Pass structured summaries between units, never raw payloads. Merge steps that lose context the earlier ones had.
    6. Shallow or inconsistent output from one large pass is a structure fault. Add a pass with a different criterion; a bigger model (DISCARD) or longer instructions (REPAIR) leave the structure as it was.

    Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)

    Sheet
    D1-6
    Exam weight
    17%
    Domain
    Solution Design & Architecture
    Corpus sections
    1.12
    Reading time
    ≈ 8 min
    Position
    6 of 6 in D1

    An invoice pipeline processes 50,000 invoices a month, and three people judge it in three different units. The finance director asks what an invoice costs: $2.10 by hand, now $0.49, made of $0.11 of compute and $0.38 of residual human review.

    The operations director asks how long an invoice takes a person: 11 minutes before, 2 now. The CIO asks whether the pipeline keeps its promise: a p95 of 7.5 seconds against a limit of 10.

    Those three answers belong to three of the five pillars the guide names: cost, efficiency and performance SLAs, meaning stated commitments such as a response-time limit. A scenario names one pillar, and the design that moves that pillar is the answer. This chapter separates the pillars and shows how the named one constrains the architecture.

    Name the pillar first, then let it constrain the design§1.12

    The guide names five pillars, and each is a different unit. The unit is what lets you tell them apart, because the same project reads differently under each.

    PillarThe unitThe question it answers
    EfficiencyInput per unit of output, such as minutes per invoiceIs the same work done with less?
    TransformationA capability that did not exist beforeCan we now do something we could not do at all?
    ProductivityOutput per person, or what the freed time goes toAre the same people producing more, or better?
    CostTotal unit economics, such as cost per transactionWhat does the solution itself cost to run?
    Performance SLAA stated commitment on speed, availability or accuracyIs the promise kept?

    Efficiency and productivity sit close together. Efficiency reduces the input for a fixed output: an invoice takes 2 minutes of a person where it took 11. Productivity changes what the freed capacity does: the team that stopped keying invoices now works exceptions and vendor disputes. Which one to lead with depends on who is listening.

    Cost is more than the inference bill. Total cost includes inference, retrieval infrastructure, human review time, error remediation and maintenance. A design that halves inference cost and doubles human review time has made the total worse. At high volume the lever that moves cost is routing by difficulty, with the smallest model that clears the bar for each tier, the split described in O1.5.

    A performance SLA behaves differently from the other four. It is a filter applied before designs are compared, not a tiebreaker after. It is written against the tail, the slowest few percent of requests, so a design whose average meets it can still miss it.

    A workflow's cost per request is close to one number because its steps are fixed. An agent's cost is a distribution, since the number of calls varies, so the budget has to cover the tail.

    Here is a worked example with invented figures. The commitment is a p95 of 3 seconds, and each model call takes about 0.8 seconds at p95. Treat the times as additive, which is a simplification. The chain has five calls: two enrichment calls (E1 and E2) that depend only on the stored document, then retrieval (R), a draft (D) and a check (V), each using the result before it.

    In series the chain takes 4.0 seconds and fails. Running E1 and E2 together saves one slot and leaves 3.2 seconds, still over. Precomputing them at ingest takes them off the request path. Three calls remain, taking 2.4 seconds, with 0.6 seconds to spare.

    The SLA removed designs before quality came up. A commitment of a 3-second p95 rules out a nine-call agent at the start, because tuning does not bring a nine-call agent to a 3-second p95. The same logic removes whole patterns from the ladder of O1.3, which is why a stated figure in a scenario is read first.

    The scenario names one pillar, and the correct design moves that pillar. An answer that cites a general virtue, such as accuracy or elegance, instead of the stated requirement is the distractor. When two designs both work and only one meets the stated commitment, pick that one. The technically superior design that misses the SLA is the trap.

    Transformation is argued differently. If the capability did not exist before, there is no baseline cost to compare against, so efficiency has no denominator and forcing the comparison understates the case. Finally, state the architecture in the unit the listener measures in: minutes, dollars, throughput or a commitment met. Accuracy and other model metrics are inputs to the business case.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A p95 latency commitment of 3 seconds meets a proposed 5-step serial chainParallelise the independent steps and move enrichment off the request path by precomputing it at ingest.The SLA eliminates serial depth before quality is compared.
    • Cost is the named pillar at high volumeRoute by confidence tier, with the smallest model that clears the bar for each tier.Difficulty-based routing is the lever that moves cost.
    • A design halves inference cost and doubles human review timeReject it.Total cost includes human time, so this is a regression.
    • The capability did not previously existArgue transformation.Efficiency has no denominator, and forcing a per-unit comparison understates the case.
    • A non-engineer stakeholder asks whether it is workingAnswer in minutes, dollars, throughput or the commitment met.Model metrics are an input to the business case, not the case.
    • Two designs both work and only one meets the stated commitmentPick the one that meets the commitment.The technically superior design that misses the SLA is the trap.
    Go deeper: the invoice pipeline in dollars, and a cost trap

    A worked example with invented figures, not a corpus rule. At 50,000 invoices a month, handling by hand at $2.10 an invoice costs $105,000 a month, or $1,260,000 a year. The pipeline at $0.49 an invoice costs $24,500 a month, or $294,000 a year, with the human review already inside that figure.

    Both costs price a minute of a person at about $0.19: 11 minutes cost $2.10, and the 2 minutes of review cost $0.38.

    Now the trap. Halve the compute, from $0.11 to $0.055, and double the review, from $0.38 to $0.76. An invoice then costs $0.815 against today's $0.49, a rise of 66%. The inference line looks cheaper while the total is dearer.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three sample questions cover Domains 3, 2 and 4, so Domain 1 has no official sample. The shape below comes from this project's own scenario set, not from Anthropic. Each wrong option carries a family label, and the Trap families page defines all eight. InferenceExpect stems with two workable designs and one named pillar, and stems that ask how to justify a design to a stakeholder.

    A team must meet a stated p95 latency commitment. Its agentic design has a mean latency that fits, and a tail that does not.

    • CorrectRestructure to a workflow with the independent steps parallelised and enrichment precomputed at ingest, keeping the agent only for the exception population.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEKeep the agentic design and tune prompts to reduce the average number of tool calls. It improves the mean, while the commitment is written against the tail.
    • WrongREPAIRAdd caching, retries and a monitoring alert on SLA breaches. It instruments and mitigates a breach that the architecture will keep producing, and leaves its cause in place.
    Say it backA team proposes an agent that averages nine model calls for a request with a p95 commitment of 3 seconds, and the average looks fine in testing. What do you check, and what do you change?

    The commitment is written against the tail, so the average does not settle it, and nine calls will not reach 3 seconds by tuning. Move to a workflow: run the independent steps together, precompute enrichment at ingest, and keep the agent only for the exception population.

    Connections

    • O1.3, §1.3 and §1.4: this chapter leans on the pattern ladder. A stated commitment removes rungs of it at design time, and workflow cost is a point where agent cost is a distribution.
    • O1.5, §1.11: the confidence-tier split is the cost lever named here, and the smallest model that clears the bar for each tier is the choice made inside it.
    • O1.4, §1.8: independent work fans out in parallel and the wall clock is the longest branch, which is the arithmetic behind the SLA example.
    • O2.1, §2.1: choosing the model for each tier is the trade-off that chapter works through.
    • O6.3, §6.9: how a service commitment is worded for a system whose output varies is covered there. This chapter treats the commitment as a filter on designs.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 1, sixth objective. Course corpus §1.12. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states design rules and no product facts. All dollar, minute and second figures are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Five pillars, five units: efficiency (input per output), transformation (a capability that did not exist), productivity (output per person), cost (total unit economics) and performance SLA (a stated commitment).
    2. The scenario names one pillar, and the design that moves it wins. An answer that cites a general virtue in its place is the distractor.
    3. An SLA is a filter applied before designs are compared. It is written against the tail, so a good average does not meet it.
    4. Cost is total: inference, retrieval infrastructure, human review, error remediation and maintenance. Halving inference while doubling review is a regression.
    5. At volume, route by confidence tier with the smallest model that clears the bar for each tier. When the capability is new, argue transformation.
    6. Answer a stakeholder in their own unit: minutes, dollars, throughput or the commitment met.
