    Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs

    Sheet
    D2-1
    Exam weight
    13%
    Domain
    Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering
    Corpus sections
    2.1
    Reading time
    ≈ 6 min
    Position
    1 of 5 in D2

    A support team classifies 2,000,000 tickets a month, each into one of 12 queues. The answer is a single label that must come back in under a second. A test on 500 hand-labelled tickets shows that a small model reaches the accuracy the team set as its bar. A stakeholder still asks for the biggest model, to be safe.

    On Anthropic's models page, read on 2026-10-25, the largest current model lists at $10 per million input tokens and the smallest at $0.10, a ratio of 100 to 1. At 2,000,000 tickets a month, that ratio is the whole argument. The chapter is about when the gap buys something and when it is headroom nobody asked for.

    Match the model to the task, not to the ceiling§2.1

    The discriminator is the task's complexity and ambiguity, set against cost and latency at the volume the task actually runs. A narrow, bounded task such as choosing one of 12 labels does not need the most capable tier. The answer is the smallest, fastest model that clears the accuracy bar, because cost and latency compound at volume.

    Complexity can run the other way. Multi-step synthesis across ambiguous sources, at low volume, calls for the higher-capability model. Here task complexity, not volume, is the binding constraint, and a small model would be the wrong saving.

    Suppose a stakeholder asks for "the biggest model, to be safe" and names no complexity driver. Push back and ask what specifically requires it. Headroom bought without a requirement is unpriced cost.

    A workload that already meets its accuracy bar does not need a newer, more capable model because one exists. Upgrade only when a specific unmet requirement drives it, such as an accuracy gap or a missing capability, and run a benchmark before switching: a test of the candidate on representative inputs.

    A switch with no gap behind it adds cost and latency risk for no proven gain, and can silently change behaviour on edge cases.

    A second rule is about reasoning depth. Suppose one step needs deep multi-step reasoning across ambiguous, high-stakes trade-offs, and latency is not gated. Enable extended thinking for that step. Do not move the whole workload to a larger model, because extended thinking targets the bottleneck, reasoning depth, without paying to upsize every other call.

    Current API versions expose this capability as adaptive thinking with an effort setting. The fold at the end of this section gives the dated detail.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A narrow, bounded, high-volume classification task with a latency limitChoose the smallest, fastest model that clears the accuracy bar.Cost and latency compound at volume, and the task does not need frontier reasoning.
    • Multi-step synthesis across ambiguous sources, at low volumeChoose the higher-capability model.Task complexity, not volume, is the binding constraint here.
    • A stakeholder asks for "the biggest model, to be safe" and states no complexity driverPush back and ask what specifically requires it.Headroom bought without a requirement is unpriced cost, not safety.
    • A production workload already meets its accuracy bar and a newer, more capable model becomes availableUpgrade only if a specific unmet requirement drives it, and benchmark before switching.A switch not tied to an actual gap adds cost and latency risk for no proven gain, and can silently change behaviour on edge cases.
    • A task needs deep multi-step reasoning across ambiguous, high-stakes trade-offs, and latency is not stated as gatedEnable extended thinking for that step instead of moving the whole workload to a larger model.It targets the actual bottleneck, reasoning depth, without paying to upsize every other call.
    Go deeper: the ticket classifier in dollars, and what the docs say about thinking now

    A worked example, not a corpus rule. Assume each ticket is 500 input tokens and 20 output tokens (invented figures). Two million tickets a month is 1,000 million input tokens and 40 million output tokens. At the prices on the models page (read 2026-10-25), Haiku 5.5 charges $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, so the month costs $120.

    Sonnet 5.5 ($2 and $10) costs $2,400 on the same traffic, Opus 5.5 ($4 and $20) costs $4,800, and Fable 5.1 ($10 and $50) costs $12,000. The page lists Haiku 5.5 as "from" its price, so treat $120 as the floor of the range.

    On thinking, the same page describes the current models as using adaptive thinking, where the model decides how much to think and an effort setting steers it. The manual form of extended thinking, a fixed thinking budget, is deprecated on the 4.6 models and rejected on later ones (extended-thinking page, read 2026-10-25). The corpus rule stands as written: spend reasoning on the one step where it is the bottleneck.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three sample questions cover Domains 3, 2 and 4. The Domain 2 sample is about prompt caching and is worked through in O2.5, so this objective has no sample of its own, though one of that sample's wrong options, the smallest model regardless of task fit, touches model selection.

    The shape below comes from this project's own scenario set, not from Anthropic, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a stem that gives the volume, a latency limit and an accuracy bar, with options that differ in size.

    A team must classify a high volume of support tickets under a latency limit. Which model choice fits?

    • CorrectSelect the smallest, fastest model that clears the accuracy bar on representative tickets, benchmarked before committing.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDDefault to the most capable model available, to be safe. It sounds more thorough, but nothing about a bounded, high-volume, latency-gated classification calls for extra reasoning, and the extra cost and latency compound at volume.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEFine-tune a smaller model, which means training it further on your own examples, without first testing whether a base model already clears the bar. Fine-tuning is a legitimate lever, but it is the expensive answer to a problem a base-model evaluation might already solve.
    Say it backA classifier already meets its accuracy bar on the current model, and a larger model has just been released. Separately, one step in another workflow needs deep reasoning over ambiguous trade-offs, with no latency limit. What do you do in each case?

    In the first case, do not upgrade unless a specific unmet requirement drives it, and benchmark before any switch. In the second, enable extended thinking for that step and leave the rest of the workload on the model it already uses.

    Connections

    • O1.5, §1.11, and O1.6, §1.12: confidence-tier routing sends routine cases to the smallest model that clears the bar and hard ones to a stronger model. This chapter leans on them for where the split falls, and chooses the model inside each tier.
    • O4.1, §4.1: the accuracy bar used here is a threshold declared in advance. Without it, "clears the bar" has no meaning.
    • O3.3, §3.4: accuracy-latency budgeting is the same trade-off argued at the level of a configuration.
    • O2.3, §2.4: reasoning cues in a prompt are the prompt-level way to ask for step-by-step reasoning. Inference: extended thinking is the model-level setting for the same need.
    • O2.5, §2.8: prompt caching is another lever on cost and latency at volume, applied to a repeated prefix and not to the choice of model.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 2, first objective, and section 8 for the Domain 2 sample question (prompt caching, O2.5). Course corpus §2.1. Live documents read on 2026-10-25: the models overview (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview) for model names, prices and thinking modes, and the extended-thinking page (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking) for the deprecation. The ticket counts, token counts and accuracy figures are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Match capability to the task's complexity at its real volume, not to the model's ceiling. A narrow, bounded, high-volume, latency-gated task takes the smallest, fastest model that clears the accuracy bar.
    2. Multi-step synthesis across ambiguous sources at low volume takes the higher-capability model. Complexity, not volume, is the binding constraint.
    3. "The biggest model, to be safe" with no stated complexity driver: ask what requires it. Headroom without a requirement is unpriced cost.
    4. A workload that meets its bar needs no upgrade. Upgrade for a specific unmet requirement, and benchmark before switching.
    5. Deep reasoning on one step means extended thinking for that step, not a larger model for every call.

    Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails

    Sheet
    D2-2
    Exam weight
    13%
    Domain
    Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering
    Corpus sections
    2.2
    Reading time
    ≈ 5 min
    Position
    2 of 5 in D2

    Suppose a bank's assistant handles 40,000 conversations a month, 14 turns each on average, which is 560,000 turns in all. The team wants every reply formal, and wants any refund above $500 sent to a person. They write both rules into the first message of each conversation. On a long call, a customer asks for $620 at turn 12 and the assistant, by then casual, approves it.

    The rules were written down and they were still not in force. Where a rule lives decides whether the model treats it as an instruction on turn 12.

    Put persistent rules in the system prompt, and scope each guardrail to its layer§2.2

    The system prompt is the instruction block set before the user speaks. It is the only location with durable authority across the whole conversation, so tone, persona and response-format rules for the whole conversation belong there.

    The other places fail, each in its own way. A rule stated in the first user message is not durable: it loses authority once the conversation moves past that turn. A rule "set" through an environment variable has no effect at all, because environment variables configure infrastructure and never reach the model.

    Guardrails follow the same placement. A guardrail is a refusal boundary or an escalation trigger, and it belongs in the system prompt. It is a design decision made when the system prompt is written, and a monitoring alert added later does not replace it.

    Scope matters as well. Suppose a guardrail must react differently depending on which tool or sub-agent is active. Put it in a per-tool or per-agent system prompt, at the layer where the risk occurs, and leave the top level with what applies everywhere. One blanket top-level rule either over-restricts the contexts that do not need it or under-restricts the one that does.

    The guide's objective also names templates, meaning prompts with fixed text and slots for variable content. The corpus rules for this section are about where rules live and how guardrails are scoped, and the corpus has no separate rule for templates. Modular prompts are covered in O2.5.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A tone, persona or response-format rule must hold for the whole conversationPut it in the system prompt.It is the only location with authority across every turn.
    • A rule is stated in the first user messageIt is not durable.It loses authority once the conversation moves past that turn.
    • A rule is "set" through an environment variableIt has no effect at all.Environment variables do not reach model behaviour.
    • A refusal boundary or an escalation trigger is neededPut it in the system prompt.A guardrail is a design decision made at system-prompt time, not a monitoring afterthought.
    • A guardrail must react differently depending on which tool or sub-agent is activeScope it to the relevant layer, such as a per-tool or per-agent system prompt, and avoid one blanket top-level rule.A single global guardrail either over-restricts contexts that do not need it or under-restricts the one that does. Guardrails belong at the layer where the risk occurs.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three sample questions cover Domains 3, 2 and 4. The Domain 2 sample is about prompt caching and is worked through in O2.5, so this objective has none. The shape below comes from this project's own scenario set, not from Anthropic, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect options that all state the right rule and differ only in where it is placed.

    A team needs a behavioural rule to hold for the whole conversation. Where does it belong?

    • CorrectIn the system prompt.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISIn the first user message. The idea is right, since the rule is stated, but the location is wrong, because it loses authority mid-conversation.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISIn an environment variable set at deploy time. It confuses infrastructure configuration with a model-facing instruction, and it never reaches the model at all.
    Say it backA formal-tone rule sits in the first user message and an escalation limit sits in an environment variable. Where does each belong, and what changes if one agent needs a stricter guardrail than the rest?

    Both belong in the system prompt. The first message loses authority as the conversation moves on, and an environment variable never reaches the model. For the stricter agent, scope the guardrail to that agent's own layer with a per-agent prompt, instead of tightening one global rule.

    Connections

    • O1.2, §1.10: a step that must always happen is enforced by a precondition in code, because a prompt cannot guarantee it. Inference: a guardrail that cannot afford a miss wants both a system-prompt rule and a check in code.
    • O2.4, §2.5: the model sees only what each request carries. That is the reason a rule that never reaches the request has no effect.
    • O2.5, §2.9: modular prompts and Skills are how the same instructions are reused across prompts.
    • O5.1, §5.1: guardrail layering is worked through there. This chapter fixes where the prompt-level layer sits.
    • O7.1, §7.8: hooks and permission rules are the deterministic layer for a rule that cannot rely on the model's compliance.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 2, second objective, and section 8 for the Domain 2 sample question (prompt caching, O2.5). Course corpus §2.2. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states placement rules and no product facts. The bank's volumes and the $500 and $620 figures are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Tone, persona, response format, refusal boundaries and escalation triggers live in the system prompt, the only location with authority across every turn.
    2. A rule in the first user message loses authority once the conversation moves on. A rule in an environment variable has no effect on the model at all.
    3. A guardrail is a design decision made when the system prompt is written, not a monitoring afterthought.
    4. Scope a guardrail to the layer where the risk occurs, with a per-tool or per-agent prompt, instead of one blanket top-level rule.
    5. A rule the model never receives has no effect, whatever the deployment settings say.

    Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)

    Sheet
    D2-3
    Exam weight
    13%
    Domain
    Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering
    Corpus sections
    2.3 2.4
    Reading time
    ≈ 8 min
    Position
    3 of 5 in D2

    A support agent has two tools that overlap: search_orders and lookup_account. In one week the routing log shows 300 wrong calls out of 5,000 requests, which is 6%. Every one of the 300 is a request that both tools could answer, such as "where is my refund?", which can mean an order's status or a billing record. The other 4,700 route correctly.

    One engineer proposes adding twelve examples of obvious requests to the prompt. Another proposes five examples of requests like the refund one. The first group of examples describes cases that already work, and the second describes the cases in the log.

    Aim the examples at the cases that fail§2.3

    Few-shot prompting puts worked examples in the prompt. Use it when prose instructions produce inconsistent output, or when a specific case is ambiguous. A prompt with instructions and no examples is zero-shot, and the guide's objective names it next to few-shot. The corpus gives no decision rule for it, so this chapter states none.

    The corpus sets two sizes. When a model formats output inconsistently despite clear instructions, add 3 to 4 examples of the exact required format. When it misroutes an ambiguous request between two tools, add 4 to 6 examples aimed at exactly that ambiguity, each with a stated rationale for the tool chosen. In the opening case, the five examples go on requests that fit both tools.

    The proposal to add 10 to 15 examples of clear-cut, unambiguous cases is rejected. Examples teach by pattern-matching to what they show, and the clear-cut requests are the 4,700 that already route correctly. Volume spent there takes context window space and leaves the 300 where they were.

    The same logic applies to examples already in the prompt. If they were drawn from the easiest, most common cases, replace them with examples drawn from the observed failure distribution, whatever their count. At the other end, when a single well-chosen example already resolves an ambiguous formatting case in testing, ship with it. Padding to an arbitrary count adds nothing.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Model inconsistently formats output despite clear instructionsAdd 3 to 4 examples of the exact required format.Instructions have already failed; examples fix format precision directly.
    • Model misroutes an ambiguous request between two toolsAdd 4 to 6 examples targeted at exactly that ambiguity.Targeting the failure case is what fixes it, not example volume.
    • Proposal to add 10 to 15 examples of clear-cut, unambiguous casesReject.It does not touch the actual ambiguous cases causing the error.
    • Few-shot examples are already in place but drawn from the easiest, most common cases, not the cases causing failuresReplace them with examples drawn from the observed failure distribution.Examples teach by pattern-matching to what they show, so ones that do not resemble the failure mode do not transfer to it, regardless of count.
    • A single well-chosen example already resolves an ambiguous formatting case in testingShip with that one targeted example instead of padding to an arbitrary count.Targeting the ambiguity is the lever, and one example that resolves the case in testing needs no padding.
    Go deeper: what Anthropic's prompting guidance says about examples

    This is a dated note, not a corpus rule. Anthropic's prompting guidance (live docs, read 2026-10-25) asks for examples that are relevant, diverse and structured. Diverse means they cover edge cases and vary enough that the model does not pick up an unintended pattern.

    Structured means each example sits in an <example> tag, with several wrapped in <examples>. The page says to "Include 3-5 examples for best results", and also notes that worked examples shape how Claude reasons inside its thinking.

    The page's range of 3 to 5 sits close to the corpus's 3 to 4 and 4 to 6 and does not match either. Answer exam items with the corpus numbers. Guides are due to be updated on 17 November 2026, so watch for a change in wording.

    A worked example, not a corpus rule: one example for the opening case reads as an input and a decision. Input: "Where is my refund?" Tool chosen: lookup_account. Reason: the customer asks about money returned, which sits on the billing record, and gives no order number. The stated reason is what lets the model separate this request from one that names an order.

    Add a reasoning cue only where the task has steps§2.4

    A chain-of-thought cue asks the model to write out its reasoning before the answer. Add one when the task has several steps to get through: multi-step math, multi-stage analysis, a comparison across N items, or a stepwise transformation. Leave it off a single-step task, such as translating one sentence. There is nothing to reason through, and the cue only adds tokens (the word pieces the model reads and writes) and latency.

    A multi-step task does not always need the cue. If it already reasons correctly and consistently without one, verified in testing, don't add it. The cue's cost in tokens and latency is paid for by a measured accuracy gap, and a task that already performs correctly has no gap to close.

    Sometimes the task shape calls for deliberation and a latency budget limits it. Then use a bounded or structured cue, such as a scratchpad of fixed length, instead of open-ended chain-of-thought. It keeps most of the accuracy benefit inside the budget.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Multi-step reasoning or comparison taskAdd a "think step by step" cue.It improves accuracy on tasks that require deliberation.
    • Single-step task, such as translating one sentenceDon't add a reasoning cue.It adds latency and cost with no accuracy benefit on a task with no steps to reason through.
    • A multi-step task already reasons correctly and consistently without an explicit cue, verified in testingDon't add the cue.The cue's cost in tokens and latency is justified only by a measured accuracy gap, and a task already performing correctly doesn't need it added by default.
    • A multi-step reasoning task also carries a latency budget the extra reasoning tokens would breachUse a bounded or structured reasoning cue, such as a short fixed scratchpad, instead of open-ended chain-of-thought.The task shape still calls for deliberation, and a bounded version keeps most of the accuracy benefit inside the budget.
    Go deeper: pricing a cue, and what the API calls thinking

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule. A translation feature handles 200,000 requests a month. Suppose a cue made each reply carry 150 extra output tokens, an assumption chosen for the arithmetic. That is 30,000,000 tokens a month. Anthropic's model overview (live docs, read 2026-10-25) lists Claude Sonnet 5.5 output at $10 per million tokens, so the cue costs $300 a month and the translations come out no better.

    For latency, assume the model writes 80 tokens a second, again an assumption. An open-ended chain of 600 tokens of reasoning takes 7.5 seconds before the answer starts. A scratchpad capped at about 120 tokens takes 1.5 seconds, which fits a 3-second budget.

    The API also has a separate thinking feature. Live docs read on 2026-10-25 say the manual form, set with budget_tokens, is deprecated on the Claude 4.6 models and rejected with a 400 error from 4.7 onward. Adaptive thinking, with depth set by an effort setting, replaces it. Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens and count toward the context window.

    Inference: the corpus rows above concern a cue written in the prompt, and the thinking parameter is a separate control, covered with model choice in O2.1.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three sample questions cover Domains 3, 2 and 4. The Domain 2 sample is about prompt caching and is worked through in O2.5, so this objective has none. The two scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect options that all sound like improvements and differ in what they target: the failing cases, or something that merely adds volume.

    An agent misroutes an ambiguous request between two tools.

    • CorrectAdd 4 to 6 few-shot examples targeted at exactly this kind of ambiguous phrasing, each with a stated rationale for the tool chosen.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEAdd 10 to 15 examples covering a broad range of clear, unambiguous requests. These are more examples, and the wrong ones, because none touches the failure case.
    • WrongREPAIRRewrite the system prompt instructions to be more explicit. The instructions are already failing, and more prose does not fix a consistency problem that examples exist to solve.

    A single-step translation feature is being specified.

    • CorrectDon't add a chain-of-thought cue. The task is single-step and gains nothing from one.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDAdd it anyway "for consistency with other features". It sounds thorough and uniform, and it adds cost and latency to a task the corpus treats as not needing it.
    • WrongREPAIRAdd it only after accuracy is observed to drop. This is a reactive patch to a symptom, instead of matching the technique to the task shape from the start.
    Say it backAn agent still misroutes requests that fit two tools, and a teammate proposes twelve more examples of clear-cut requests. A separate feature translates single sentences, and another teammate wants a step-by-step cue on it for consistency. What do you do with each?

    Reject the twelve. They describe cases that already work, so they leave the failures untouched. Add 4 to 6 examples aimed at the ambiguous phrasing, each with a stated reason for the tool chosen. Leave the cue off the translation feature: it has a single step, so the cue adds tokens and latency and gains no accuracy.

    Connections

    • O2.2, §2.2: instructions and examples both travel in the prompt, and §2.3 starts from instructions that have already failed. The system prompt remains where durable rules live.
    • O2.1, §2.1: the choice of model and the API's thinking setting sit beside the prompt cue. A task that needs deeper reasoning can be met at either level, and the cost of each is weighed there.
    • O1.6, §1.12: a stated latency commitment filters designs before they are compared, which is how a latency budget limits the open cue in §2.4.
    • O4.3, §4.3: that section puts coverage over count for evaluation datasets. Inference: it is the same logic as targeting over volume for examples, applied to a different artefact.
    • O4.5, §4.11: a cue is a token and latency cost, and the case for adding one rests on a measured gap, which is the kind of evidence that section asks for.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 2, third objective, and section 8 for the Domain 2 sample question (prompt caching, O2.5). Course corpus §2.3 and §2.4, including the rows added on 1 September 2026. The corpus holds no zero-shot rule, so none appears here. Live checks, read 2026-10-25: Anthropic prompting guidance (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) for the first fold; Anthropic extended-thinking documentation (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking) and model overview (platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview) for the second fold. The request volumes, the 150-token cue, the 80 tokens a second and the 3-second budget are assumptions chosen for the arithmetic.

    Remember

    1. When instructions have already failed, add examples. Use 3 to 4 for output format and 4 to 6 aimed at an ambiguity. Examples teach by resemblance to what they show.
    2. Reject 10 to 15 clear-cut examples. Replace convenient examples with ones drawn from the observed failures, and ship a single example that resolves the case in testing.
    3. A reasoning cue belongs on multi-step tasks: math, analysis, comparison across N items, stepwise transformation. A single-step task gets none.
    4. If a multi-step task is already correct and consistent without a cue, verified in testing, leave the cue out. A measured accuracy gap is what pays for it.
    5. When a latency budget would be breached, use a bounded or structured cue such as a short fixed scratchpad, instead of open-ended chain-of-thought.

    Optimize context windows and manage token usage

    Sheet
    D2-4
    Exam weight
    13%
    Domain
    Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering
    Corpus sections
    2.5 2.6 2.7
    Reading time
    ≈ 11 min
    Position
    4 of 5 in D2

    A support chat runs for 50 turns, and each turn, a customer message and the reply, adds about 300 tokens (a token is a word or a piece of a word). The first call sends 300 tokens. The fiftieth sends 15,000. Added up over the whole chat, the calls send 382,500 tokens, which is 25.5 times the 15,000 the conversation contains. The figures are illustrative.

    One fact about the API produces that multiple: it keeps nothing between calls. The same fact explains why the model can seem to forget something said two turns ago. Once history has to be resent, a second problem follows: what to keep as it grows, and where to place the parts that must not be missed.

    Resend the whole history on every call§2.5

    Claude's API is stateless: every call stands alone, with no server-side memory. So every request must carry the complete conversation history in the messages array. All continuity is the application's job to build and resend on every request.

    Two symptoms look alike and have different causes. If Claude "forgot" something from two turns ago in a short conversation, the application is not including the prior messages. The context window (the most tokens a request may hold) cannot be full that early.

    If latency and cost rise as a conversation passes 50 turns, the full history is being resent every call, so more turns mean more tokens. Longer model responses and a slow database do not explain it.

    To cut the tokens resent without losing continuity, summarise or truncate older turns, and keep resending the full messages array, summary included, on every call. Full here means everything that was kept: the summary plus the turns that remain.

    Two client sessions for one user need the same handling: the application merges their histories and passes the combined history explicitly. The API will not correlate sessions, because a stateless API has no session identity and a shared identifier on the request does not create one.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Claude "forgot" something from 2 turns ago, in a short conversationThe application isn't including prior messages in the messages array.Rules out: the context window being exceeded, which is impossible this early.
    • Latency and cost rise as a conversation passes 50 turnsThe full history is resent every call, so more turns mean more tokens.Rules out: the model generating longer responses, or a database slowdown.
    • A team wants to reduce the tokens resent every call as a conversation grows, without losing continuitySummarise or truncate older turns, and keep resending the full messages array, summary included, on every call.Statelessness isn't the thing to remove, since every call still needs complete context. The fix shrinks what is resent and does not skip the resend.
    • Two separate client sessions for the same user, hitting the API independently, need to share conversation contextThe application merges the histories and passes the combined history explicitly in messages.There is no server-side session identity in a stateless API. Cross-session continuity is an application responsibility, and a shared identifier on the request does not enable it.

    Put what matters where attention holds§2.6

    "Lost in the middle" names a pattern in long inputs. The model uses the beginning and the end reliably, and its attention to the middle is weaker. A synthesis agent given a long document can therefore miss a critical finding that sits halfway through it. The mitigation is structural: key findings first, explicit section headings, and structured data instead of verbose prose.

    Shortening the input under an arbitrary token limit is the wrong fix. It risks cutting exactly the information that was missed. The structural fix puts the findings where the model reads closely. Rotating which source appears first across runs only changes whose content sits in the weak middle position.

    The scope of the fix varies. If one precision-critical fact sits mid-document and the failure is fabricating that single value, pull the fact into a short structured highlight near the top or end, and leave it in place as well. If many facts matter equally and none dominates, convert the input to explicit headed sections grouped by topic, even without one findings-first summary.

    If the total input is short, well under the model's effective context, ordering does not matter. The effect is a function of total input length, and a short input does not trigger it. Applying restructuring to such input is overhead with no measured benefit.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Long synthesis input misses critical mid-document findingsRestructure: findings first, headings and structured facts.It fixes the attention pattern directly, at the source.
    • A single precision-critical fact sits mid-document, and the failure is fabricating that one valuePull that fact into a short structured highlight near the top or end, in addition to leaving it in place.Restructuring everything targets pervasive degradation. One known critical fact needs surfacing at the positions where attention holds.
    • The question is whether ordering matters when the total input is short, well under the model's effective contextNo.The phenomenon depends on total input length relative to the attention pattern, and a short input does not trigger it. Restructuring there is unneeded overhead.
    • Scattered facts of equal importance, with no single dominant findingConvert to explicit headed sections grouped by topic, even without one findings-first summary.Structure is the fix, and it is not limited to a top summary. Section-level organisation restores retrievability across the middle.
    Go deeper: a highlight block, and what the documentation adds

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule. An agent summarises a 120-page contract, and the notice period of 90 days sits in a clause on page 61. The summary states 60 days. Leave the clause where it is, and add a block at the top of the input: Key terms: notice period 90 days (clause 14.2, page 61). The model now meets the value at a position where attention holds.

    Anthropic's prompting guidance (live docs, read 2026-10-25) advises placing long documents of 20,000 tokens or more near the top of the prompt, above the query and instructions, and wrapping each in document tags. It reports that a query at the end improved quality by up to 30 percent in its tests.

    The context-window page also names "context rot", a decline in accuracy and recall as the token count grows, which is why curating the context matters as much as having room.

    Extract what must stay exact, compress the rest§2.7

    The tested pattern is a hybrid. Extract the critical facts into a structured block, summarise the general discussion, and keep the recent turns verbatim, meaning word for word. A long session might hold amounts, identifiers and an allergy alongside general chatter. Summarising everything uniformly blurs those facts into vague paraphrase. Keeping only the most recent tokens drops any critical fact mentioned early.

    A decision made early may need to hold for hundreds of turns. Pin it into a persistent structured block that is included on every call, separate from the rolling summary, the running summary of older turns. A rolling summary can drift or drop a fact across repeated summarising passes. A pinned fact has a stable slot that the summarising process never touches.

    Summarising should run incrementally, as new turns roll off the retained window. One pass at the very end of the conversation either handles an unbounded amount of history at once or arrives too late to control token growth during the conversation.

    When retrieved documents and conversation history share one bounded window, give each source its own budget. Truncating whichever was added last lets one source crowd out the other unpredictably, depending on assembly order. An explicit per-source budget keeps both available.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Long conversation with precision-critical facts (amounts, IDs, allergies) plus general chatterExtract the critical facts into a structured block, summarise the rest, keep recent turns verbatim.It preserves precision where it matters and compresses where it doesn't.
    • An early-conversation decision, such as a chosen configuration, must never change for the rest of a session that runs for hundreds of turnsPin it into a persistent structured block, re-included on every call, separate from the rolling summary.A rolling summary can drift or drop a fact across repeated passes. A fact that must never change needs a slot that summarising never touches.
    • A team plans to summarise older turns automatically but is unsure how often to re-run the summarising stepRe-summarise incrementally as new turns roll off the retained window, not once at the very end.A single end-of-conversation pass either processes unbounded history at once or arrives too late to control token growth.
    • Retrieved documents and conversation history both need space in one bounded context windowBudget each source independently against the window rather than truncating whichever was added last.Truncating by insertion order lets one source crowd out the other unpredictably. A per-source budget keeps both available regardless of assembly order.
    Go deeper: what the documentation says about windows and overflow

    These are dated notes, not corpus rules (live docs, read 2026-10-25). The four current models have a 1M-token context window by default, with a 128K-token maximum output. Everything counts toward the window: the system prompt, every message including tool results, images and documents, tool definitions, and the model's own output including thinking. A cached prefix still counts, because caching changes the price of a prefix and not its size.

    For long conversations the page names server-side compaction as the primary strategy, a beta feature on Claude 4.6 and later, and describes context editing, which clears old tool results or thinking blocks. An input already over the window returns a 400 error. On Claude 4.5 and newer models, an input plus max_tokens that goes over the window is accepted, and generation can stop with the reason model_context_window_exceeded.

    The corpus examples use bounded windows. A window of 1M tokens makes the budgeting problem rarer in practice and leaves the rules above in force, because the pinned block, the verbatim facts and the per-source budgets address accuracy and cost as well as capacity.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three sample questions cover Domains 3, 2 and 4. The Domain 2 sample is about prompt caching and is worked through in O2.5, so this objective has none. The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a symptom with a tempting model-side explanation, and check whether the application sent the context before choosing it.

    Claude has no memory of a fact mentioned two turns earlier.

    • CorrectThe application is not including the full prior message history in the messages array.
    • WrongDISCARDThe context window was exceeded. This swaps a plain application-layer fix for a model-capacity explanation that cannot fit a short conversation.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISClaude needs a session_id parameter for persistent memory. That invents a mechanism the stateless API does not have.

    A long assistance session mixes a safety-critical fact with general chatter.

    • CorrectExtract the critical fact and quantities into a compact structured block, summarise the chatter, and keep the most recent exchanges verbatim.
    • WrongREPAIRSummarise the entire history. It compresses everything uniformly and degrades the critical fact into unsafe vagueness.
    • WrongDISCARDKeep only the most recent portion of the conversation. It drops the critical fact entirely if it was mentioned early and falls outside the retained window.

    Design shapeA synthesis agent misses critical findings buried in the middle of a long input. The answer places a key-findings summary at the start and adds explicit section headings throughout.

    Summarising the whole input to a much shorter length is DISCARD, because it risks cutting the information the agent is missing. Alternating which source appears first across runs is HALF-MOVE: it rotates whose content sits in the weak middle and leaves the attention pattern alone.

    Say it backA chat assistant forgets an order number given two turns earlier. Separately, a 40-page report synthesis misses a finding on page 22. What does each point to, and where does each fix go?

    The forgotten order number points to the application, which did not include the prior messages in the messages array. The fix is to send the history on every call, since the API keeps nothing. The missed finding on page 22 points to position. Restructure the input with a key-findings summary at the start and explicit headings, and do not just shorten it.

    Connections

    • O2.5, §2.8: the history resent on each call is a repeated prefix, and prompt caching is built for repeated prefixes. Inference: that is why this chapter and the next belong together.
    • O1.4, §1.7: a subagent knows only what the coordinator passed it, the same rule as a stateless API. Context not sent does not exist for the receiver.
    • O2.2, §2.2: the system prompt is part of every request, which is how it keeps authority on every turn. A rule never sent has no effect.
    • O3.8, §3.14: progressive discovery against a monolithic context is the other way to manage what the window holds, by loading less up front.
    • O4.4, §4.10: diagnosis checks the data and retrieval before the model. Inference: §2.5's root-cause table follows the same order, checking what the application sent before blaming the model.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 2, fourth objective, and section 8 for the Domain 2 sample question (prompt caching, O2.5). Course corpus §2.5 to §2.7, including the rows added on 1 September 2026. Live checks, read 2026-10-25: Anthropic, "Context windows" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows) for the window, counting, compaction and overflow notes; Anthropic prompting guidance (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) for the placement of long documents. The 300-token turns, the 60,000-token window, its five budgets and the contract example are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. The API is stateless. Every call carries the whole history in the messages array, and cost grows with it.
    2. A fact forgotten two turns ago means the application did not send it. A cost climbing past 50 turns means the full history is resent. Summarise or truncate old turns and still resend the array.
    3. Two sessions share context only if the application merges the histories. No session identifier does it.
    4. Attention is strong at the start and end of a long input. Fix a lost finding with findings first, headings and structured facts, not by shortening.
    5. One critical mid-document fact gets a short highlight near the top or end. A short input needs no restructuring.
    6. Extract exact facts, summarise the chatter, keep recent turns verbatim. Pin fixed decisions, re-summarise incrementally, and budget each source on its own.

    Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)

    Sheet
    D2-5
    Exam weight
    13%
    Domain
    Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering
    Corpus sections
    2.8 2.9
    Reading time
    ≈ 9 min
    Position
    5 of 5 in D2

    An application sends the same 8,000-token policy prompt with every request, followed by a customer message of about 100 tokens. Each request is therefore 98.8% identical to the one before it. At 100,000 requests a day, 800,000,000 of the tokens the service sends are repeats. The figures are illustrative.

    Two kinds of repetition appear in this objective. The first is repeated text inside one application, which caching can reuse. The second is repeated prompts across teams, where each team keeps its own copy of something similar and the copies slowly drift apart.

    Put the static part first and keep it identical§2.8

    Prompt caching lets Claude reuse a cached prefix, the opening stretch of a prompt, across requests. The prefix has to be byte-identical and stable. That means static content goes first and dynamic content goes last, outside the cached prefix. Caching cuts latency, measured as time-to-first-token (how long until the reply begins), and cost together.

    For an identical large system prompt and policy followed by a varying user message, order the static content first and enable caching. Truncating the policy loses content the application needs. Moving it into a few-shot block (§2.3) creates no stable prefix to reuse. Caching also does not store replies: it reuses an input prefix, and only while that prefix is identical and first.

    Any change inside the prefix invalidates the cache for the whole block, even a single token. Suppose a block is byte-identical except for a timestamp at its very start. Move the timestamp out to after the cached prefix. Dynamic content must sit strictly after the stable part.

    Caching only pays within its retention window, the time a cached prefix stays available, 5 minutes by default (the fold below has the dated detail). If a large static prefix is a caching candidate but requests arrive only once every 20 minutes, longer than that window, accept that caching will not help and evaluate other cost and latency levers. Each request recomputes the prefix from scratch.

    When two downstream tools each need a different static block, structure the prompt as the shared prefix, then the per-tool static block, then the dynamic content. Putting the common part first keeps the cache hit rate on the shared portion across tool variants, where the per-tool part first would force a full-prompt divergence for each.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Identical large system prompt and policy sent on every request, with a varying user message after itOrder the static content first and enable prompt caching.A stable prefix gets reused, and it cuts latency and cost together.
    • A byte-identical static block has a small dynamic timestamp inserted at the very startMove the dynamic timestamp out of the static block, to after the cached prefix.Any change inside the supposedly static prefix, even one token, invalidates the cache for the whole block.
    • A large static prefix is a caching candidate, but requests reach it only once every 20 minutes, longer than the cache's retention windowAccept that caching won't help this workload, and evaluate other cost and latency levers.Caching pays off only within its retention window. A longer cadence recomputes the prefix from scratch regardless.
    • A stable prefix is shared, but two downstream tools each need a different static block appended before the shared dynamic contentOrder it as shared prefix, then per-tool static block, then dynamic content.Ordering the common part first preserves the cache hit rate on the shared portion across tool variants.
    Go deeper: what the caching documentation adds, with the sums

    These are dated notes, not corpus rules (live docs, read 2026-10-25; the first 100,000 of 162,264 characters of the caching page were read). The prefix is built in the order tools, then system, then messages, and a change at one level invalidates that level and every later one.

    The minimum cacheable prompt is 512 tokens on the four current models, and a shorter prompt runs uncached with no error. The default lifetime is 5 minutes, or 1 hour with "ttl": "1h", and each use refreshes it at no extra cost. Caching is requested by adding a cache_control marker, {"type": "ephemeral"}, at the end of the part to be cached, and a request may carry up to 4 such breakpoints.

    Price multipliers on the base input price are 1.25 times for a 5-minute write, 2 times for a 1-hour write, and 0.05 times for a read on Sonnet 5.5.

    A worked example, with the Sonnet 5.5 input price of $2 per million tokens from the model overview: the 8,000-token prefix costs $0.016 a request uncached and $0.0008 as a read. At 100,000 requests a day that is $1,600 against $80, a saving of $1,520 a day, plus a write whenever the cache expires, which steady traffic rarely allows.

    The 20-minute row differs in practice. At the default lifetime, a request every 20 minutes writes the prefix each time, at $0.02 against $0.016 uncached, so caching would cost more. The page's 1-hour option keeps such a prefix warm, at a 2 times write price. Inference: the corpus rule assumes the default window. Answer exam items with the corpus rule, and test the 1-hour option in a real design.

    Share versioned components instead of private copies§2.9

    A modular prompt is assembled from shared parts. A Skill packages instructions that Claude loads when a task needs them. The team-scale answer for either is versioned, shared, reviewable components, instead of per-project copy-paste. Domain 7 applies the same logic to Claude Code configuration.

    When several teams each keep their own copy of a similar system prompt, behaviour drifts silently, with no single source of truth. Consolidate them into versioned shared components. A change in behaviour then becomes one reviewable event, instead of a separate silent drift in each of N copies.

    Version the shared component explicitly. When one is updated and some consumers are deliberately still pinned to the older version for a staged rollout, explicit versions let each team pin and upgrade independently. Without versions, every consumer has to accept every edit immediately, and everyone gets every change the moment it is made.

    Suppose a team needs 90% of an existing shared Skill and one constraint differs. Parameterise or extend the Skill for that constraint, and do not fork a full copy. A fork becomes a second, silently drifting copy, which is the failure versioned reuse exists to prevent.

    With many small single-purpose snippets and no way to find them, teams re-author the same snippet independently. Keep a discoverable, indexed catalog of shared components. Version control fixes drift once a component is found. It does nothing for a team that never learns the component exists.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Multiple teams each maintain their own copy of similar system promptsConsolidate into versioned, shared modular prompts or Skills.A behaviour change becomes one reviewable event, instead of N silent drifts.
    • A shared component is updated, but some consuming teams are deliberately pinned to an older version for a staged rolloutVersion the component explicitly so teams can pin and upgrade independently, and do not force every consumer onto the latest edit at once.Versioned reuse means controlled adoption. An unversioned shared prompt forces every consumer to accept every edit immediately.
    • A team needs 90% of a shared Skill's behaviour, with one differing constraintParameterise or extend the existing Skill for that constraint, and do not fork a full copy.A fork becomes a second, silently drifting copy, the exact failure versioned reuse exists to prevent.
    • Many small single-purpose prompt snippets have no discovery mechanism, and teams keep re-authoring the same oneMaintain a discoverable, indexed catalog of shared components, in addition to version control on each one.Version control solves drift once a component is found, and does nothing for teams who never find it.
    Go deeper: how Skills load, and what they cost in tokens

    These are dated notes, not corpus rules (live docs, Agent Skills overview, read 2026-10-25). A Skill is a directory with a SKILL.md file, loaded in three levels. The name and description of every Skill are always loaded, about 100 tokens each. The body of SKILL.md, under 5,000 tokens, loads when the Skill triggers. Bundled files and scripts load only when needed, and a script's output enters the context and its code does not.

    A worked example, with assumed sizes. A team has 20 Skills with 4,000-token bodies. Loading every body up front would put 80,000 tokens in the context. Loading by level puts 2,000 tokens of descriptions there and adds a 4,000-token body when one Skill triggers, 6,000 in all.

    The page limits a name to 64 characters of lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens, and a description to 1,024 characters that must say what the Skill does and when to use it.

    Custom Skills do not sync across surfaces: the API, Claude Code and claude.ai each hold their own. Claude Code reads .claude/skills/ in a project and shares Skills through plugins. The page also warns to use Skills only from trusted sources, and to audit them like installed software.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's Sample 2 is this chapter's caching question, and it is the one official Domain 2 sample. An application sends the same 8,000-token system prompt and policy document on every request, followed by a short, varying user message, and both latency and cost are concerns. The answer places the static prompt and policy before the dynamic content and enables prompt caching.

    The guide's reason is that stable content first lets a repeated prefix be reused, which reduces both time-to-first-token and per-request cost without discarding required context. Its wrong options truncate the policy to 1,000 tokens, which loses needed policy. They switch to the smallest model regardless of task fit, which risks quality. They move the policy into a few-shot block, which creates no cacheable, reusable prefix. The Trap families page defines the labels used below.

    The project's corpus words the same scenario with different wrong options, and tags them:

    An identical large policy preamble is sent on every request, and both latency and cost are concerns.

    • CorrectOrder the static preamble first and enable prompt caching.
    • WrongHALF-MOVESplit the preamble across two requests. It relocates the same token cost and does not touch caching.
    • WrongREPAIRSummarise the preamble with the model at request time. It adds a whole extra model call to solve a problem caching already solves, and it risks losing policy precision.

    A partner team wants to adopt your prompt and tooling setup.

    • CorrectVersion-controlled shared configuration, prompts and Skills, with an onboarding path new team members actually follow.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEA recorded walkthrough. It transfers knowledge once and does not stay current as prompts evolve.
    • WrongREPAIRA shared chat channel for questions. It is reactive support, where a durable, versioned artifact is needed.

    InferenceExpect the caching items to turn on small details of ordering, such as a timestamp at the top of a static block, and the reuse items on a choice between a copy and a version.

    Say it backA service sends the same 8,000-token policy on every request, and a developer has added the current time as the first line of it. Caching has stopped saving anything. Why, and what is the fix? Separately, a team wants a shared Skill but needs one constraint changed.

    The time changes the first token of the block on every request, so the prefix is never identical and the whole block misses the cache. Move the time after the cached prefix, with the other dynamic content. For the Skill, parameterise or extend it for the one constraint, because a fork would become a second copy that drifts.

    Connections

    • O2.4, §2.5: a stateless API resends the whole history each call, and that history is a repeated prefix. Inference: it is the natural candidate for caching. A cached prefix still counts toward the window, because caching changes the price and not the size.
    • O2.2, §2.2: the system prompt is a block that is often identical across requests. Inference: that makes it a natural part of the cached prefix.
    • O4.5, §4.11: the title of that section names caching as the first lever for cost and latency, ahead of the others.
    • O3.8, §3.14: the three-level loading of Skills is a small case of progressive discovery against a monolithic context.
    • O7.1, §7.1: the same rule for Claude Code configuration. Shared, versioned and scoped settings persist, where one person's local copy does not.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 2, fifth objective, and section 8, Sample 2 with its rationale, paraphrased above. Course corpus §2.8 and §2.9, including the rows added on 1 September 2026. Live checks, read 2026-10-25: Anthropic, "Prompt caching" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching), first 100,000 of 162,264 characters; "Models overview" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview) for the price; "Agent Skills overview" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview). The request volumes, token counts and the 20-Skill example are assumptions chosen for the arithmetic.

    Remember

    1. Caching reuses a byte-identical input prefix, never a reply. Put static content first and dynamic content last, outside the prefix. It cuts latency and cost together.
    2. One changed token inside the prefix invalidates the whole block. A dynamic timestamp goes after the cached prefix.
    3. Caching helps only within its retention window. A 20-minute cadence means look at other levers. With two tools, order shared prefix, per-tool block, then dynamic content.
    4. Teams that keep private copies drift silently. Share versioned components, so a change is one reviewable event.
    5. Version so teams can pin and upgrade on their own schedule. Parameterise or extend a Skill for one differing constraint, and do not fork it.
    6. A catalog solves finding what exists, and version control solves drift. A walkthrough or a chat channel is neither.

    Domain 3 is the heaviest at 19%, about 12 of the 63 items, and it has more objectives than any other domain: eight. Domains 1 and 2 are about the system you design. Domain 3 is about everything that system has to touch and that you did not design.

    Think of an identity provider configured years ago, a document store whose refresh job runs at 02:00, a downstream service that is slow on one request in a hundred, and a ticketing API that predates REST conventions.

    The eight objectives look scattered. One question runs through all of them: what gets admitted into the model's context or reach, what does the admission cost, and what record do you keep of it? The table below is the course's reading of the domain, not the guide's wording.

    ObjectiveThe question it answers
    Capability bloatHow many capabilities enter the agent's decision space?
    Authentication and authorizationWhose privileges does the agent exercise when it reaches out?
    Accuracy and latencyWhat does each admitted thing cost in time?
    Observability at scaleWhat record do you keep of what was admitted, and why?
    RAG chunking and indexingWhat shape does admitted knowledge arrive in?
    Retrieval strategyWhich knowledge is admitted for this query?
    Connection protocolsThrough which door does anything get admitted at all?
    Progressive discovery and monolithic contextDoes everything get admitted up front, or on demand?

    Questions in this domain rarely ask what something is. They give you a production system that is misbehaving, or a design proposal with a cost or an SLA attached, and ask which change addresses the cause. The one official Domain 3 sample shows the pattern: the right answer removes two tools, and the wrong answers add logging, a confirmation prompt or a larger model.

    Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat

    Sheet
    D3-1
    Exam weight
    19%
    Domain
    Integration
    Corpus sections
    3.1
    Reading time
    ≈ 6 min
    Position
    1 of 8 in D3

    An operations agent has collected 22 tools over three quarters, because each new integration was added to the agent that already existed. Each tool definition, with its name, description and input schema, averages about 200 tokens. The agent therefore carries 4,400 tokens of definitions before it reads a word of the request. At 40,000 requests a day, that is 176,000,000 tokens a day spent describing tools.

    A week of traces shows the misroutes sitting in three near-duplicate pairs: get_customer with get_account, search_tickets with search_knowledge, and send_notification with create_alert. On requests that touch those pairs the agent picks the wrong tool 11% of the time. On the other sixteen tools the rate is under 2%. The figures are illustrative.

    Shrink the decision space before polishing descriptions§3.1

    A tool costs three things. It costs tokens on every request, because tool definitions are a fixed per-request tax paid whether the tool is called or not. It costs discrimination on every turn, since the model must pick between candidates by reading their descriptions. And it costs blast radius when misused, since every tool is also a capability the agent can use.

    Misroutes concentrate in near-duplicate pairs, and the error rate rises faster than the tool count. Pairs grow faster than tools, because each new tool can pair with every tool already there: 10 tools make 45 possible pairs, and 22 tools make 231.

    The corpus discriminator is whether the failure comes from the size of the decision space or from the quality of individual descriptions. Cut the number of candidate tools first. Sharpen descriptions only for the confusable pairs that survive the cut.

    With 20 or more tools spanning several unrelated roles, split into role-scoped agents of 4 to 6 tools each. That moves confusable pairs into different agents, and the discrimination problem disappears where mitigation would only shrink it. If two tools inside one scoped agent are still confused, expand both descriptions with input formats, boundaries and when-not-to-use. Once the decision space is small, descriptions are the primary selection lever.

    A generic tool such as fetch_url, used outside its intended scope, is replaced with a constrained tool that validates its own inputs. The boundary then holds at the interface, where an instruction in a prompt would hold it only probabilistically.

    One exception is sanctioned. A scoped agent that needs a simple cross-role lookup on nearly every turn gets a narrowly scoped cross-role tool, because coordinator round-trips on a high-frequency need cost more than the scoping saves. Complex cross-role cases still route through the coordinator.

    A stakeholder may ask to keep every tool available "for flexibility". Push back with the per-request token cost and the measured misroute rate. Flexibility on a tool surface cannot be told apart from ambiguity.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • One agent holds 20+ tools spanning several unrelated roles, misrouting between near-duplicatesSplit into role-scoped agents of 4 to 6 tools each.It moves confusable pairs into different agents, and the discrimination problem disappears rather than being mitigated.
    • Two tools in the same scoped agent are still confusedExpand both descriptions with input formats, boundaries and when-not-to-use.Descriptions are the primary selection lever once the decision space is already small.
    • A generic tool (fetch_url) is being used outside its intended scopeReplace it with a constrained tool that validates its own inputs.It enforces the boundary at the interface, not probabilistically in a prompt.
    • A scoped agent needs one simple cross-role lookup on nearly every turnGive it a narrowly scoped cross-role tool.Coordinator round-trips on a high-frequency need cost more than the scoping buys.
    • A stakeholder asks to keep all tools available "for flexibility"Push back with the per-request token cost and the measured misroute rate.Flexibility on a tool surface is indistinguishable from ambiguity.
    Go deeper: the arithmetic of the split, and what Anthropic's documentation says about descriptions

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the 200 tokens a tool is an assumption. The largest of the four agents has 6 tools, which is 1,200 tokens of definitions. Against 4,400, each request saves at least 3,200 tokens. At 40,000 requests a day, that is 128,000,000 tokens a day, before any gain from fewer wrong tool calls.

    The figure ignores the routing step that picks an agent for each request. Its tokens, time and own misroute rate have to be counted before the saving is claimed.

    Anthropic's documentation on defining tools (live docs, read 2026-10-26) says the API builds a system prompt from the tool definitions, so every definition is input on every request. It calls the description "by far the most important factor in tool performance" and asks for at least 3 to 4 sentences per tool: what it does, when to use it and when not, and what each parameter means.

    It also advises consolidating related operations into fewer tools, and prefixing tool names with the service when tools span several services.

    Inference: that advice fits the corpus order of work. Fewer candidates first, then fuller descriptions for the pairs that remain.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's Sample 1 is filed under Domain 3 and is worked through in O3.2, yet it shares this chapter's logic. A support agent holds tools to read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds and delete accounts, and staff need only the first two. The answer removes the refund and delete tools from the configuration. The wrong options add logging, add a confirmation prompt or swap in a larger model.

    The Trap families page defines the labels below.

    An agent with 22 tools misroutes 11% of requests touching three near-duplicate tool pairs.

    • CorrectSplit the agent into role-scoped agents, so each request sees only the 4 to 6 tools its role uses, then tighten descriptions on any pair still confusable inside one agent.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEWrite more detailed descriptions for all 22 tools. It improves discrimination and leaves the decision space, the token tax and the privilege surface as they were.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDPut a routing classifier in front of the agent. It sounds like separation of concerns, and it adds a component, a hop and a failure mode to compensate for a configuration problem that scoping solves outright.

    InferenceExpect the options to differ on whether they reduce the number of candidates or only describe them better.

    Say it backAn agent holds 22 tools and misroutes between three near-duplicate pairs. A teammate proposes rewriting all 22 descriptions, and a stakeholder wants every tool kept "for flexibility". How do you answer each?

    Split the agent into role-scoped agents of 4 to 6 tools, so the pairs land in different agents and each request pays for far fewer definitions. Rewrite descriptions only for a pair that is still confused inside one agent. To the stakeholder, show the per-request token cost and the measured misroute rate, since flexibility on a tool surface reads as ambiguity.

    Connections

    • O1.4, §1.5: privilege separation is one of the three reasons for more than one agent, and role-scoped tool sets are how it is built. Here the split is chosen to shrink the decision space.
    • O3.8, §3.14: for 60 tools across 8 systems the corpus answer is an index with expansion, where §3.1 splits into agents. Inference: a split removes tools from an agent's reach, and discovery keeps every tool reachable but out of view until it is asked for.
    • O3.2, §3.2: the blast radius cost leads there. Removing a capability beats compensating controls such as logging.
    • O2.3, §2.3: a misroute between two tools can also be answered with 4 to 6 targeted examples. This chapter says to cut the candidates first.
    • O3.3, §3.4: tool definitions add input tokens to every request, so a latency and cost budget has to count them. Inference: that section does not itself mention tool tokens.
    • O5.1, §5.2: least privilege in tool scoping is worked through there, from the safety side.
