The 22 tools, the 200-token average, the request volume and the misroute rates are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. A tool costs tokens on every request, discrimination on every turn and blast radius when misused. Misroutes concentrate in near-duplicate pairs.
    2. Cut the decision space first. With 20+ tools across unrelated roles, split into role-scoped agents of 4 to 6 tools.
    3. Descriptions are the lever once the space is small: input formats, boundaries and when-not-to-use.
    4. Replace a generic tool with a constrained one that validates its own inputs, so the boundary holds at the interface.
    5. A high-frequency cross-role lookup earns a narrow cross-role tool. "For flexibility" is answered with the token cost and the misroute rate.

    Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps

    Sheet
    D3-2
    Exam weight
    19%
    Domain
    Integration
    Corpus sections
    3.2 3.3
    Reading time
    ≈ 8 min
    Position
    2 of 8 in D3

    An HR assistant serves 4,000 employees. Its document store holds three tiers: general policy for all staff, manager guidance for about 400 people managers, and compensation planning for 12 HR business partners, which is 0.3% of staff. The figures are illustrative. A review finds two gaps.

    The first is a delete_document tool that no workflow uses.

    The second is that every search runs under one service account with read access to all three tiers, and a filter drops restricted chunks after the search. When an ordinary employee asks about pay bands, the compensation plan ranks first, the filter removes it, and the answer is built from the chunks ranked fourth and fifth. The plan's text has still been in the model's context and in the trace store.

    Remove the capability when the scenario says it is not needed§3.2

    Least privilege means the capability does not exist. Compensating controls are logging, confirmation prompts, time-window restrictions and rate limits. They are correct when the privilege is genuinely required and its risk must be managed. They are wrong when the scenario states that the capability is not needed. The tell is in the scenario's wording: if it says the agent does not need the capability, remove it.

    Take an agent that holds a write or delete capability no workflow uses. Remove it from the tool set. The privilege is the gap, and nothing else closes it. Logging records afterwards that the unwanted action happened and never prevents it. Restricting the capability to business hours narrows a time window and leaves the privilege whole, so the unwanted action is acceptable at 2 pm.

    When a workflow genuinely requires a consequential capability, keep it and add human confirmation and audit logging. Confirmation is the right control for an action that is needed and consequential. When the capability is needed only for one narrow case, replace the broad one with a narrow capability scoped to that case, since narrowing the privilege beats gating the broad one.

    Compliance may require proof of who did what. Add audit logging for that, together with removal of unneeded privileges. Logging satisfies an audit requirement and is no substitute for scoping.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Agent holds a write or delete capability no workflow usesRemove it from the tool set.The privilege is the gap, and nothing else closes it.
    • Agent needs a consequential capability that a workflow genuinely requiresKeep it and add human confirmation and audit logging.Confirmation is the right control for needed-but-consequential actions.
    • Agent needs a capability only for a specific narrow caseReplace the broad capability with a narrow one scoped to that case.Narrowing the privilege beats gating the broad one.
    • Compliance requires proof of who did whatAudit logging, in addition to removal of unneeded privileges.Logging is an audit requirement, not a substitute for scoping.

    Enforce entitlement in the query, as the user§3.3

    Authentication establishes who is calling. Authorization establishes what that caller may reach. The default gap in an agent system is that the agent calls tools under its own service credential, so the user's entitlements are stripped at the tool boundary. Every user collapses into one identity at the point where data is reached.

    Security people call this the confused deputy: a privileged component acting for a less privileged caller whose limits were lost on the way.

    The corpus discriminator is whether entitlement is enforced in the query or after the content has been retrieved. When it is enforced afterwards, restricted content enters context and the trace store even though it is filtered out of the answer.

    Auditors require enforcement that can be proved at the point of access. A filter in the query is enforced where the data is reached, under the propagated identity, while a filter in application code is only asserted.

    With a multi-tier document store, one service account and post-retrieval filtering, propagate the user's identity and apply an entitlement filter as part of the retrieval query. Restricted chunks are then never candidates, never ranked and never traced.

    If the vector store cannot filter at query time, keep separate indexes per entitlement tier and route each request by the caller's tier. That takes more infrastructure, and enforcement becomes structural and no longer depends on a code path.

    A shared third-party integration may need each action attributable to the person who took it, which the corpus calls the operator. Substitute a per-user credential for the one shared service token, because both attribution and revocation need a per-user identity.

    If someone proposes a system-prompt rule stating what the agent may not access, reject it. Prompt-level rules are probabilistic, and security enforcement must be deterministic.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Multi-tier document store, one service account, post-retrieval filteringPropagate user identity and apply an entitlement filter as part of the retrieval query.Restricted chunks are never candidates, never ranked, never traced.
    • The vector store cannot filter at query timeSeparate indexes per entitlement tier, routed by caller tier.It is more infrastructure, but enforcement is structural rather than dependent on a code path.
    • A shared third-party integration where actions must be attributable to the operatorPer-user credential substitution rather than one shared service token.Attribution and revocation both require a per-user identity.
    • Someone proposes a system-prompt rule stating what the agent may not accessReject.Prompt-level rules are probabilistic, and security enforcement must be deterministic.
    Go deeper: three gaps in the filter-after design, and the cost of a probabilistic rule

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its figures are invented. The post-retrieval filter in the opening has three gaps. It spoils answers: when a restricted chunk ranks first, the filter drops it and the answer rests on lower-ranked material, with no sign to the user that this happened.

    It lives in application code, so any path to the index that bypasses that code has no authorization at all, such as a debugging endpoint or a batch summarising job. And the trace store holds chunks that were filtered out of the answer, in a system whose own access controls were never designed for compensation data.

    A system-prompt rule has a cost in numbers too. A control that holds 99% of the time fails 400 times a day at 40,000 requests a day. A deterministic filter in the query has no such failure rate.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's Sample 1 is this chapter's least-privilege question. A support agent can read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds and delete user accounts, and staff only ever need to read tickets and draft replies. The question asks which change best reduces risk, applying least privilege. The answer removes the refund and delete tools from the agent's configuration.

    The guide's reason is that least privilege removes capabilities the role does not require, which eliminates the attack surface rather than monitoring or guarding it. Adding logging and adding a confirmation prompt are detective or compensating controls. Swapping in a larger model has nothing to do with authorization scope. This project tags the logging and the confirmation prompt DETECTIVE-FOR-PREVENTIVE. The Trap families page defines each label below.

    The corpus words the same rule as its own scenario:

    An agent has a capability the scenario states it does not require.

    • CorrectRemove the capability from the agent's configuration.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEKeep it and log every use for audit review. Logging records afterwards that the unwanted thing happened and never prevents it.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISKeep it but restrict it to business hours. It narrows a time window and leaves the privilege whole.

    A multi-user assistant reaches a tiered document store under a single service account and filters restricted results out of the answer.

    • CorrectPropagate the requesting user's identity to the retrieval layer and apply the entitlement filter inside the query.
    • WrongREPAIRKeep post-retrieval filtering and add a second review pass over the drafted answer. It fixes downstream what the query could have prevented upstream, and the restricted content is already in context and in traces.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISAdd an instruction to the system prompt telling the agent which tiers it may cite. This treats an access-control problem as an instruction-following problem.
    Say it backAn agent has a delete tool that no workflow uses, and the team proposes logging every delete. Separately, a RAG assistant searches under one service account and drops restricted chunks from the answer. What do you recommend in each case?

    Remove the delete tool. The scenario says nothing needs it, so logging would only record a misuse after it happened. For the assistant, propagate the user's identity to retrieval and put the entitlement filter in the query, so restricted chunks are never retrieved, ranked or traced. Filtering the answer is too late, because the content has already reached context and the traces.

    Connections

    • O3.1, §3.1: blast radius is the third cost of a tool. Splitting an agent into role-scoped agents shrinks that surface the same way removal does here.
    • O3.5, §3.10: separate indexes per entitlement tier are an index design, and a refresh has to keep every tier's index consistent with its source.
    • O3.4, §3.6: observability stores what was retrieved, which is why a restricted chunk in a trace is a second leak beyond the answer.
    • O1.2, §1.10: a rule that must always hold is enforced in code, since a prompt cannot guarantee it. The system-prompt rejection here is the same principle.
    • O7.1, §7.8: hooks and permission rules are the deterministic layer in Claude Code.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 3, second objective, and section 8, Sample 1 with its rationale, summarised above. Course corpus §3.2 and §3.3. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states access-control rules and no product facts. The employee counts, the ranks and the request volume are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Least privilege means the capability does not exist. If the scenario says it is not needed, remove it. Logging, confirmation, time windows and rate limits manage a privilege you keep.
    2. Needed and consequential: keep it with human confirmation and audit logging. Needed for a narrow case: replace it with a narrow capability.
    3. Logging serves an audit requirement alongside removal and never substitutes for it.
    4. An agent on a service account collapses every user into one identity. Propagate the user's identity and put the entitlement filter in the retrieval query.
    5. If the store cannot filter at query time, use separate indexes per tier. Use per-user credentials where actions must be attributable.
    6. A system-prompt rule about access is probabilistic. Security enforcement must be deterministic.

    Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions

    Sheet
    D3-3
    Exam weight
    19%
    Domain
    Integration
    Corpus sections
    3.4 3.5
    Reading time
    ≈ 8 min
    Position
    3 of 8 in D3

    A document-triage assistant has a contractual p95 limit of 3,000 ms end to end, meaning 95% of requests must finish within it. At p95 the stages take 120 ms for the edge and identity, 180 for the query embedding, 240 for the vector search, 300 for reranking, 1,900 for generation and 60 for assembly. That totals 2,800 ms, leaving 200 ms of slack.

    Quality is 91% on the evaluation set, and the business wants 95%. The figures are illustrative.

    Three proposals arrive, each with a good accuracy story and a time cost. Which of them can the assistant afford, and what should it do with the 200 ms?

    Spend latency only where the stated requirement pays for it§3.4

    Accuracy and latency are both budgets, and most levers that buy accuracy spend latency: a larger model, more retrieved chunks, reranking, reasoning cues, self-critique passes and multi-hop retrieval. The method is a stage-level budget table at the percentile the SLA names. The corpus discriminator is whether an option satisfies the stated requirement or maximises an unstated one. The most accurate option is often the one that breaks the SLA.

    Take the proposals in turn. A self-critique pass costs about 1,400 ms and breaks the SLA. A proposed change that exceeds the stated SLA is rejected, or the SLA is reopened explicitly with the stakeholder. A breach is a decision to make with the business, never one to absorb silently. Reducing the retrieved chunks to make room for the pass removes a working mechanism and usually loses more accuracy than it buys.

    Look first for latency that is being wasted. One lever improves two things at once: put the static content first and enable prompt caching, which cuts time-to-first-token and cost together with no accuracy cost (§2.8). When the budget is tight and no slack exists, look for wasted latency in ordering, caching and redundant hops before cutting retrieved context. Cutting context loses more accuracy per millisecond saved than restructuring does.

    When there is slack and accuracy is short of target, spend the slack on the stage with the highest accuracy per millisecond, usually reranking. If accuracy is already above the target and an option offers more at triple the latency, reject it, because accuracy bought outside a requirement is unpriced cost. To a stakeholder, present the stage table and the measured accuracy change, not a preference.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Stated p95 budget with slack, accuracy short of targetSpend the slack on the highest accuracy-per-millisecond stage, usually reranking.It buys the requirement inside the budget.
    • Proposed change exceeds the stated SLAReject it, or reopen the SLA explicitly with the stakeholder.An SLA breach is a decision to be made with the business, not absorbed silently.
    • Latency and cost both named, large identical preamble on every requestOrder static content first and enable prompt caching.A stable reused prefix cuts both, with no accuracy cost.
    • Accuracy already above the stated target, and an option offers more at triple the latencyReject.Accuracy purchased outside a requirement is unpriced cost.
    • Budget is tight and no slack existsLook for wasted latency (ordering, caching, redundant hops) before cutting retrieved context.Cutting context costs more accuracy per millisecond saved than restructuring does.
    Go deeper: the three proposals priced, and what caching has to free

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and every timing is invented. The self-critique pass adds 1,400 ms, so the total is 4,200 ms, which is 40% over the limit. A larger generation model raises generation from 1,900 to 2,600 ms, which adds 700 and gives 3,500 ms. Retrieving the top 50 instead of the top 20 adds 90 ms to the search and 210 to the rerank, giving 3,100 ms.

    The larger model needs 700 ms and the slack is 200, so the other changes must free at least 500 ms. Moving a 3,100-token static preamble to the front and caching it is the candidate. No source here says it frees that much. The saving has to be measured on the real system, and if it falls short, the model change does not fit.

    One caution that is not a corpus rule: stage p95 figures do not add up to the end-to-end p95, because the p95 of a total is not the sum of the stage p95s. Use the table to see where time goes, then measure the end-to-end p95 itself.

    Match the fix to the consumer and the percentile§3.5

    Streaming changes time-to-first-token, how long a reader waits before the first words appear. It does not change total end-to-end latency. The discriminator is whether the consumer reads incrementally or waits for the complete response.

    For a human-facing chat surface where users say the system "feels slow", enable streaming. The complaint is about time-to-first-token. For a downstream service that consumes the whole response before it acts, streaming buys nothing, because the consumer cannot start early. Reduce total latency instead. When an interactive surface and a batch path share the pipeline, stream the interactive path only and optimise total time for the batch path.

    Budget at the percentile the SLA names, usually p95 or p99, and not at the mean. If a dashboard shows mean latency improved and users still complain, measure and optimise p95 or p99, because the SLA and the complaint both live in the tail.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Human-facing chat surface, users complain the system "feels slow"Enable streaming.Time-to-first-token is what the complaint is actually about.
    • Downstream service consumes the complete response before actingStreaming buys nothing. Reduce total latency instead.The consumer cannot start work early.
    • Dashboard shows mean latency improved but users still complainMeasure and optimise p95 and p99.The SLA and the complaint both live in the tail.
    • Both an interactive surface and a batch path share the pipelineStream the interactive path only, and optimise total time for the batch path.Two consumers have two different latency definitions.
    Go deeper: a mean that improves while the tail stays put

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its numbers are invented. Of 1,000 requests, 940 take 1.0 second and 60 take 9.0 seconds. The mean is 1.48 seconds. The p95 is 9.0 seconds, because 95% of requests (950) are only covered once the 9-second requests are included.

    A change makes the 940 fast requests 0.2 seconds quicker. The mean falls to 1.292 seconds, a visible improvement on a dashboard. The p95 is still 9.0 seconds, and the 60 users in the tail notice nothing.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's one Domain 3 sample is about least privilege and is worked through in O3.2, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The shapes below come from this project's own scenario set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a stem that names an SLA or a latency complaint, sometimes with a cost figure, and options that differ in accuracy and time.

    A system runs at 2,800 ms against a 3,000 ms p95 SLA and needs 4 more accuracy points. A proposed self-critique pass costs 1,400 ms.

    • CorrectReject the self-critique pass. Reorder the static preamble to the front, enable prompt caching, and spend the recovered budget on a higher-capability generation model that fits inside the SLA.
    • WrongOVERSPECAdd the pass and raise the SLA to 4,500 ms without consulting the business. It buys more accuracy than anyone asked for by breaking a contractual latency guarantee that was stated.
    • WrongDISCARDReduce the number of retrieved chunks to make room for the pass. It removes a working mechanism instead of tuning the pipeline, and usually loses more accuracy than the pass returns.

    A service-to-service integration misses its latency SLA, and someone proposes enabling streaming.

    • CorrectReject streaming for this consumer and reduce total latency at the slowest measured stage.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISEnable streaming and report the improved time-to-first-token against the SLA. It has the right vocabulary and the wrong metric, because the consumer waits for the complete response either way.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEReport the improved mean latency after a change that leaves p95 unchanged. It is a real improvement, measured at the wrong percentile, which is not the one the SLA names.
    Say it backA service is at 2,900 ms against a 3,000 ms p95 limit, and a teammate proposes a critique pass for 1,200 ms. Another proposes streaming for a downstream parser that reads only complete responses. What do you say to each?

    Reject the critique pass, since 2,900 plus 1,200 is 4,100 and the SLA is a stated requirement. Reopen the SLA with the business if the accuracy is truly needed. Reject streaming for the parser: it waits for the whole response, so only total latency matters, and the work is to cut it at the slowest stage. Report p95, the percentile the SLA names.

    Connections

    • O2.5, §2.8: static content first with caching is the one lever that improves latency and cost together, and that section holds the rule and the timestamp trap.
    • O1.6, §1.12: an SLA is a filter applied before designs are compared, and it is written against the tail. This chapter applies that filter stage by stage.
    • O2.3, §2.4: a reasoning cue is an accuracy lever that costs latency, and a bounded cue is the answer when the budget is tight.
    • O4.5, §4.11: cost and latency optimisation is worked through there, with caching first.
    • O3.4, §3.6: a stage table needs stage timings, and trace depth decides whether you can measure them.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 3, third objective. Course corpus §3.4 and §3.5. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states budgeting rules and no product facts. The stage timings, the quality figures and the request counts are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Check each option against the stated SLA. The most accurate option is often the one that breaks it.
    2. Use a stage-level budget table at the percentile the SLA names. Spend slack on the highest accuracy-per-millisecond stage, usually reranking.
    3. An SLA breach is decided with the business. Reject the change or reopen the SLA explicitly.
    4. Find wasted latency before buying accuracy or cutting retrieved context: ordering, caching, redundant hops. Static content first with prompt caching cuts latency and cost together.
    5. Streaming moves time-to-first-token for a reader and leaves total latency alone. A consumer that waits for the whole response gains nothing from it.
    6. Budget at p95 or p99, and fix the tail when the mean improves and users still complain.

    Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale

    Sheet
    D3-4
    Exam weight
    19%
    Domain
    Integration
    Corpus sections
    3.6 3.7
    Reading time
    ≈ 8 min
    Position
    4 of 8 in D3

    A claims assistant handles 200,000 requests a day, and its escalation rate is rising. A full trace of one request, with the prompt, the retrieved chunks, the tool arguments and the tool results, averages 30 KB. Tracing everything stores 6 GB a day, about 2.2 TB a year, and copies claimant data into a second store. The figures are illustrative.

    Tracing 1% of all requests at random stores 60 MB a day and catches about 20 of the 2,000 escalations that happen daily. Neither policy answers the team's question, which is why the escalation rate is rising.

    Trace the decision path, not only the output§3.6

    The unit of observability is the trace, not the log line. A useful trace captures the tool calls with their arguments and results, the retrieved chunk IDs with document versions and scores, the decision points and guardrail firings, and one correlation ID from the first hop to the last.

    The corpus discriminator is whether the capture explains why the output was produced or only that it was. Without the decision path, a confidently wrong answer looks the same as a correct one at the response layer. A log of requests and responses says what happened and nothing about why.

    When wrong answers are intermittent and the team sees only inputs and final outputs, instrument the tool calls, the retrieved context with document versions, and the decision points. That tells you which stage produced the error. When there is a latency regression and only end-to-end timing exists, add per-stage timing. That turns "the system got slow" into "the reranker got slow".

    A request that spans several agents and tools needs one correlation ID propagated through every hop. Without it the trace fragments and cannot be reassembled. Traces also hold prompts and retrieved documents, which makes the trace store a second copy of sensitive data. Design its redaction, retention and access control at the same time as the pipeline, because the observability system inherits the sensitivity of what it captures.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Intermittent wrong answers, team can see only inputs and final outputsInstrument tool calls, retrieved context with document versions, and decision points.It tells you which stage produced the error, rather than that one did.
    • Latency regression, only end-to-end timing capturedAdd per-stage timing.It turns "the system got slow" into "the reranker got slow".
    • A request spans several agents and toolsPropagate one correlation ID through every hop.Without it, the trace fragments and cannot be reassembled.
    • Traces will contain regulated contentDesign redaction, retention and access control on the trace store at the same time as the pipeline.The observability system inherits the sensitivity of what it captures.

    Sample by stratum so the rare events are all kept§3.7

    The corpus discriminator is whether the events you need to see are common or rare. Uniform sampling is calibrated to the common case, and failures are rare. So capture all of the high-information events and only a slice of the routine traffic. The stratified policy keeps 100% of errors, escalations, low-confidence paths and audit-relevant requests, and a small percentage of routine successes.

    For baselines and regression detection, a small uniform sample of routine successes is enough, since baselines need only enough samples to be stable. For regulated data, audit needs the fact of access and not the content, so keep 100% of access metadata with the payload redacted. Retention is set per stratum: short for routine samples, regulation-length for audit metadata.

    Metrics follow a separate rule. They carry low-cardinality dimensions (a small, fixed set of values) such as tool name, model, tenant tier and outcome class. User, session and document IDs belong in traces. If someone proposes labelling metrics by user ID for per-user slicing, reject it and serve that need from traces. High-cardinality labels make the metrics backend slow and expensive.

    Reject a proposal for 100% full-fidelity capture "and we'll optimise later". At these volumes it is unaffordable, and it creates a second sensitive store.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • High volume, need to characterise failures100% of errors, escalations and low-confidence paths, and 1 to 5% of successes.It captures every high-information event at a fraction of full-capture cost.
    • High volume, need baseline distributions and regression detectionA small uniform sample of routine successes.Baselines only need enough samples to be stable.
    • Regulated data accessed, audit requires proof of access100% of access metadata with a redacted payload.Audit needs the fact of access, not the content.
    • Someone proposes labelling metrics by user ID to enable per-user slicingReject, and serve that need from traces.High-cardinality labels make the metrics backend slow and expensive.
    • Someone proposes 100% full-fidelity capture "and we'll optimise later"Reject, on cost and on data-protection exposure.At these volumes it is unaffordable and creates a second sensitive store.
    Go deeper: the storage arithmetic of the three policies

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the 30 KB trace and the stratum sizes are assumptions. Tracing everything stores 200,000 traces of 30 KB, which is 6 GB a day, and 2,190 GB, about 2.2 TB, over a year. Tracing 1% uniformly stores 60 MB a day and keeps 1% of the 2,000 escalations, which is 20.

    The stratified policy traces 10,860 requests. At 30 KB each that is 325.8 MB a day, a bit over five times the uniform sample, and it holds all 2,000 escalations, all 1,000 errors and all 4,000 low-confidence paths. Alongside it, metrics with low-cardinality labels show that something moved. The traces show why, for the strata kept.

    Inference: a request is known to have failed or escalated only when it ends, so the keep-or-drop decision for those strata is made after the request finishes, and its trace has to be held until then.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's one Domain 3 sample is about least privilege and is worked through in O3.2, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The shapes below come from this project's own scenario set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a stem that names a production symptom, a volume or a cost limit, and options that differ in what is captured and how much.

    A RAG-backed agent intermittently returns wrong answers, and the team has request and response logging only.

    • CorrectAdd tracing that records retrieved chunk IDs with document versions and scores, every tool call and result, and the decision points, all tied to one correlation ID.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEIncrease log retention and add full request and response bodies at 100%. It is more volume of the same low-information capture, and it still records outcomes and not causes.
    • WrongREPAIRAdd a user feedback widget and triage from reported issues. It reacts after the fact, and confidently wrong answers are the failure users are least likely to report.

    A service handles 200,000 requests a day, full tracing is unaffordable, and the team needs to diagnose a rising escalation rate.

    • CorrectStratify: trace 100% of errors, escalations and low-confidence paths, 2% of routine successes, and keep redacted metadata for every regulated-data access.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISSample uniformly at 1% across all traffic. It is the textbook answer to a volume problem, applied to a rare-event problem, and it captures almost none of the escalations.
    • WrongOVERSPECTrace everything at full fidelity and revisit storage cost next quarter. It buys total coverage nobody asked for, at a cost the scenario says is unavailable, and it duplicates sensitive data into a new store.
    Say it backA team logs every request and response and still cannot explain intermittent wrong answers. At 200,000 requests a day they also say they will sample 1% to save money. What do you change in each case?

    Move from logs to traces: tool calls with results, retrieved chunk IDs with document versions and scores, and decision points, tied by one correlation ID, so the stage that produced the error can be found. Replace the uniform 1% with strata: keep every error, escalation and low-confidence request, and a small share of routine successes, because the failures are rare and a uniform slice catches few of them.

    Connections

    • O3.2, §3.3: a retrieved chunk that a user may not see is still written to the trace when a filter runs after retrieval. The trace store holds a second copy of what was retrieved.
    • O3.3, §3.4: a stage budget table needs per-stage timings, and the per-stage timing rule here is what supplies them.
    • O1.4, §1.7: provenance passed as separate fields is what lets a trace or an audit record show a claim's source. A correlation ID does the same job across hops.
    • O4.4, §4.10: diagnosis checks data and retrieval before the model, and the trace is where that evidence lives.
    • O4.6, §4.12: logging for attribution continues the same subject on the evaluation side.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 3, fourth objective. Course corpus §3.6 and §3.7. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states monitoring rules and no product facts. The request volume, the 30 KB trace, the stratum sizes and the escalation counts are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. The unit of observability is the trace. Capture tool calls with results, retrieved chunk IDs with document versions and scores, decision points and guardrail firings, under one correlation ID.
    2. A log of requests and responses says that a wrong answer happened and not why. Add per-stage timing so a slow system becomes a named slow stage.
    3. The trace store is a second copy of sensitive data. Design its redaction, retention and access control with the pipeline.
    4. Failures are rare, so sample by stratum: 100% of errors, escalations, low-confidence paths and audit metadata, and a small share of routine successes.
    5. Metrics carry low-cardinality labels. User, session and document IDs go in traces. Retention is set per stratum.
    6. Reject full-fidelity capture "to optimise later": it is unaffordable and creates a second sensitive store.

    Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies

    Sheet
    D3-5
    Exam weight
    19%
    Domain
    Integration
    Corpus sections
    3.8 3.9 3.10
    Reading time
    ≈ 9 min
    Position
    5 of 8 in D3

    An insurance operations team puts four kinds of content behind one assistant: policy manuals with numbered clauses, an API reference for the claims system, a support-ticket archive, and a product specification table with 12,000 rows. No single chunking strategy fits all four. The objective is matching how you cut and index each kind of content to the shape it already has.

    RAG, or retrieval-augmented generation, exists because the model's weights hold general knowledge, while your organisation's specifics live elsewhere, change on their own schedule and carry access rules. A RAG pipeline fetches those specifics at request time and puts them in front of the model.

    It has five stages. Ingestion loads and cleans the documents. Chunking cuts them into pieces. Embedding turns each piece into a list of numbers, a vector, that places similar meanings close together. Indexing stores the vectors so the nearest ones can be found quickly. Retrieval fetches the best matches for a question. Diagnosing RAG starts by asking which stage failed.

    Cut where the document already has seams§3.8

    Define a chunk as the smallest span of a document that still makes sense when read completely out of context. That rules out a fixed 512-token window (a token is a word or part of a word) as a universal default, because a window cuts wherever the 512th token lands: mid-clause, mid-table, mid-function.

    It also tells you where to cut instead. A human author already marked the seams, in clauses, endpoints, tickets and functions, and those are the places where meaning is self-contained. A support ticket stays whole for the same reason: one reply makes no sense without the problem statement above it. Overlap of 10 to 15% is insurance against a sentence straddling a boundary. Good boundaries still come first.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A policy manual with numbered clauses and a heading hierarchyChunk on clause boundaries, and carry clause number, heading path, effective date and jurisdiction as metadata.Version and jurisdiction are a correctness requirement for time-sensitive lookups.
    • An API reference with one regular section per endpointChunk per endpoint, whole.Splitting parameters from the description produces two unusable chunks.
    • Support threads of 3 to 40 messagesChunk per ticket, not per message.A single reply is unanswerable without the problem statement above it.
    • A wide relational table of product specificationsDo not embed it. Expose it as a structured query tool.Row embeddings are mostly noise, and aggregation has no vector-space answer.
    • Unstructured prose with no headings at allUse fixed-size windows with overlap, as the fallback.The fallback is correct only where no structure exists to follow.

    Put the missing context into the chunk§3.9

    A chunk pulled from the middle of a long document loses the title and heading hierarchy that made it interpretable. "This limit does not apply to renewals" means nothing on its own. Ask one question: is the chunk missing context, or missing content? If it is on topic but ambiguous, prepend the document title and heading path to the chunk text before embedding, so the context lands inside the vector and not only in metadata.

    Enlarging chunks looks like a shortcut and costs precision. A bigger chunk spreads its embedding across more topics, so it matches queries less sharply. Contextualization adds what was missing without adding unrelated text to the same vector.

    Metadata keeps its own job, which is filtering, for example down to the policy version in force on a claim's date. It does not influence semantic similarity, so a heading path held only in metadata should also be prepended to the embedded text.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Retrieved chunks are on topic but ambiguous out of contextPrepend the title and heading path before embedding.It puts the missing context into the vector, not only into metadata.
    • Retrieved chunks are genuinely cut off mid-ideaFix the boundary so it follows the document's structure.The problem is the cut, not the size.
    • Precision drops as chunk size growsReduce the size and contextualize instead.A larger chunk spreads its embedding across more topics.
    • Metadata already holds the heading path but it is not embeddedAlso prepend it to the embedded text.Metadata can be filtered on, but it does not influence semantic similarity.
    Go deeper: what Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval adds

    This is not a corpus rule. It comes from Anthropic's post of 19 September 2024. The title-and-heading prefix described above is the cheap, structural version. Contextual Retrieval has Claude write a short explanation specific to each chunk, usually 50 to 100 tokens. That explanation is prepended to the chunk before embedding and before the keyword index (BM25, which matches exact terms) is built.

    In Anthropic's tests the top-20 retrieval failure rate, the share of relevant chunks that miss the top 20 results, fell from 5.7% to 3.7% with contextual embeddings alone, a reduction of 35%. Adding contextual BM25 took it to 2.9%, a reduction of 49%, and reranking on top (a second pass that re-orders the retrieved chunks by relevance) took it to 1.9%, a reduction of 67%.

    The post gives no recommended chunk size. It says only that chunk size, boundaries and overlap can all affect retrieval.

    Keep chunking, embeddings and index in step§3.10

    An index is a coupled unit of three things: the chunking scheme that produced the chunks, the embedding model version that turned them into vectors, and the vector index that stores the result. Change one without the others and the space becomes inconsistent.

    At query time the user's question is embedded too, and it must be embedded by the same model version as the index. Vectors from a different embedding model sit in a different geometry, so similarity scores between them are not reliable. The system raises no error and keeps answering fluently, with wrong answers.

    So when a RAG system turns confidently wrong the morning after a document refresh, start with retrieval and indexing. The model and the prompt did not change, and the refresh is the only thing that moved.

    Work through four checks in order: was the re-index complete, did the chunk schema change, did the embedding model version change, and were stale vectors for deleted documents left behind. Look at the prompt and the model only after all four have cleared.

    You can catch this before users do. After every re-index, run golden queries (a fixed list of real questions whose correct chunk IDs you already know) and block promotion when the hit rate, meaning how often the known-right chunk comes back, drops.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Quality falls right after a nightly document reloadInvestigate the index: completeness, chunk schema, embedding version, stale vectors.The refresh is the only variable that moved.
    • Answers cite clause numbers that do not match the quoted textSuspect a chunk-schema change or a partial re-index.Content and metadata have come apart.
    • Retrieval scores dropped across the board with no content changeSuspect embedding model version drift.Vectors from a different model live in a different geometry.
    • Quality degraded gradually, with no deployment or refreshNow the model, the prompt or a drifting query distribution is in scope.There is no indexing event to correlate against.
    Go deeper: the refresh incident, step by step

    Six weeks after launch, a nightly reload of the policy manuals runs, and the manuals themselves have not changed. The next morning the assistant answers coverage questions confidently, and retrieval scores have dropped across the board. This is a worked example, not a corpus rule.

    Check 1 compares the chunk count in the index with the count the source should produce. If the source should yield 10,000 chunks and the index holds 7,000, the shortfall is 30%, which points at a partial run. Check 2 diffs the chunk-schema version.

    Check 3 compares the embedding model version recorded on the index with the one used at query time, and a mismatch there is a silent failure. In this example check 3 finds it: the ingestion job used a floating model version, an alias that points at whatever the latest version is, and it moved. The fix pins the version to the index and re-embeds the whole corpus.

    To build golden queries, collect real questions users ask, record the chunk IDs that should come back for each, and keep the list fixed. Take the hit rate of the last good index as the baseline, and block promotion of any new index that falls below it.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's Sample 3 is this chapter's failure. It files the question under Domain 4, Evaluation and Optimization, and asks where to look first when a RAG system returns confident but incorrect answers after a document refresh while latency and model version are unchanged. The answer is the retrieval and indexing step.

    The other three options blame silent weight changes, a low temperature and a shrunken context window. The guide's reason is that none of them would be triggered specifically by a document refresh, and the stem also says the model version is unchanged.

    The Trap families page tags the first two EVIDENCE-MISMATCH, because the evidence in the stem does not support them. The shrunken context window fails the same test, though the page does not name it. The Trap families page defines each label.

    The project's corpus words the same scenario with different wrong options, and tags them differently:

    A stable RAG system returns confident, fluent, incorrect answers the morning after a document refresh.

    • CorrectInvestigate retrieval and indexing: re-index completeness, the chunking configuration, the embedding model version pinned to the index, and removal of superseded vectors.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISLower the sampling temperature. Temperature governs token selection and says nothing about which documents were retrieved.
    • WrongDISCARDMove to a higher-capability model. It replaces a working component, and a better model reading the wrong document still gives a wrong answer, only a more fluent one.

    Design shapeTwo more shapes come from the project's scenario set. In the first, a knowledge base mixes clause-numbered manuals, threaded tickets and a 12,000-row table. The answer chunks the manuals on clauses and the tickets per thread, and gives the table a structured query tool.

    Uniform 512-token windows are WRONG-AXIS, because they treat size as the decision when the decision is where the boundary falls. Embedding the table row by row is ARCHITECTED, because one index sounds cleaner and no retrieval tuning answers a counting question.

    In the second, retrieved chunks are on topic but too ambiguous to answer from, and someone proposes doubling the chunk size. Keep the size and prepend the title and heading path. Doubling is WRONG-AXIS. Holding the heading path in metadata and showing it in the prompt afterwards is HALF-MOVE: it helps the model read what it got and does nothing for which chunks are retrieved.

    Say it backRetrieved chunks are on topic but too ambiguous to answer from, and a colleague proposes doubling the chunk size. What do you do instead, and why does the proposal backfire?

    Keep the size and prepend the document title and heading path to each chunk before embedding. Doubling spreads each embedding across more topics, so precision drops. The problem is missing context, and the fix adds context without adding unrelated text.

    Connections

    • O1.2, §1.9: wrong citations after a document refresh are routed to this layer as a feedback signal.
    • O4.4, §4.10: the same failure is the case for checking data and retrieval before the model. The guide files its Sample 3 under Domain 4, and §4.10 checks retrieval with Recall@k against gold passage IDs, which measures how often the known-right passages appear in the top k results.
    • O3.6, §3.11: the next decision is the retrieval mechanism. The structured query tool for the 12,000-row table comes back there as the SQL case.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 3, fifth objective, and section 8, Sample 3 (filed under Domain 4). Course corpus §3.8 to §3.10; the 10 to 15% overlap range is the corpus's figure, and the guide gives none. Live check: Anthropic, "Introducing Contextual Retrieval", 19 September 2024, read 2026-10-24, for the figures in the first fold.

    Remember

    1. A chunk is the smallest span that still makes sense read out of context. Let the document's structure set the boundaries: clauses, endpoints, tickets.
    2. Fixed windows are the fallback for prose with no structure. Overlap of 10 to 15% insures against a cut sentence and does not replace good boundaries.
    3. Data queried by filter or count is not embedded. Give it a structured query tool.
    4. On topic but ambiguous: prepend title and heading path before embedding. Cut off mid-idea: fix the boundary. Bigger chunks dilute the embedding.
    5. Chunking scheme, embedding model version and vector index are one coupled unit. Version them together.
    6. Confidently wrong right after a refresh: check re-index completeness, chunk schema, embedding version and stale vectors, then the prompt and the model.

    Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern

    Sheet
    D3-6
    Exam weight
    19%
    Domain
    Integration
    Corpus sections
    3.11 3.12
    Reading time
    ≈ 8 min
    Position
    6 of 8 in D3

    Field technicians use an assistant built on 8,000 troubleshooting articles. One asks why ERR_5521 happens after an upgrade. Search returns five articles about upgrade errors, each on topic and none mentioning ERR_5521. The one article that explains the code ranks far down, because every upgrade article sits in the same tight cluster of meaning and the code itself carries almost none.

    On queries that mix plain description with an exact code, the dense search finds the right article 34% of the time. With a second search that matches exact terms, and the two rankings fused, an invented test of the same queries reaches 89%, a gain of 55 points. The same assistant also gets questions that no search over articles can answer.

    Pick the mechanism from the data shape and the query pattern§3.11

    Choose on two axes: what the data is, and what the query does. A single mechanism across a mixed corpus is wrong for most of its query types. "RAG means a vector database" is a habit, and the vector search is one mechanism among several.

    Dense retrieval is strong on paraphrase and conceptual similarity, and weak on exact identifiers, codes, part numbers and rare proper nouns. A rare identifier carries almost no distributional meaning, so its vector is near-noise. Lexical retrieval is the opposite: strong on exact terms and identifiers, weak on paraphrase.

    Hybrid retrieval earns its place when the corpus and the query mix contain both prose and exact identifiers: run both searches and combine them with fused ranking, one ordering built from the two. Where the corpus is pure narrative with no identifiers, queried in natural language, use dense only. A lexical index and a fusion step there buy nothing.

    Some questions are not retrieval problems. Counting, summing, filtering and joining belong to a structured query against the relational source, because aggregation has no vector-space answer. A relationship lookup such as what superseded a part is foreign-key or graph traversal. A graph is for multi-hop relationship questions only, and it is expensive to build and maintain. A metadata filter is part of the query itself.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Prose corpus, conceptual questions in natural languageDense retrieval.Paraphrase tolerance is exactly what embeddings provide.
    • Query contains an exact error code or part numberLexical, or hybrid.Rare identifiers carry almost no distributional meaning, and their vectors are near-noise.
    • Corpus contains prose explanation with identifiers inline, and users query both waysHybrid with fused ranking.This is the condition hybrid exists for.
    • "How many X in region Y this quarter"A structured query against the relational source.Aggregation has no vector-space answer.
    • "What superseded part 88-2210J"Foreign-key or graph traversal.It is a relationship lookup, not a similarity problem.
    • Pure narrative corpus with no identifiers, queried in natural languageDense only.Adding a lexical index and a fusion step buys nothing.
    Go deeper: one assistant, three sources, a router

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its sources and numbers are invented. The assistant reaches three sources: 8,000 troubleshooting articles in prose with codes inline, a 45,000-row parts catalogue in a relational database, and an equipment hierarchy with sub-assemblies, compatible parts and superseded-by links.

    A router classifies each query by shape and sends it on. "Compressor is short-cycling on a model 400" goes to dense retrieval over the articles, filtered to model 400. "What does ERR_5521 mean" goes to lexical retrieval. "Is part 88-2210J still in stock" is a SQL lookup on the catalogue and no retrieval at all. "What replaced the 88-2210J" is a traversal over the hierarchy.

    Only "why does the compressor fail after the ERR_5521 sequence" justifies hybrid, since it mixes prose and a code.

    The 34% against 89% from the opening is what justifies the second index to a stakeholder. A general claim that hybrid is better does not.

    Rerank when the right document is there but ranked low§3.12

    The standard pattern is to retrieve wide, with a fast approximate search returning the top 20 to 50 candidates, and rerank narrow. A reranker rescores the candidates, and the top 3 to 5 go into context. The discriminator is whether the right document is absent from the candidate set or present and ranked low.

    Raising top-k costs more tokens, more money, more latency and a worse attention gradient, the uneven attention across a longer context (§2.6). Reranking costs a latency stage that must fit the budget. If the correct document is consistently at rank 8 to 15, add a reranking stage over the existing candidates. If it is not in the top 50 at all, change the retrieval mechanism or the chunking, and leave the depth alone.

    If top-k has already been raised to 40 and the context is crowded, reduce the number of chunks passed on and rerank to 3 to 5, because fewer, better chunks beat more, noisier ones. If reranking would breach a stated latency SLA, reduce the candidate width, or fund the stage by recovering latency elsewhere. The budget is the constraint, and reranking is the technique.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Correct document consistently retrieved at rank 8 to 15Add a reranking stage over the existing candidate set.It is a ranking problem, and the candidates are already there.
    • Correct document not in the top 50 at allChange the retrieval mechanism or the chunking, not the depth.Depth cannot surface something the mechanism never matches.
    • Top-k already raised to 40 and context is crowdedReduce k and rerank to 3 to 5.Fewer, better chunks beat more, noisier ones.
    • Reranking would breach the stated latency SLAReduce candidate width, or fund the stage by recovering latency elsewhere.The budget is the constraint, not the technique.
    Go deeper: what raising k costs against reranking

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the chunk size and volume are assumptions. At 500 tokens a chunk, raising k from 5 to 25 adds 20 chunks, which is 10,000 tokens a request. At 30,000 requests a day that is 300,000,000 extra input tokens a day, and the document that was ranked eighth still sits among 20 weaker neighbours.

    Retrieving 20 and reranking to the top 5 keeps the context at 2,500 tokens and puts the right document near the top. The price is one more stage. If that stage takes 300 ms and the budget has 200 ms of slack, the stage needs 100 ms recovered elsewhere, or a narrower candidate set.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's one Domain 3 sample is about least privilege and is worked through in O3.2, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The two shapes below come from this project's own scenario set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect the data shape and the query pattern to sit in the stem, and options that change the wrong layer.

    Field technicians query a prose troubleshooting corpus using plain descriptions and exact error codes, and code-based queries have a 34% hit rate.

    • CorrectAdd lexical retrieval alongside dense and fuse the rankings, because the corpus and the query mix both contain exact identifiers and prose.
    • WrongHALF-MOVETune the embedding model and increase top-k until the code-based queries succeed. It raises recall by flooding context and leaves the identifier weakness in place.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDBuild a knowledge graph over the equipment hierarchy. It is an expensive answer to a lexical-matching problem, with a graph to maintain afterwards.

    The correct document is retrieved but consistently ranks eighth, and answers use the wrong source.

    • CorrectAdd a reranking stage that reorders the existing top-20 candidates down to the top 3 to 5 passed into context.
    • WrongHALF-MOVERaise top-k from 5 to 25 so the correct document is always included. It gets the document into context at the cost of 20 lower-relevance chunks, more spend and a worse attention gradient.
    • WrongDISCARDReplace the retrieval mechanism with a different embedding model. It swaps out a mechanism that is already surfacing the right document, to fix a ranking problem.
    Say it backAn assistant's technicians query by plain description and by exact error code, and code queries often miss. Separately, a team finds the right article at rank 11 and proposes raising k to 40. What do you recommend in each case?

    For the code queries, add lexical retrieval beside the dense search and fuse the rankings, since the corpus and the queries mix prose and identifiers. For rank 11, the document is already a candidate, so add reranking and pass only the top 3 to 5 into context. Raising k to 40 would flood the context with weaker chunks and worsen the attention problem.

    Connections

    • O3.5, §3.8: when the right document is not in the top 50, chunking is the other thing to change, and that chapter covers where chunk boundaries fall.
    • O3.3, §3.4: a reranking stage is the usual place to spend slack, and the budget table decides whether it fits.
    • O2.4, §2.6: a longer context weakens attention in the middle, which is the cost of raising top-k.
    • O3.2, §3.3: the metadata filter that scopes a query is also where an entitlement filter belongs, inside the query.
    • O4.4, §4.10: diagnosis checks data and retrieval before the model, and this chapter is a list of the retrieval faults to check.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 3, sixth objective. Course corpus §3.11 and §3.12. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states retrieval-selection rules and no product facts. The article counts, the hit rates of 34% and 89%, the chunk size and the request volume are invented for illustration, except that the 34% also appears in the corpus scenario.

    Remember

    1. Choose retrieval on two axes: the data shape and the query pattern. "RAG" does not mean a vector database.
    2. Dense for paraphrase and concepts. Lexical for exact codes and identifiers. Hybrid with fused ranking only when the corpus and the queries mix both.
    3. Counts, sums and joins are structured queries. Relationship lookups are foreign-key or graph traversal, and a graph is for multi-hop questions only.
    4. Retrieve wide, 20 to 50, and rerank narrow, to 3 to 5. Right document at rank 8 to 15 means rerank. Not in the top 50 means change the mechanism or the chunking.
    5. Raising top-k adds tokens, cost, latency and a worse attention gradient. Reranking is a latency stage that has to fit the budget.

    Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)

    Sheet
    D3-7
    Exam weight
    19%
    Domain
    Integration
    Corpus sections
    3.13
    Reading time
    ≈ 7 min
    Position
    7 of 8 in D3

    A claims assistant must reach five systems: a claims database, a policy document store, a fraud-scoring service, an issue tracker and a medical-necessity review. A team proposes giving the model a tool for every one of them, so that "the agent can decide". That answer is wrong for at least two of the five, and for different reasons.

    Take the fraud score, which must run on every claim above a threshold. If it is a tool and the model skips it on 1% of the 20,000 qualifying claims a day, 200 claims go through unscored every day. The skip rate is invented, and the point holds at any rate above zero.

    Ask who decides what happens next§3.13

    The corpus discriminator is one question: who decides what happens next, your code, the model, or another agent? The cost gradient runs in one direction. A direct API call is cheaper than an MCP tool call, and an MCP tool call is cheaper than an agent-to-agent handoff. Each step up buys flexibility and spends determinism, meaning the same input always taking the same path.

    Use a direct API or CLI call (a command-line tool) for a known, mandatory, deterministic step. If a record must be fetched on every request and the ID is already known, call the API in pre-processing, because no model decision exists to make.

    If a control must run on every qualifying request, call it directly from the orchestration layer and do not expose it as a tool. A tool lets the model choose not to call it.

    Use MCP when the model should choose. An MCP tool is an action the model chooses to call. If the agent should decide whether and when to search a document store, that is an MCP tool, since the decision depends on the conversation.

    An MCP resource is read-only content the model can consult. If the agent needs to know what content exists before it queries, expose a catalog as a resource, which gives it the map as readable context instead of exploratory model turns.

    For a standard third-party system such as an issue tracker, source control or chat, use an existing community MCP server, after vetting it. Claude Code's documentation warns that servers which fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection (live docs, read 2026-10-26). Custom effort belongs on workflows nothing else covers.

    Use agent-to-agent when the other side brings its own judgment, context and accountability: work that needs separate domain judgment and separate audit attribution, where the determination must be owned by the other function.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A record must be fetched on every request and the ID is already knownDirect API call in pre-processing.No model decision exists to make. It is one hop, deterministic and testable.
    • A control that must run on every qualifying requestDirect API from the orchestration layer, not a tool.Exposing it as a tool lets the model choose not to call it.
    • The agent should decide whether and when to search a document storeMCP tool.The decision depends on the conversation.
    • The agent needs to know what content exists before queryingMCP resource exposing a catalog.It provides the map as readable context instead of exploratory model turns.
    • A standard third-party system (issue tracker, source control, chat)Existing community MCP server.Custom effort belongs on workflows nothing else covers.
    • Work needing separate domain judgment and separate audit attributionAgent-to-agent.The determination must be owned by the other function.
    Go deeper: what the MCP and Claude Code documentation say

    These are dated notes, not corpus rules (live docs, read 2026-10-26). The MCP architecture page describes a host, such as Claude Code, that creates one client for each server. A server offers three primitives: tools, which are executable functions, resources, which are data sources that give context, and prompts, which are reusable templates. A client finds them with list requests such as tools/list, and the listings can change.

    The page names two transports, stdio for local servers and Streamable HTTP for remote ones, and recommends OAuth for the remote case.

    In Claude Code, claude mcp add registers a server. HTTP is recommended for remote servers, and the older SSE transport is deprecated. A server loads at local scope by default, at project scope through a .mcp.json file shared with the team, or at user scope across all projects, and Claude Code asks for approval before using project-scoped servers in an interactive session.

    The docs warn to verify that you trust each server before connecting it, because servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection.

    The protocol page also notes that a client combining many servers can use progressive tool discovery instead of loading every tool at once, which is the subject of O3.8. No agent-to-agent specification was read for this chapter. The part of the architecture page read here does not say whether the model or the application triggers the read of a resource, and the corpus rule treats a resource as content the agent can consult.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's one Domain 3 sample is about least privilege and is worked through in O3.2, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The scenario below comes from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect the stem to state whether a step is mandatory, chosen by the model or owned by another function, and to offer options one rung too high.

    A compliance scoring service must run on every claim above a threshold, and the team proposes exposing it as an agent tool.

    • CorrectCall it directly from the orchestration layer whenever the threshold is met, keeping it outside the model's discretion.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEExpose it as an MCP tool with a system-prompt rule requiring the agent to call it on every qualifying claim. It makes a mandatory control probabilistic, and adds a model decision's latency and cost to a deterministic step.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDDelegate the scoring to a dedicated compliance agent that decides when to run. It buys a full inference loop and a second failure surface to perform what is a function call with fixed inputs.

    Design shapeThe project's lesson text adds a related shape. An agent needs to know what documents exist before it searches. The answer is a catalog exposed as an MCP resource. Pasting the catalog into the system prompt bloats every request with content that goes stale when the catalog changes. A list_everything tool needs the model to remember to call it and spends a turn on what a resource supplies as context.

    Say it backAn assistant must run a fraud check on every large claim, search a policy store when a question needs it, and file a ticket in a widely used issue tracker. Which mechanism fits each, and why?

    The fraud check is a direct API call from the orchestration layer, because it is mandatory and a tool would let the model skip it. The policy search is an MCP tool, since whether and when to search depends on the conversation. The ticket goes through an existing community MCP server, because the tracker is a standard third-party system and a custom server would repeat maintained work.

    Connections

    • O1.3, §1.3: "who decides" is the pattern-ladder question in another form. Paths that can be listed belong in code, and the cost gradient here mirrors the ladder.
    • O3.2, §3.3: where actions on a shared third-party integration must be attributable to the operator, per-user credential substitution applies, so a ticket is filed as the operator and not as a shared service account.
    • O1.4, §1.5: an agent-to-agent handoff is a multi-agent boundary, with the same price in tokens and in information lost at the handoff.
    • O3.8, §3.14: a catalog exposed as a resource is the start of progressive discovery, where the agent loads detail when it needs it.
    • O3.1, §3.1: every MCP tool joins the tool surface, so the size and confusability rules there apply to tools from all configured servers.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 3, seventh objective. Course corpus §3.13. Live checks, read 2026-10-26: the Model Context Protocol architecture page (modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture), and Anthropic's Claude Code MCP page (code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp), of which the first 100,000 of about 150,000 characters were read. No agent-to-agent specification was checked. The claim volume, the skip rate and the five-system example are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. The discriminator is who decides: your code, the model or another agent. Each step up the cost gradient buys flexibility and spends determinism.
    2. A known, mandatory step is a direct API or CLI call. A control that must run on every qualifying request is called from the orchestration layer, never offered as a tool.
    3. An MCP tool is an action the model chooses. An MCP resource is read-only content, such as a catalog of what exists.
    4. For a standard third-party system, use an existing community MCP server. Build custom only for workflows nothing else covers.
    5. Use agent-to-agent only when the other side brings its own judgment and owns the determination and its audit trail.

    Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy

    Sheet
    D3-8
    Exam weight
    19%
    Domain
    Integration
    Corpus sections
    3.14
    Reading time
    ≈ 6 min
    Position
    8 of 8 in D3

    An enterprise agent can reach 60 tools across 8 systems, and each tool definition averages about 200 tokens. Every request therefore carries 12,000 tokens of tool definitions, which is 600,000,000 tokens a day at 50,000 requests. The median request uses 1.4 tools and touches exactly one system, so most of that surface is irrelevant to the request that paid for it. The figures are illustrative.

    One option is to load a short index of the eight systems and fetch the detail only for the system a request needs. That is cheaper in tokens, and it adds a step. When is the step worth taking, and when is loading everything the better answer?

    Compare the token saving with the discovery round-trip§3.14

    A monolithic surface loads everything on every request, and the full token cost is paid whether or not any of it is used. Progressive discovery loads a compact index and fetches detail on demand. The corpus discriminator is whether the surface is large enough for the token saving to exceed the cost of the discovery round-trip.

    Progressive discovery has two costs. Requests that need expansion pay one extra model turn. And there is a discovery failure mode: the agent may miss a capability that exists because the index entry did not make it visible. Two mitigations come with it. Write index entries as a usable map, and promote high-frequency capabilities into the base surface so that the common path never pays the round-trip.

    With 60 tools across 8 systems and a median request touching one system, use a namespace-level index with on-demand expansion. A namespace here is one system's group of tools, and its index entry says what lives there and when to come. If trace data shows six tools account for 61% of calls, promote those six into the base surface. The common path then stops paying the round-trip.

    Monolithic wins in three cases. First, a small stable surface: five stable tools load all at once, and below roughly ten tools discovery costs more than it saves. Second, a latency budget that cannot absorb a round-trip, because the trip costs more than the surface does.

    Third, content needed on every single request has nothing to discover: order it first and cache it, which is a caching answer. A large document catalog the agent should know about is exposed as a readable resource, so the map stays current and is consulted on demand.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • 60 tools across 8 systems, median request touches one systemNamespace-level index plus on-demand expansion.Most of the surface is irrelevant to any given request.
    • Trace data shows six tools account for 61% of callsPromote those six into the base surface.The common path stops paying the round-trip.
    • Five stable tools and a tight latency budgetLoad them all, and skip discovery.The round-trip costs more than the surface does.
    • A large document catalog the agent should be aware ofExpose it as a readable resource.The map stays current and is consulted on demand.
    • A large identical block needed on every requestOrder it first with prompt caching.Nothing is being discovered, because it is always required.
    Go deeper: the arithmetic, and what Anthropic's tool search does

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the sizes are assumptions. Eight namespace entries of 150 tokens make a 1,200-token index. A request that expands one namespace adds about 7.5 tools, which is 1,500 tokens, so such a request carries 2,700 against 12,000. Promoting six tools of 200 tokens each raises the base to 2,400 tokens, and the 61% of calls that those six serve need no expansion.

    If expansion costs an extra 250 ms, an assumption, then a request that needs it takes 250 ms longer. The saving buys that only when the surface is large. At 5 tools of 200 tokens, the whole surface is 1,000 tokens, and the index alone would be most of it.

    Anthropic's tool search tool (live docs, read 2026-10-26) is this pattern as a feature. Tools marked defer_loading: true stay out of the context until Claude finds them by search, with 5 matches returned by default, and the page advises keeping the 3 to 5 most frequently used tools non-deferred. That echoes the corpus's promotion rule, though the page says 3 to 5 tools where the corpus example promotes six.

    Every definition is still sent in the request so that the search can run, but deferred ones are kept out of the model's context until they are found. The prompt prefix is untouched, so caching is preserved.

    The page recommends tool search at 10 or more tools or more than 10,000 tokens of definitions. It suggests standard tool calling for fewer than 10 tools, or when every tool is used in every request. It says selection accuracy degrades beyond 30 to 50 tools. The corpus's figure of roughly ten tools agrees with the page.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's one Domain 3 sample is about least privilege and is worked through in O3.2, so none of them is a sample for this domain.

    The scenario below comes from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect the stem to give a size and a token cost, and to test the reverse direction as well: a small surface with a latency limit and a proposal to add discovery.

    An agent carries 60 tool definitions totalling about 12,000 tokens per request and misroutes frequently. The median request touches one of eight systems.

    • CorrectExpose eight namespace-level entries with expansion on demand, and promote the highest-frequency tools into the base surface based on the measured call distribution.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISPaste the full tool catalog into the system prompt so the agent always has visibility. It relocates monolithic context into the prompt and adds a staleness problem, while the token cost and the discrimination load stay as they were.
    • WrongDISCARDRemove the least-used tools until the surface fits. It eliminates required capabilities to solve a presentation problem, when restructuring how the surface is shown keeps them all.
    Say it backOne team has 60 tools and wants to load a short index and expand on demand. Another has five stable tools under a tight latency budget and wants to do the same. A third needs a 3,000-token policy block on every request. What do you say to each?

    The first team is right. The surface is large and a request touches little of it, so use an index with expansion and promote the busiest tools into the base. The second should load all five tools, because a round-trip costs more than the small surface does. The third is a caching case: order the block first and cache it, since nothing is being discovered.

    Connections

    • O3.1, §3.1: discovery is a second way to shrink the decision space, by showing a request fewer tools. Splitting into role-scoped agents is the first.
    • O2.5, §2.8: content needed on every request belongs at the front of a cached prefix, which is the third case where loading everything is right.
    • O2.4, §2.6: a long monolithic surface puts most of itself in the weak middle of the context.
    • O3.7, §3.13: a catalog exposed as an MCP resource is the same pattern for content, a map that is read on demand.
    • O3.3, §3.4: the discovery round-trip is latency, and the budget table says whether it fits.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 3, eighth objective. Course corpus §3.14. Live check, read 2026-10-26: Anthropic, "Tool search tool" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool), for the last fold. The tool counts, the 200-token definitions, the request volume and the 250 ms are assumptions chosen for the arithmetic.

    Remember

    1. Monolithic loads the whole surface on every request. Progressive loads an index and fetches detail on demand. Compare the token saving with the round-trip.
    2. Progressive costs one extra turn on requests that expand, and risks a missed capability. Write the index as a usable map and promote high-frequency tools into the base.
    3. Sixty tools across eight systems, one system per request: index plus expansion. Six tools carrying 61% of calls: promote them.
    4. A small, stable surface, or a latency budget with no room for a trip, loads everything. Below roughly ten tools, discovery costs more than it saves.
    5. A large catalog becomes a readable resource. Content needed on every request is ordered first and cached.

    Evaluation, Testing & Optimization

    Domain
    D4
    Exam weight
    16%
    Objectives
    6
    Scored items
    about 10
    Guide
    v1.0, section 6

    Domain 4 carries 16% of the exam, about 10 of the 63 items, across six objectives. The earlier domains build the system. This one asks whether the system works, how you would know, and what to change when it does not.

    Items usually hand you a number or a symptom: a 96% score, a 97% aggregate, a bill that tripled, confident answers that are wrong. The question is what that evidence permits. A score on a biased set, an aggregate over a failing segment and a mean over a bad tail each look like evidence and carry less than they seem to. The table below is the course's reading of the domain, not the guide's wording.

    ObjectiveThe question it answers
    Define evaluation metricsWhat counts as a pass, and who set the bar before the results?
    Datasets and test frameworksWhat is the set made of, who grades it, and how are attempts counted?
    A/B testing and iterationHow does a change reach users without hiding its effect?
    Diagnose system issuesWhich layer does the symptom point at?
    Optimise tokens, latency and costWhich lever saves, and loses nothing the requirement needs?
    Monitor with loggingWhat can a production log attribute to a layer and a release?

    The one official Domain 4 sample gives a symptom with a timing clue. A RAG system returns confident but wrong answers after a document refresh, while latency and model version are unchanged. The right answer investigates retrieval and indexing first. It is worked through in the diagnosis chapter of this domain.
