    Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)

    Sheet
    D4-1
    Exam weight
    16%
    Domain
    Evaluation, Testing & Optimization
    Corpus sections
    4.1 4.2
    Reading time
    ≈ 8 min
    Position
    1 of 6 in D4

    A business sponsor says a new support assistant "must be fast, accurate, and safe". The team's dashboard tracks three numbers: average response time, average response length and daily request volume. None of the three says whether the assistant is accurate or safe, and none can stop a launch. The sponsor has given three adjectives, and an evaluation needs numbers that can pass or fail.

    Suppose the assistant handles 12,000 tickets a month at a model spend of $3,600, and 9,000 of the tickets end resolved. The cost per resolved ticket is $0.40. A report in cost per token would not show that. The figures are illustrative.

    Fix the bar before any score is seen§4.1

    A finished metric has four parts: a named failure, a denominator (the count the failures are measured against), a segment (the slice of traffic it is reported on), and a threshold set before results are seen. The corpus discriminator is when the number was chosen. A bar fixed before any score gates a decision. A bar chosen afterwards only describes the result.

    Where does a bar come from before there are results? From the success criterion, from frontier reality (what the best systems achieve), or from the error rate of the process being replaced. If an existing manual process has a measured 8% error rate, the bar is tied to that figure and beats it. An anchored bar is still a bar, and "we'll decide later" is not one.

    If a stakeholder asks to "calibrate the threshold once we see baseline numbers", reject it. Set the bar now and revise it later as a recorded decision, because a post-hoc bar is only ever revised downward.

    A bar of 0% ("0 per N" means zero failures in the N outputs checked) is allowed only where a deterministic check can enforce it, such as a PII field present or a citation span missing. For an open-ended, model-judged property, re-anchor 0% to a small achievable rate, for example under 0.1% of 10,000 samples. An unachievable bar becomes non-binding at the first miss.

    Latency is reported at p95 or p99 (the time that 95% or 99% of requests come in at or under) and not as a mean, with time-to-first-token for an interactive surface and total time for a batch one (§3.5). Cost is reported per unit of business work, such as per resolved ticket or per claim, and not per token.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • New capability, no baseline yetSet the bar from the success criterion, frontier reality or the current process's error rate.An anchored bar is still a bar. "We'll decide later" is not.
    • Stakeholder asks to "calibrate the threshold once we see baseline numbers"Reject. Set it now, and revise it later as a recorded decision.A post-hoc bar is only ever revised downward.
    • Existing manual process with a measured 8% error rate is being replacedA bar tied to and beating 8%.The replacement's bar has a real-world anchor.
    • Open-ended safety property, proposed bar of 0%Re-anchor to a small non-zero rate (for example under 0.1% of 10,000).An unachievable bar becomes non-binding on first miss.
    • Requirement is "outputs must never contain another customer's account ID"0 per N, by a deterministic check.Code can enforce it exactly.
    Go deeper: a bar set after the result, and what 0.1% of 10,000 means

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its numbers are invented. A team plans a 95% accuracy bar, then measures a baseline of 91% and proposes to calibrate the bar to the baseline, at 90%. The bar has moved down 5 points, and the system that was going to fail now passes.

    A bar fixed at 95% before the run gates the launch, and lowering it becomes a recorded decision with a name against it.

    A bar of under 0.1% of 10,000 sampled outputs allows fewer than 10 failures in the sample. A bar of 0% fails on the first miss in a model-judged property, where the grader itself is imperfect, so the team stops treating it as binding.

    The cost line in the opening shows the denominator at work. Divided by all 12,000 tickets, $3,600 gives $0.30 a ticket. Divided by the 9,000 resolved tickets, it gives $0.40, which is the figure the business pays per unit of work.

    Score what the model says apart from what the system permits§4.2

    Safety measures what the model says: policy-violating, toxic or non-compliant output. Security measures what the system permits: an injection reaching a tool, an over-scoped credential, or data leaving through a tool result. The corpus discriminator is whether the risk is realised by what the model emits or by what the system allows it to do.

    The instruments differ with the families. Safety is a rate over a stated denominator, graded by a model or a classifier. Security is an adversarial suite: the block rate on attempted injections, the count of unauthorized tool invocations, and a least-privilege audit. A system can pass every safety metric and fail every security control.

    Classify each requirement by where the harm sits. "Must not produce discriminatory language" is safety, since the harm is in the emitted text. "A malicious instruction inside a retrieved document must not trigger a refund tool call" is security, because the harm is a permitted action. "Must not be able to read records outside the requesting customer's account" is security too, an authorization scope measured by audit and adversarial probe.

    "Outputs must not include another policyholder's identifier" is both. A deterministic PII check is the enforcing control, a content check that enforces a security property, so count it in both the safety and the security metrics, and neither report leaves it out. If someone proposes to cover a prompt-injection risk with a tone rubric, reject it, because a quality rubric cannot measure whether a tool fired.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • "The assistant must not produce discriminatory language"Safety.The harm is in the emitted text.
    • "A malicious instruction inside a retrieved document must not trigger a refund tool call"Security.The harm is a permitted action, not a sentence.
    • "The agent must not be able to read records outside the requesting customer's account"Security.It is authorization scope, measured by audit and adversarial probe.
    • "Outputs must not include another policyholder's identifier"Both. A deterministic PII check is the enforcing control.A content check enforces a security property, so log it under both.
    • Proposal to cover a prompt-injection risk with a tone rubricReject.A quality rubric cannot measure whether a tool fired.
    Go deeper: reading an adversarial suite

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its numbers are invented. A suite of 250 documents, each hiding an instruction that tries to trigger a refund call, is run against the agent. It blocks 247 of them, a block rate of 98.8%, and 3 documents trigger an unauthorized refund call. Against a bar of zero unauthorized calls, that run fails, whatever the 98.8% says.

    Inference: the count of unauthorized tool invocations is a deterministic check on the tool log, so a bar of zero is allowed for it under §4.1. The block rate across varied attacks is a rate over a suite, so it takes a threshold set before the run. The same suite shows nothing about tone. That is why a tone rubric cannot stand in for it.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's one Domain 4 sample asks where to look first when a RAG system returns confident, wrong answers after a document refresh. It is worked through in O4.4 (and the chapter on RAG indexing, O3.5), so this objective has no official sample.

    The shapes below come from this project's own scenario set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect options that look like measurement and fail one of the four parts of a metric, or that use the wrong instrument for the family.

    A business sponsor states the assistant "must be fast, accurate, and safe".

    • CorrectConvert each adjective into a metric with a named failure, a denominator, a reporting segment and a threshold agreed before measurement begins.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISTrack average response time, average response length and daily request volume. These are collectable telemetry and not decision-gating metrics: none has a named failure, a denominator and a threshold, and a mean response time is the wrong form for "fast".
    • WrongARCHITECTEDDefine one composite quality score and set its pass bar after establishing a baseline. A single tidy number sounds like executive reporting, but it cannot be diagnosed when it moves, and the bar is chosen after the result.

    A RAG agent with tool access ingests third-party documents, and the risk raised is instruction injection.

    • CorrectBuild an adversarial suite of injected documents and measure the block rate on unauthorized tool invocations, alongside a least-privilege audit of the agent's tool set.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISAdd prompt-injection wording to the safety rubric the model grader scores. It has the right vocabulary and the wrong instrument, since a content rubric cannot observe whether a tool call fired.
    • WrongHALF-MOVELog every tool invocation and review the logs weekly. It detects after the fact, with no measured block rate and no reduction of the permitted capability.
    Say it backA stakeholder wants to agree the accuracy bar "once we see the baseline", and a teammate wants a tone rubric to cover prompt injection. What do you say to each, and where does each requirement sit?

    Reject the delayed bar. Set it now from the success criterion, frontier reality or the error rate of the process being replaced, and revise it later as a recorded decision, because a bar set after the results is only ever lowered. Reject the tone rubric as well. Injection is a security risk, the harm being a permitted action, and it needs an adversarial suite that counts unauthorized tool invocations and a least-privilege audit.

    Connections

    • O1.6, §1.12: a metric is stated in the unit the listener measures, and a latency commitment is written against the tail. This chapter turns that into the four parts of a metric.
    • O3.3, §3.5: time-to-first-token for an interactive surface and total time for a batch one, the latency form used here.
    • O3.2, §3.2: the least-privilege audit that measures security is the same removal-first reasoning, and a removed tool cannot be invoked by an injection.
    • O4.2, §4.3: a metric needs a dataset to be measured on, and that objective covers how the dataset is built.
    • O5.1, §5.1: guardrail layering is the build side of these safety and security families.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 4, first objective. Course corpus §4.1 and §4.2. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states metric-definition rules and no product facts. The ticket volume, the spend, the 95%, 91% and 90% figures and the 250-document suite are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. A finished metric has a named failure, a denominator, a segment and a threshold set before results are seen. A bar chosen afterwards describes the result and does not gate it.
    2. Anchor the bar in the success criterion, frontier reality or the process being replaced. Refuse to calibrate it to the baseline.
    3. A hard zero is allowed only where a deterministic check enforces it. For an open-ended, model-judged property, use a small non-zero rate.
    4. Latency at p95 or p99, with time-to-first-token for interactive and total time for batch. Cost per unit of business work.
    5. Safety scores what the model says. Security scores what the system permits, with an adversarial suite and a least-privilege audit. A tone rubric cannot measure a tool call.

    Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies

    Sheet
    D4-2
    Exam weight
    16%
    Domain
    Evaluation, Testing & Optimization
    Corpus sections
    4.3 4.4 4.5 4.6 4.7 4.8
    Reading time
    ≈ 17 min
    Position
    2 of 6 in D4

    An extraction system reads four types of document, and its evaluation set reports 97.6% overall accuracy. The four types make up 78%, 15%, 5% and 2% of traffic, and they score 99%, 98%, 90% and 60%. The 2% type fails 40% of the time. The team proposes to auto-process everything the model is confident about, and customers keep reporting errors the dashboard cannot see.

    The evaluation set has only 50 cases. At natural frequency the rarest type gets 1 of them, and one case cannot measure a rate. The figures are illustrative. Six corpus sections cover what went wrong: what is in the set, how it is reported, who grades it, how far the grader can be trusted, which layers it scores, and how repeated attempts are counted.

    Fix the composition of the set before its size§4.3

    A set built from cases the system already handles overstates performance. Source them in order: real production traces first, then synthetic cases, then hand-written cases for failures that are expected and not yet seen. A working set of 20 to 50 hand-verified cases beats hundreds of unverified synthetic ones. Keep roughly equal numbers of should-fire cases, where the check ought to trigger, and shouldn't-fire cases, where it ought to stay quiet.

    The corpus discriminator is whether the set's composition or its size is the defect. A set that is missing failure modes is never repaired by adding more of what it already contains. A 500-case set reports 96% while customers still report failures: rebuild it from real production failures and report by segment. Expanding it to 2,000 cases drawn the same way multiplies the bias and tightens the interval around a wrong number.

    Unverified cases add a score and no information, so 600 synthetic cases with an unknown label error rate are cut to 40 hand-verified ones. A set of only failure cases hides false alarms, and a set of only clean cases hides misses, so add the matching cases to each.

    For a genuinely new capability with no production traces, hand-write cases and label the whole set provisional. Failure modes taken from the spec are hypotheses until real traces confirm them.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A 500-case set reports 96%, and customers still report failuresRebuild from real production failures and report by segment.The set omits the failure classes that are occurring.
    • Same situation, with a proposal to expand to 2,000 cases drawn the same wayReject.It is the same sampling process, four times the bias, and a tighter interval on a wrong number.
    • The set has 600 unverified synthetic cases with an unknown label error rateCut to 40 hand-verified cases.An unverified case adds a score without adding information.
    • The set contains only failure casesAdd matched shouldn't-fire cases.An all-negative set hides false alarms.
    • The set contains only clean casesAdd should-fire cases per known failure mode.An all-positive set hides misses.
    • A genuinely new capability, and no production traces exist yetHand-write cases, and label the whole set provisional until real traces confirm the failure modes.Spec-derived failure modes are hypotheses, not findings.

    Report by segment, because an aggregate hides the failing one§4.4

    An aggregate of 97% can conceal a 40% failure rate on a rare segment. Build the evaluation set to answer per-segment questions and not to mirror production frequency. Over-sample the rare, high-cost segments relative to their share of traffic. A segment needs enough cases to support a rate, about 30 as a working floor, and one case is not enough.

    Inference: a report on four segments therefore needs about 120 cases, more than the working size of 20 to 50 in §4.3, which is the minimum for a first hand-verified set.

    An over-sampled set stops mirroring traffic, so its overall figure differs from the production figure. A single production number needs the segments re-weighted by traffic share.

    The gate on reducing oversight is that every segment clears the bar independently, and not the weighted average. If a team proposes auto-processing everything above an aggregate confidence threshold, analyse accuracy by document type and field first. The aggregate averages away the segment that fails 40% of the time.

    The same logic runs live. For an ongoing audit of an automated path, take a stratified random sample across document types and field categories, since novel error patterns surface first in the high-confidence stream. Reviewing only the lowest-confidence extractions leaves the automated path unmeasured where volume is highest. Sampling only the most common document type under-samples the worst segments by construction.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A 50-case set, with a document mix of 78/15/5/2 across four typesRebuild with enough cases per type to support a rate.At natural frequency the 2% segment gets one case, and one case cannot measure a rate.
    • Team proposes auto-processing everything above an aggregate confidence thresholdAnalyse accuracy by document type and field first.The aggregate averages away the segment that fails 40% of the time.
    • Ongoing audit of an automated extraction pathA stratified random sample across document types and field categories.Novel error patterns surface first in the high-confidence stream.
    • Proposal to review only the lowest-confidence extractionsReject as the sole audit.The automated path goes unmeasured exactly where volume is highest.
    • Proposal to sample only the most common document typeReject.It under-samples the worst-performing segments by construction.

    Use code wherever the answer is exact§4.5

    Layer the graders in order. Deterministic code checks filter first, a model grader scales the judgement of subjective quality, and humans calibrate periodically. The corpus discriminator is whether the property has an exact, machine-decidable answer. If it does, a model grader is a strictly worse instrument, however good its rubric.

    Code reaches schema validity, field match, numeric comparison, regular expressions, forbidden-pattern and PII scans, execution against tests, tool-call ordering, refusal when required, and the existence of a citation span. Check citations with a verbatim string comparison and not a model grader, since judges are near chance on citation validity. The corpus cites roughly 38% as the score judges reach on citation validity in studies, a figure not checked here.

    Subjective properties go to a model grader. "The answer must be in the right register for a regulated communication" takes a model grader with a binary rubric, since no code check reaches tone. "The summary must be faithful to the source" takes a model grader for faithfulness, with an overlap metric as a cheap floor, and the overlap metric alone is not enough.

    A human's job is to label ground truth and to calibrate the grader.

    The corpus sets one solvability bar. If two domain experts would not independently reach the same verdict, no automated grader is trustworthy at any threshold. Where two adjusters disagree on the verdict, use human adjudication and re-scope the evaluation row, because unstable ground truth defeats every automated grader.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • "Every output must be valid JSON matching this schema"Deterministic schema validation.It is exact, free and reproducible.
    • "Every cited passage must exist verbatim in the cited document"A deterministic verbatim string check.Judges are near chance on citation validity.
    • "No output may contain another customer's account identifier"A deterministic pattern or field scan.It is enforceable as a hard zero.
    • "The answer must be in the right register for a regulated communication"A model grader with a binary rubric.No code check reaches tone.
    • "The summary must be faithful to the source"A model grader for faithfulness, with an overlap metric as a cheap floor.Faithfulness is semantic, and the overlap metric alone is not sufficient.
    • Ambiguous cases where two adjusters disagree on the verdictHuman adjudication, and re-scope the evaluation row.Unstable ground truth defeats every automated grader.

    Measure the grader before believing its scores§4.6

    Write a model-graded rubric as binary sub-criteria, where the whole output passes only if every hard criterion passes. A 1 to 5 scale hides mid-scale uncertainty, drifts between runs, needs larger samples and aggregates poorly. The grader must come from a different model family than the generator. A same-family grader brings self-preference bias and shared blind spots, and the failures it cannot see are the generator's own.

    The discriminator is whether the grader itself has been measured. An unvalidated grader's scores describe the grader and not the system. Before believing any score, hand-label a sample and measure agreement between grader and human, with about 75% as a starting bar and not a settled constant. For a new tone grader, hand-label 20 to 50 cases, run the grader, compute agreement, then decide.

    Several cases follow from that. An agreement of 0.62, meaning 62%, calls for rebuilding the criterion as binary sub-criteria and re-validating, because a fuzzy scalar is the most common cause of low agreement.

    If agreement is still below the bar after rework and no deterministic fallback exists, drop the row and record why. If only a same-family grader is available, use it, mark the row degraded, and never report it as ground truth. A grader six months in production with no re-audit needs periodic human calibration again.

    The known biases are position (favouring the first or last option), verbosity (rewarding length) and self-preference. The guards are to randomise and swap the order of options and aggregate both runs, to use binary criteria that control for length, and to use an out-of-family grader.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A new model grader is proposed for tone and helpfulnessHand-label 20 to 50 cases, run the grader, compute agreement, then decide.The grader is the measuring instrument and has not been calibrated.
    • Agreement measured at 0.62Rebuild the criterion as binary sub-criteria and re-validate before use.A fuzzy scalar is the most common cause of low agreement.
    • Agreement is still below the bar after rework, and no deterministic fallback existsDrop the row and record why.An untrustworthy grader shipped as validated is worse than no row.
    • Only a same-family grader is availableUse it but mark the row degraded, and never report it as ground truth.Self-preference bias and shared blind spots.
    • The grader has been in production six months and was never re-auditedResume periodic human calibration.Agreement drifts, and a grader that was trusted is not permanently trusted.
    Go deeper: what a 40-case agreement check can and cannot show

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its counts are invented. A team hand-labels 40 cases and the grader agrees with the human on 31. That is 77.5% agreement, above a starting bar of 75%. If it agrees on 25, the figure is 62.5%, below the bar.

    With 40 cases, one case moves the figure by 2.5 points. Inference: a 20 to 50 case sample therefore works as a screen. It separates a grader that is clearly poor from one that is plausible, and it cannot settle a close call, which is why the corpus calls the bar a starting point.

    Grade each layer, so a blended score cannot hide the broken one§4.7

    A RAG system has two layers. Retrieval is scored with Recall@k (the share of the gold passages found in the top k results) and context precision, against gold passage IDs. Generation is scored with faithfulness (whether the answer follows its sources) and answer relevancy. Both layers must clear their own bar. A single blended score is a defect.

    Faithfulness computed over the wrong passages means nothing, and retrieval is the more common failure. With Recall@5 of 0.55 and faithfulness of 0.97, read both bars: the system fails on retrieval, because high faithfulness to the wrong passages is not quality.

    An agentic system has two layers as well: the trajectory, meaning the tool selection and step order, and the outcome, meaning the final state and task completion. A correct result reached by a wrong or irreversible path is a failure. An agent that completes the task but deleted a record on the way fails the trajectory row. An agent with correct tools in the correct order and the wrong final state fails the outcome row.

    For multi-turn systems, attribute the first failing turn and not only the final state. An assistant that recovers by turn 6 from a turn-2 error still reports the turn-2 failure, since a late correction masks a defect that will not always correct itself.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A RAG assistant with one overall quality score, and a regression that cannot be locatedSplit into retrieval and generation rows.The blended score cannot say which layer moved.
    • Retrieval Recall@5 = 0.55, generation faithfulness = 0.97Both bars are read, and the system fails on retrieval.High faithfulness to the wrong passages is not quality.
    • An agent completes the task but deleted a record on the wayFail.The trajectory row exists precisely for this.
    • An agent selects the correct tools in the correct order but the final state is wrongFail.The outcome row exists precisely for this.
    • A multi-turn assistant recovers by turn 6 from a turn-2 errorReport the turn-2 failure.A late correction masks a defect that will not always self-correct.

    Count attempts by what a failed one costs§4.8

    pass@k passes when at least one of k attempts succeeds, so it measures reachable success. pass^k passes only when all k attempts succeed, so it measures reliability. The discriminator is whether a failed attempt is absorbed by a downstream check or reaches the world.

    Use pass@k where a validator or a test catches failures and triggers a retry, such as code generation with a test runner that reruns on failure, or a tool call behind a schema validator that retries on rejection. Use pass^k where every attempt is visible to a user or acts in the world: an answer shown directly to a customer has no retry, so each attempt is the product.

    Any step that takes an irreversible action is a gate, whatever the aggregate score says. An agent that must confirm with a human before an irreversible action is graded pass^k = 1.0, since one silent irreversible action in k attempts is a failed control. Reject a confirmation gate reported as pass@5 = 1.0, because a gate that fires once in five attempts would score as passing.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Code generation with a test runner that reruns on failurepass@k.The test runner absorbs failures, so reachable success is what matters.
    • A tool call behind a schema validator that retries on rejectionpass@k.It has the same structure.
    • An agent must confirm with a human before any irreversible actionpass^k = 1.0.One silent irreversible action in k attempts is a failed control.
    • Every generated answer is shown directly to a customerpass^k.There is no retry, and each attempt is the product.
    • A confirmation gate is reported as pass@5 = 1.0Reject the framing.A gate that fires once in five attempts would score as passing.
    Go deeper: the same system under both readings

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule. Suppose a step succeeds on 90% of attempts and attempts are independent, which is an assumption. The chance that at least one of five attempts succeeds is 1 minus 0.1 five times over, which is 99.999%. The chance that all five succeed is 0.9 five times over, which is 59.0%.

    The same step is nearly certain to succeed at least once in five tries, yet all five succeed only 59% of the time. Behind a retrying validator the first number is the one that matters. In front of a customer, or on a step that acts in the world, the second is.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's one Domain 4 sample asks where to look first when a RAG system returns confident, wrong answers after a document refresh. It is worked through in O4.4 and O3.5, so this objective has no official sample. The shapes below come from this project's own scenario set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect options that look like rigour and fail on composition, segment, instrument or aggregation.

    An evaluation set scores 96% while production complaints continue.

    • CorrectRebuild the evaluation set from real production failures, stratified by segment, and report accuracy per segment.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEExpand the set from 500 to 2,000 cases using the same collection process. More data is the right reflex almost everywhere else, and here it scales the sampling bias.
    • WrongDISCARDGenerate the additional cases with the same model that serves production. It replaces human-verified grounding with the model's own competence, so the set can hold nothing the model cannot already do.

    A team proposes an LLM-graded rubric for "output conforms to the required JSON schema and cites only real document sections".

    • CorrectRoute both properties to deterministic checks, schema validation and a verbatim citation-span check, and reserve the model grader for the subjective criteria.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDBuild a detailed grading rubric and have a model score both properties. An elaborate rubric reads as rigorous, and it brings grader error into two properties that code settles exactly and for free.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISHave humans review a sample of outputs for schema and citation errors. Humans are the calibration instrument and not the scaling one, so this spends the scarcest resource on the cheapest check.

    Design shapeFour more shapes come from the corpus. A 97% extraction system proposes auto-processing everything above the aggregate confidence threshold. The answer analyses accuracy by document type first, and auto-processes only segments with independently validated accuracy. Using the aggregate for a per-segment decision is WRONG-AXIS, and trusting raw self-reported confidence is HALF-MOVE.

    A team reports 4.2 out of 5 from a same-family grader. The answer rebuilds the rubric as binary sub-criteria, switches to an out-of-family grader and validates against a hand-labelled sample. Reporting the 4.2 with a bar of 4.0 is HALF-MOVE, and enlarging the sample from 100 to 1,000 is WRONG-AXIS, because the defect is the grader.

    A RAG system's single quality metric drops. The answer splits the evaluation into a retrieval row and a generation row, each with its own bar. A better rubric on the blended score is HALF-MOVE, and a larger model is DISCARD.

    An agent that issues refunds must confirm with a human first. The answer grades the gate as pass^k. Grading it as pass@k is WRONG-AXIS, and demanding pass^k = 1.0 on every row is OVERSPEC, since a retrying validator sits behind task completion.

    Say it backAn evaluation set of 500 cases scores 96% and customers still complain, and someone proposes 2,000 more cases from the same source. Separately, a model grader scores a summary task. How do you handle the set, the grader and a refund agent's confirmation step?

    Rebuild the set from real production failures and report by segment, because more cases from the same source only repeat the bias. Validate the grader against 20 to 50 hand-labelled cases before trusting it, use binary criteria, and take a grader from another model family. Grade the confirmation step as pass^k, since one silent refund in k attempts is a failed control.

    Connections

    • O4.1, §4.1: the metrics defined there are what these datasets and graders measure. A hard zero is allowed only where a deterministic check enforces it, which is this chapter's code-first rule.
    • O3.6, §3.12: Recall@k is the retrieval row here, and reranking and depth are the levers when that row fails.
    • O4.3, §4.9: regression and A/B testing run on the datasets and graders built here.
    • O4.4, §4.10: diagnosis checks data and retrieval before the model, and the retrieval row is the one that measures that layer.
    • O5.3, §5.8: human-in-the-loop routing is where the adjudicated and calibrated human work from §4.5 and §4.6 is used.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 4, second objective. Course corpus §4.3 to §4.8. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states evaluation-design rules and no product facts. The document mix, the accuracies, the agreement counts and the 90% success rate are invented for illustration. The figures of roughly 38% for judges on citation validity and about 75% as a starting agreement bar are the corpus's own, and neither was checked against a source here.

    Remember

    1. Fix the composition before the size: real traces first, 20 to 50 hand-verified cases, balanced should-fire and shouldn't-fire. A bigger set drawn the same way is the same bias.
    2. Report by segment. Over-sample rare, high-cost segments to about 30 cases each, and let every segment clear the bar before oversight is reduced.
    3. Code first for anything exact: schema, verbatim citations, PII. A model grader for tone and faithfulness. Humans label and calibrate.
    4. Validate a model grader against 20 to 50 hand-labelled cases, with binary criteria and a different model family. Mark a same-family grader degraded and re-audit periodically.
    5. Grade RAG as retrieval plus generation and agents as trajectory plus outcome, and attribute the first failing turn.
    6. pass@k where a retry absorbs failure, pass^k where an attempt is visible or acts in the world, and any irreversible-action gate is pass^k = 1.0.

    Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements

    Sheet
    D4-3
    Exam weight
    16%
    Domain
    Evaluation, Testing & Optimization
    Corpus sections
    4.9
    Reading time
    ≈ 6 min
    Position
    3 of 6 in D4

    A support team rewrites its assistant's prompt. On ten examples that someone picked by hand, the new version reads better, and the team wants to ship it to every user. Ten hand-picked examples are persuasive, and they are not evidence. Nobody chose them at random, nobody declared in advance what "better" means, and nothing says the edit did not break a rare case.

    What does a prompt change need before it reaches all users? The corpus answers with an order, and every step in it exists because the step before it cannot answer one particular question.

    Regression first, then A/B, then staged rollout§4.9

    The order is a regression evaluation on the fixed set, then a controlled A/B test on metrics defined in advance, then a staged rollout.

    A regression evaluation replays a fixed test set to check that nothing that worked has got worse. A controlled A/B test splits live traffic between the current prompt and the new one. Regression comes first because the A/B costs live traffic and only the fixed set over-samples rare segments. The A/B comes second because the fixed set cannot report on the live distribution, real load or production latency.

    The corpus discriminator is whether the change was checked before it touched traffic, and whether a result could be attributed to it. Change one variable per variant. If a variant changes the prompt, the model and the retrieval depth together, split it into separate variants. Otherwise a win is unattributable, and the next regression has three suspects.

    Randomise by user or session and never per request. A per-request split flips a conversation between prompts mid-thread, which corrupts the behaviour and the metric together. Declare the primary metric and the guardrails before launch, and let the guardrails only block. A variant that improves the primary metric and breaches the declared latency guardrail is not shipped.

    Fix the duration and the sample size in advance. A test that looks favourable at day 4 of a planned 14 runs to day 14, because stopping on good news inflates the false-positive rate, the chance of declaring a win that is only noise.

    The corpus gives no rule for sizing the duration or the sample, and a real test sizes them from the smallest difference worth detecting.

    Report by segment as well as in aggregate. If the aggregate improves by 1.5 points and one segment regresses by 12, do not ship on the aggregate, since segment masking applies to A/B results as it does to accuracy.

    If a change has already shipped to 100% with no control arm, state that no clean comparison exists. A before-and-after reading is confounded by everything else that changed in the window.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A prompt edit looked better on ten hand-picked examplesRun the regression set first, then a controlled A/B.Ten non-randomly chosen examples is persuasive and is not evidence.
    • A variant changes prompt, model and retrieval depth togetherSplit into separate variants.A win is unattributable, and the next regression has three suspects.
    • The A/B is randomised per requestRe-randomise by user or session.Conversations flip prompts mid-thread, corrupting behaviour and metric together.
    • The test looks favourable at day 4 of a planned 14Run to the declared duration.Stopping on good news inflates the false-positive rate.
    • A variant improves the primary metric but breaches the declared latency guardrailDo not ship.Guardrails were declared to block precisely this.
    • The aggregate improves 1.5 points, and one segment regresses 12Do not ship on the aggregate.Segment masking applies to A/B results as it does to accuracy.
    • A change has already shipped to 100% with no control armState that no clean comparison exists.Before and after is confounded by everything else in the window.
    Go deeper: how an aggregate gain and a segment loss fit together

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its shares are invented. Suppose the regressing segment carries 10% of traffic and falls by 12 points. For the aggregate to rise by 1.5 points, the other 90% of traffic has to gain 3.0 points on average, because 1.5 is the weighted sum of the two changes.

    Nothing in the aggregate hints at the 12-point loss. Inference: looking at the result every day for 14 days gives noise 14 chances to cross the threshold, which is why the corpus fixes the duration in advance.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's one Domain 4 sample is about diagnosing a RAG failure after a document refresh and is worked through in O4.4, so this objective has no official sample. The scenario below comes from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a stem where a change looks good on a few examples and the options differ in what is checked before and after exposure.

    A prompt change improves output on a set of examples the team reviewed manually.

    • CorrectRun the change against the fixed regression set first, then a controlled A/B against the current prompt with the primary metric and guardrails declared in advance, then roll out in stages.
    • WrongREPAIRDeploy to 100% and monitor the quality dashboard for regressions. It catches damage after users absorb it, and with no control arm the comparison is confounded.
    • WrongHALF-MOVESkip the regression set and go straight to a live A/B because live traffic is more representative. Live traffic delivers rare segments at natural frequency, so a regression confined to one of them will not surface.
    Say it backA prompt edit wins on a day-4 reading of a planned 14-day test, with an aggregate gain of 1.5 points, while one segment is down 12. The test also randomised each request. What do you tell the team?

    Do not ship. Run to day 14, because stopping on good news inflates false positives. Do not read the aggregate alone, since the segment that lost 12 points is hidden inside it. Re-run with randomisation by user or session, so a conversation stays on one prompt, and change one variable per variant so a result can be attributed.

    Connections

    • O4.1, §4.1: the primary metric and the guardrails need thresholds declared before launch, which is the same rule applied to a test.
    • O4.2, §4.4: segment reporting is why one segment's 12-point loss is visible, and the regression set is the fixed set built there.
    • O3.3, §3.4: a declared latency guardrail is the SLA of that section, and a variant that breaches it does not ship.
    • O4.4, §4.10: when a regression does appear in production, diagnosis checks data and retrieval before the model.
    • O4.5, §4.11: Inference: caching, routing and retrieval changes are production changes too, so the same path applies to them.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 4, third objective. Course corpus §4.9. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states release-process rules and no product facts. The traffic shares in the fold and the 14-day plan are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. The order is regression on the fixed set, then a controlled A/B on metrics declared in advance, then a staged rollout. Ten hand-picked examples are not evidence.
    2. One variable per variant. A variant that changes prompt, model and retrieval depth together is split.
    3. Randomise by user or session, never per request.
    4. Declare the primary metric and the guardrails before launch. A breached guardrail means do not ship.
    5. Run to the declared duration. Report by segment, since a good aggregate can hide a 12-point loss. With no control arm, say that no clean comparison exists.

    Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)

    Sheet
    D4-4
    Exam weight
    16%
    Domain
    Evaluation, Testing & Optimization
    Corpus sections
    4.10
    Reading time
    ≈ 6 min
    Position
    4 of 6 in D4

    On Monday morning, the share of sampled answers marked wrong from a support assistant jumps from 4% to 19%, a rise of 15 points. The knowledge base was re-indexed on Sunday night. The model version, the prompt and the response times are unchanged. The answers are fluent and confident, and they are wrong. The figures are illustrative.

    Someone proposes moving to a more capable model, since "the model has started hallucinating". The model is the layer that changed least and costs most to swap, so what does the symptom point at?

    Check data and retrieval first, and the model last§4.10

    The corpus gives an order: data and retrieval, then prompt and context, then model mismatch. Each earlier layer poisons everything downstream, and checking it is far cheaper. The discriminator is which layer the symptom's timing and shape point at, and not which layer is quickest to swap. By the timeline rule, a sharp drop with a change immediately before it makes the change the hypothesis.

    Match the symptom to the layer. Confidently wrong right after a refresh or re-index points at retrieval and indexing, and the model, which did not change, is not the cause. Wrong on one document or query type and correct elsewhere points at data coverage or chunking and not a general capability deficit. Correct facts with the required format or steps missing points at the prompt.

    Format that varies across runs despite explicit instructions needs few-shot examples (§2.3), and more prose has already failed. Failing only on long inputs, with mid-document facts missed, is context structure and position (§2.6), not an exceeded window.

    Forgetting a fact from two turns ago in a short conversation is the application not resending history (§2.5), since the API is stateless: it keeps nothing between calls, and the application must send the history each time. Failing broadly on multi-step reasoning, with retrieval verified and the prompt clean, is model mismatch.

    "Hallucination" names three faults in the corpus. If the context contained the answer and the claim was unsupported, the fault is grounding or the prompt, and the fix is cited spans plus a verbatim check.

    If retrieval returned nothing relevant, fix retrieval and add an explicit refusal or escalation path. If the claim was fabricated under truncation or compaction, it is a context-management fault (compaction means summarising older context to make room), and the fix is to extract the critical facts verbatim into a structured block that the summary never touches.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Confidently wrong right after a document refresh or re-indexRetrieval and indexing.Rules out: the model, which did not change.
    • Wrong on one document or query type, correct elsewhereData coverage or chunking.Rules out: a general capability deficit.
    • Facts correct, required format or steps missingPrompt and instructions.Rules out: retrieval.
    • Format inconsistent across runs despite explicit instructionsFew-shot examples are needed.Rules out: too little prose instruction, which has already failed.
    • Fails only on long inputs, and misses mid-document factsContext structure and position.Rules out: the context window being exceeded.
    • Forgets a fact from two turns ago in a short conversationThe application is not resending history.Rules out: a context limit, since the API is stateless.
    • Fails broadly on multi-step reasoning, with retrieval verified and the prompt cleanModel mismatch.Everything upstream has already been cleared.
    Go deeper: what checking retrieval first looks like

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its counts are invented. The team keeps 50 questions with gold passage IDs. Before the re-index, the gold passage was in the top five results for 44 of them, a Recall@5 of 0.88. After the re-index it is in the top five for 30, a Recall@5 of 0.60.

    That is a drop of 28 points in a layer that sits before the model, and it accounts for the wrong answers without any change to the model.

    An upgrade to a larger model would have kept the same missing passages and produced fluent answers on top of them. The check is one script run against a fixed question set.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's Sample 3 is this chapter's failure, and it is the one official Domain 4 sample. A RAG system suddenly returns confident but incorrect answers after a document refresh, while latency and model version are unchanged, and the question asks where to investigate first. The answer is the retrieval and indexing step.

    The guide's reason is that confident-but-wrong answers after a refresh, with the model and latency unchanged, point to retrieval feeding the model poor context, for example a broken re-index or mismatched embeddings. The other options blame silent weight changes, a low temperature and a shrunken context window, and none of them would be triggered specifically by a document refresh. O3.5 covers why indexes degrade after a refresh. The Trap families page defines the labels below.

    The project's corpus words the same scenario with different wrong options:

    A RAG assistant becomes confidently wrong in the week following a corpus refresh.

    • CorrectCheck retrieval first: measure Recall@k against gold passage IDs and inspect how the refreshed documents were chunked and indexed.
    • WrongDISCARDMove to a higher-capability model. It replaces a component that was never implicated, and produces more fluent answers built on the same missing passages.
    • WrongREPAIRAdd an instruction to the system prompt not to state facts it cannot support. It patches the symptom downstream of a data fault, and cannot conjure material that was never retrieved.
    Say it backAfter a re-index, a RAG assistant gives confident wrong answers, and a teammate says the model has started hallucinating. Separately, an assistant forgets a customer's name from two turns ago. Where does each investigation start?

    For the re-index, start with retrieval and indexing: measure Recall@k against gold passages and inspect the chunking of the refreshed documents. The model did not change, and the timeline names the re-index as the hypothesis. For the forgotten name, check whether the application resends the conversation history, because the API keeps nothing between calls and a short conversation cannot have exceeded the window.

    Connections

    • O3.5, §3.10: index coupling and post-refresh degradation are the cause behind the guide's sample, and that chapter says why the embedding model and the index must match.
    • O2.4, §2.5 and §2.6: forgetting in a short conversation and missing a mid-document fact are the two context rows here, with their fixes.
    • O2.3, §2.3: inconsistent format despite instructions is the few-shot row, and examples are the fix that prose has not delivered.
    • O4.2, §4.7: a retrieval row scored apart from a generation row is the measurement this chapter's first check uses.
    • O3.4, §3.6: traces with retrieved chunk IDs and document versions are the evidence this diagnosis reads.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 4, fourth objective, and section 8, Sample 3 with its rationale, summarised above. Course corpus §4.10. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states diagnosis rules and no product facts. The error rates, the question counts and the Recall@5 values are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Diagnose in this order: data and retrieval, then prompt and context, then model mismatch. Each earlier layer poisons the ones after it, and checking is cheaper.
    2. A sharp drop right after a change makes the change the hypothesis. Confidently wrong right after a refresh means retrieval and indexing.
    3. Wrong on one document or query type means coverage or chunking. Right facts with wrong format means the prompt. Inconsistent format despite instructions needs few-shot examples.
    4. Long-input misses are structure and position. Forgetting two turns back is the application not resending history.
    5. Three hallucination causes, three fixes: grounding with cited spans, retrieval plus a refusal path, and context management with verbatim critical facts. Model mismatch is a conclusion, never an opening move.

    Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs

    Sheet
    D4-5
    Exam weight
    16%
    Domain
    Evaluation, Testing & Optimization
    Corpus sections
    4.11
    Reading time
    ≈ 6 min
    Position
    5 of 6 in D4

    A service has a p95 limit of 2,800 ms and gets a latency complaint. Nobody has stage timings. A team decides to halve the retrieval step. A profile, which nobody has run yet, would show that it takes 224 ms, or 8% of the budget. Halving it saves 112 ms, which is 4% of the total, and the complaint stays.

    Generation takes 2,016 ms, 72% of the budget, and nobody looked. The figures are illustrative.

    Every token is a cost line and a latency line at once. Which levers cut both, which cut one, and which only look like savings?

    Profile first, cache first, and remove nothing the requirement needs§4.11

    Profile which stage dominates the budget before optimising anything. The fields that make a profile possible are listed in O4.6. With no stage-level timing, a latency complaint is answered by profiling first, since halving a stage worth 8% of the budget buys only 4%. The corpus discriminator is whether a saving preserves everything the requirement demands. Reordering for cache reuse loses nothing, and truncation loses content.

    The highest-value lever is prompt caching: static content first and dynamic content last (how long a cache lasts, the smallest prompt it works on and the write premium are covered in O2.5), which cuts time-to-first-token and cost together with no quality loss (§2.8).

    Any variation in the prefix, such as a timestamp, a session ID or a user name, destroys reuse. If a large identical policy preamble is sent on every request and latency and cost are both named, order it first and cache it.

    Cutting the preamble by 60% is a compliance regression where the removed sections are required. Summarising it with an extra model call adds a full invocation and degrades precision.

    For a quality floor plus a budget ceiling with mixed task difficulty, use a cascade: a smaller model for the routine class, escalation for the rest, with the trigger validated for each segment and not assumed. The trigger is the rule that decides a request needs the larger model, such as a confidence signal or a failed check (§5.8 lists the valid signals).

    A nightly batch job with a latency complaint wants batch or async processing and output shaping (trimming what the model is asked to write, so fewer output tokens are generated), because nobody is watching a cursor and streaming changes nothing there.

    If retrieval fetches the top 20 passages, reduce it to those that clear the relevance floor (a minimum retrieval score, set in advance like any bar), since noise in the middle of the window costs tokens and accuracy.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Identical large policy preamble on every request, with latency and cost both namedOrder static content first and enable prompt caching.The stable prefix is reused, both metrics improve and nothing is lost.
    • Same situation, with a proposal to cut the preamble by 60%Reject if the removed sections are required.It is a compliance regression and not a saving.
    • Same situation, with a proposal to summarise the preamble with an extra model call at request timeReject.It adds a full model invocation with its own cost and latency, and degrades policy precision.
    • A quality floor plus a budget ceiling, with mixed task difficultyA cascade: a small model for the routine class, escalate the rest, with the trigger validated per segment.It matches capability to what each class actually requires.
    • Nightly batch job, latency complaintBatch or async, and output shaping.Nobody is watching a cursor, and streaming changes nothing here.
    • Retrieval fetches the top 20 passagesReduce to the passages that clear the relevance floor.Noise in the middle of the window costs tokens and accuracy.
    • A latency complaint, with no stage-level timing collectedProfile first.Halving a stage worth 8% of the budget buys 4%.
    Go deeper: a cascade priced, and the batch rate in the documentation

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the prices are invented. A service makes 100,000 requests a day, and 80% are routine. A large model at $0.02 a request would cost $2,000 a day.

    A cascade sends the 80,000 routine requests to a small model at $0.002, which costs $160, and the other 20,000 to the large model, which costs $400. The total is $560 a day, a saving of $1,440, or 72%.

    That saving holds only if the small model clears the quality floor on the routine class. The corpus says to validate the escalation trigger for each segment, because a segment where the small model falls short has to escalate or the saving becomes a regression.

    On batch, Anthropic's model documentation (live docs, read 2026-10-25) says Batch API requests are 50% cheaper. A nightly job that costs $2,000 on demand would cost $1,000 as a batch, a case where nobody waits for the result.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's Domain 2 sample is the top lever of this chapter. It describes an 8,000-token system prompt sent on every request with a short varying message, and asks which optimisation addresses latency and cost together. The answer is to place the static prompt and policy first and enable prompt caching, and O2.5 works it through. The scenario below comes from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label.

    InferenceExpect options that save a number by removing content, and one that reuses it.

    An identical large system preamble is sent on every request, and both p95 latency and monthly cost are over target.

    • CorrectReorder so the static preamble comes first and the varying input last, and enable prompt caching.
    • WrongDISCARDTruncate the preamble to the sections used most often. It removes required content to solve a problem that reuse solves without any loss.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISEnable response streaming to bring the latency number down. Streaming changes perceived latency and not total completion time, and it does nothing for cost.
    Say it backA team halves a 224 ms stage to fix a latency complaint, and another wants to cut a 60% share of the policy preamble to save tokens. What do you ask for, and what do you recommend instead?

    Ask for stage timings first. Halving a stage worth 8% of the budget buys 4%, and the dominant stage may be elsewhere. Reject the cut if the removed sections are required, because it is a compliance regression. Put the static preamble first and enable prompt caching, which reuses the same content and lowers both latency and cost.

    Connections

    • O2.5, §2.8: the caching rule and the timestamp trap are worked through there. This chapter ranks caching first among the levers.
    • O3.3, §3.4: the stage budget table is how the profile is read, and the same section says to look for wasted latency before cutting retrieved context.
    • O1.5, §1.11: routing by confidence tier is the cascade, and the validated trigger is the same measured split.
    • O3.6, §3.12: fewer, better passages after reranking are the retrieval lever.
    • O4.3, §4.9: Inference: each of these is a change to production, so it goes through the regression set and a controlled A/B before it reaches everyone.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 4, fifth objective, and section 8, Sample 2, summarised above. Course corpus §4.11. Live check, read 2026-10-25: Anthropic, "Models overview" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview), for the 50% batch discount in the last fold. The stage timings, the request volumes and the model prices are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. A token is a cost line and a latency line. Profile which stage dominates before optimising, because halving an 8% stage buys 4%.
    2. Prompt caching is the highest-value lever: static first, dynamic last. A timestamp, session ID or user name in the prefix destroys reuse.
    3. Do not cut required preamble content or add a summarising model call. Neither is a saving.
    4. Cascade a small model for the routine class and validate the escalation trigger per segment. Use batch or async for a nightly job, since streaming changes nothing there.
    5. Fewer, better passages are often cheaper and more accurate than the top 20. An optimisation that breaches a stated quality, policy or compliance constraint is not one.

    Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools

    Sheet
    D4-6
    Exam weight
    16%
    Domain
    Evaluation, Testing & Optimization
    Corpus sections
    4.12
    Reading time
    ≈ 6 min
    Position
    6 of 6 in D4

    One morning the daily bill for an assistant is three times what it was, response times are up, and the quality score has not moved. Nothing was announced. The team's logs hold the final answer and a timestamp for each request, which is enough to show that the bill rose and not enough to say why.

    The logs did not capture which prompt version served each request, or how many input tokens were read from the cache. If they had, the cause would take a minute to find. What should a production log contain so that a metric that moves can be tied to a layer and a release?

    Log for attribution, so a moving metric can name its cause§4.12

    Evals measure a frozen set, and monitoring measures the distribution nobody anticipated. Both are required, and a system that passed its evals can still drift in production. The corpus discriminator is whether the logged fields let you say which layer and which release moved a metric.

    The one field that cannot be left out is the prompt version and model identifier on every request. Without it, no change in a metric can be tied to a release.

    That is the corpus's minimum log. It also names online proxies, such as the escalation rate, retry rate, thumbs-down rate, conversation length and abandonment, which move before the offline metrics do. Sample live traffic for quality in strata, across segments and across verdict classes, and include the high-confidence automated stream. Alert on rates, on segment rates and on leading indicators, and not on individual events.

    Two fields in that record need a gloss. A guardrail verdict records whether each guardrail layer allowed or blocked the request. The outcome signal is the online proxy for how the request ended, such as an escalation, a retry or a thumbs-down.

    The signature to learn is cost and latency moving together while quality holds. That points at the token or caching layer and not at model behaviour. When the quality metric moves and the cause is unknown with only final outputs logged, add the prompt and model version, the retrieved IDs, the tool calls and the staged latency. Output alone cannot name the layer that produced it.

    A dashboard of aggregate averages needs per-segment breakdowns, since it reproduces the masking trap in real time. Alerting on every individual error gets ignored within a week, so alert on rates. If only complaints and flagged outputs are sampled, add stratified sampling of the high-confidence stream, because novel error patterns appear first where nobody is looking.

    After an incident, "add monitoring" is accepted as prevention and not as the root-cause fix, since instrumentation diagnoses the next incident and not this one. In a regulated sector, redact real-traffic logs at write time, define retention and restrict access. The evaluation sample inherits the same obligations.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A quality metric moved, the cause is unknown, and only final outputs are loggedAdd prompt and model version, retrieved IDs, tool calls and staged latency.Output alone cannot name the layer that produced it.
    • Cost tripled overnight, latency is up, and quality is flatCheck cache-read token counts and the prompt-version field.That combination points at the caching or token layer.
    • The dashboard shows aggregate averages onlyAdd per-segment breakdowns.It is the masking trap reproduced in real time.
    • Alerting is configured to fire on every individual errorAlert on rates and segment rates instead.Per-event alerting is ignored within a week.
    • Only complaints and flagged outputs are sampled for qualityAdd stratified sampling of the high-confidence stream.Novel error patterns appear first where nobody is looking.
    • Post-incident, the proposed remedy is "add monitoring"Accept it as prevention, not as the root-cause fix.Instrumentation diagnoses the next incident, not this one.
    • Regulated sector, with real-traffic logsRedact at write, define retention, and restrict access.It is a control with an auditor attached.
    Go deeper: why a lost cache raises the bill about threefold

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the 75% share is invented. Anthropic's model documentation (live docs, read 2026-10-25) prices a cache read at 0.1 times the base input price for most current models, and at 0.05 times on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. Take 0.1 times. If 75% of input tokens were cache reads, the input cost per unit was 0.325 of the full price.

    Suppose a new prompt version puts a timestamp at the start of the static block, so the cache never hits. The input cost becomes 1.0, which is 3.1 times the earlier figure.

    Output tokens and quality are unchanged, so where input tokens are most of the bill, the whole bill follows that ratio. The prefix is also processed again on every request, which fits the higher latency. Only the cache-read count and the prompt-version field make this visible in a minute.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's one Domain 4 sample is about diagnosing a RAG failure after a refresh and is worked through in O4.4, so this objective has no official sample. The scenario below comes from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a production symptom with no explanation in the logs, and options that differ in whether the new capture can attribute a cause.

    A system that performed well in pre-production degrades in production, and the team cannot say why.

    • CorrectInstrument for attribution (prompt and model version, retrieved document IDs, tool calls, staged latency, split token counts, outcome signals) and add stratified sampling of live traffic through the grading stack.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISExpand the pre-production evaluation set. The eval set is a frozen distribution and cannot observe production drift, which is the actual gap.
    • WrongHALF-MOVELog every request and response in full and review them when problems arise. It is volume without the attribution fields, and in a regulated sector it creates a retention and PII exposure of its own.
    Say it backCost tripled overnight, latency rose and quality is flat, and the proposed remedy is to "add monitoring". Which fields would you check, and how do you treat the monitoring proposal?

    Check the cache-read token counts and the prompt-version field, since cost and latency moving together with quality holding points at the caching or token layer. Accept more monitoring as prevention for the next incident and not as the root-cause fix for this one, which comes from reading those two fields and correcting what changed in the prompt.

    Connections

    • O3.4, §3.6 and §3.7: traces and stratified sampling are the same capture seen from the integration side, and both chapters say the store inherits the sensitivity of what it holds.
    • O2.5, §2.8: a cache that stops hitting is the cause behind the signature in this chapter, and the timestamp trap there is how it happens.
    • O4.2, §4.4: per-segment reporting is the cure for the aggregate dashboard here, and stratified sampling of the automated stream carries over.
    • O4.4, §4.10: diagnosis needs the fields this chapter logs, and the order of layers there decides which field to read first.
    • O5.4, §5.5: retention and auditability set the rules for the redaction and retention steps in the regulated overlay.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 4, sixth objective. Course corpus §4.12. Live check, read 2026-10-25: Anthropic, "Models overview" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview), for the cache-read price multipliers in the fold. The 75% cache-read share and the overnight cost change are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Evals measure a frozen set, and monitoring measures what nobody anticipated. Both are required.
    2. Log for attribution: trace ID, prompt and model version, retrieved IDs and scores, tool calls, token counts split input, output and cache-read, latency by stage, guardrail verdicts and an outcome signal.
    3. Cost and latency up with quality flat means the token or caching layer. Check cache-read counts and the prompt-version field.
    4. Per-segment dashboards, alerts on rates and leading indicators, and stratified sampling that includes the high-confidence stream.
    5. "Add monitoring" after an incident is prevention and not the root-cause fix. In a regulated sector, redact at write, set retention and restrict access.

    Governance, Safety & Risk Management

    Domain
    D5

    14%

    about 9
    Guide
    v1.0, section 6

    Domain 5 carries 14% of the exam, about 9 of the 63 items, across five objectives. It is about what a system must refuse, what it must be able to prove, and who it must answer to.

    Items here tend to offer a control that sounds responsible and acts at the wrong moment or on the wrong thing.

    Examples are a log written after the data left, a prompt instruction against an absolute rule, a model checking its own work, and a confidence figure the model reports about itself. The test is whether the control is deterministic, independent of the model and early enough. The table below is the course's reading of the domain, not the guide's wording.

    ObjectiveThe question it answers
    Guardrails and safety controlsWhich independent layers stand between a bad input and a consequential action?
    Risks, limitations and failure modesWhat is the symptom's signature, and which control is independent of the model?
    Human-in-the-loop validationWhich items need a person, and how is the rest checked?
    Regulatory complianceDoes the control act before the data crosses, and which constraint binds?
    Ethical AIWhich group is the aggregate hiding, and what record explains a decision?

    The guide's three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4, so Domain 5 has none of its own. Two of them bear on it. The least-privilege item, Sample 1, is the logic of the least-privilege section of the guardrails chapter. The RAG-after-refresh item, Sample 3, is the first rule in the risks chapter's failure-mode list.
