    Implement guardrails and safety controls

    Sheet
    D5-1
    Exam weight
    14%
    Domain
    Governance, Safety & Risk Management
    Corpus sections
    5.1 5.2
    Reading time
    ≈ 8 min
    Position
    1 of 5 in D5

    A support assistant's only safety control is an output classifier, and it has started taking actions that users never requested. Suppose a document in a customer's upload contained an instruction, and the assistant followed it. The classifier, which reads what the assistant says, saw nothing wrong with the sentence. The assistant can also issue refunds of up to $10,000 with no one in the loop.

    The team's instinct is to retrain the classifier on the new failure. That makes the one existing layer better, and it leaves the design at one layer. What would a design look like in which this failure could not reach a refund?

    Stack independent layers, matched to consequence§5.1

    The corpus names four layers: input validation before the call, output filtering after it, scoped permissions, and human approval on consequential actions. The discriminator is whether the design has independent layers or one control carrying everything. The layers fail independently, so an incident has to clear all four. Adding a fifth flavour of one layer adds almost nothing, since it shares that layer's blind spot.

    Most layers are cheap: input validation, schema checks and permission scoping are small deterministic checks. One tuned safety classifier costs more to build and covers less.

    The failure mode of a single control is that it is bypassed by exactly the case it was not written for, with nothing behind it to catch the miss. Replacing four simple checks with one fine-tuned safety model gives correlated coverage from one mechanism, and independence is what layering buys.

    Match the layers to the consequence. Where an output classifier is the only control on a customer-facing assistant, add pre-call input validation, tool scoping and a human gate on consequential actions.

    If input validation, output filtering and scoped tools exist and the assistant can still issue refunds of up to $10,000 unattended, the uncovered layer is human approval on that irreversible action. A low-consequence internal drafting tool with no external output and no tools needs only input validation and output schema checks.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • An output classifier is the only safety control on a customer-facing assistantAdd pre-call input validation, tool scoping and a human gate on consequential actions.A single layer is a single point of failure, and the other three catch different classes.
    • A team proposes replacing four simple checks with one fine-tuned safety modelReject.It gives correlated coverage from one mechanism, and independence is what the layering buys.
    • The assistant already has input validation, output filtering and scoped tools, and can issue refunds up to $10,000 unattendedAdd the human-approval layer on the consequential action.The irreversible action is the uncovered layer.
    • A low-consequence internal drafting tool with no external output and no toolsInput validation and output schema checks are sufficient.Layers are matched to consequence, and permission scoping and human gates have nothing to cover here.
    Go deeper: what independence is worth in numbers

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and every figure is invented. If each of four layers misses 10% of attempts and the misses are independent, the share that gets past all four is 0.1 four times over, which is 0.01%. Out of a million attempts, one layer lets 100,000 through and four let about 100 through.

    The result depends on the independence. If two layers share a blind spot, such as two checks built on the same classifier, their misses overlap, and more gets past both than the product suggests. That is the corpus's point about replacing four simple checks with one tuned model, and about adding a fifth flavour of one layer.

    Remove the capability, or take it out of the model's hands§5.2

    Least privilege means removing an unneeded capability, and not logging or confirming its use. If the task does not require the capability, delete it, because monitoring, confirming and rate-limiting all presuppose that the capability still exists. This matches the answer logic of the guide's sample on least privilege, covered in O3.2.

    When the agent needs the capability sometimes and misuse is consequential, use the strongest form: move the model out of the action path. The model emits a structured request, and a separate service that holds the credential validates it and executes. The privilege stays outside the model while the capability remains available. The stakeholder answer is: "The assistant cannot do X. It proposes; the existing system decides."

    The cases follow from consequence. If an agent holds a write or delete tool it has never legitimately needed, remove the tool, and the failure class disappears instead of being mitigated.

    If it needs the capability routinely and misuse is low-consequence and reversible, keep the tool and add logging, since removal would break the task. A proposal to keep a dangerous tool and log every invocation is rejected as the primary control, because logging is detection and the action still executes.

    A confirmation step is the right control when the capability is needed and consequential (§3.2). It is a half-move when the scenario says the capability is not needed, because then it should be removed.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • An agent has a write or delete tool it has never legitimately neededRemove the tool.The failure class disappears rather than being mitigated.
    • The agent needs the capability sometimes, and misuse is consequentialThe model emits a structured request, and a separate service holding the credential validates and executes it.Privilege stays outside the model while the capability remains available.
    • The agent needs the capability routinely, and misuse is low-consequence and reversibleKeep the tool, and add logging.Removal would break the task, and the consequence does not justify a gate.
    • Proposal: keep the dangerous tool and log every invocationReject as the primary control.Logging is detection, and the action still executes.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's only sample that touches this objective is Sample 1, filed under Domain 3, and it is the same removal-first logic: a support agent holds refund and delete tools that staff never need, and the answer removes them from the configuration. Logging and confirmation prompts are the compensating controls it rejects. O3.2 works through it. The two scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label.

    A support assistant's only safety control is an output classifier, and it has begun taking actions users did not request.

    • CorrectAdd independent layers: validate and delimit untrusted input before the call, scope the tool set to what the task requires, and gate consequential actions on human approval.
    • WrongHALF-MOVERetrain the output classifier on the new failure examples. It improves the one layer that already exists, leaves the design at one layer, and does nothing about the action path.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISAdd detailed logging and alerting on unexpected tool calls. It is detection and not prevention, and a log records the action after it happened.

    An agent has a delete_records tool it does not need for its stated task.

    • CorrectRemove delete_records from the agent's tool definitions.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISKeep the tool and log every invocation for audit. It has the right vocabulary and the wrong mechanism, since the deletion still happens.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEKeep the tool but require a confirmation step before it executes. It is a partial version of the right answer that leaves the capability in place and depends on whoever confirms.
    Say it backA team wants to retrain its output classifier after an assistant followed an injected instruction. Separately, an agent needs to issue a refund once a day, and a teammate wants to keep the refund tool and log each call. What do you recommend for each?

    Do not rely on the classifier alone. Add input validation, tool scoping and human approval for the consequential action, so that the layers fail independently. For the refund, have the model emit a structured request and let a separate service that holds the credential validate and execute it, with human approval for a consequential amount. Logging only records the refund after it happened.

    Connections

    • O3.2, §3.2: the same rule from the integration side. Removal comes first, and logging, confirmation and time windows manage a privilege that is kept.
    • O4.1, §4.2: the adversarial suite and the least-privilege audit there are how the security layers in this chapter are measured.
    • O5.3, §5.8: human approval is the fourth layer, and that chapter covers how to route work to people.
    • O3.1, §3.1: blast radius is a tool-surface cost, and role-scoped agents shrink it.
    • O2.2, §2.2: a guardrail written into the system prompt is one layer among these, and it stays probabilistic.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 5, first objective, and section 8, Sample 1, summarised above. Course corpus §5.1 and §5.2. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states control-design rules and no product facts. The attempt counts, the 10% miss rate and the refund limits other than the corpus's $10,000 are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Four layers: input validation before the call, output filtering after it, scoped permissions, and human approval on consequential actions. They fail independently, so an incident has to clear all four.
    2. One strong classifier is a single point of failure. Replacing four simple checks with one tuned model gives correlated coverage.
    3. Match layers to consequence: an unattended $10,000 refund needs a human gate, and a low-consequence drafting tool needs only input and schema checks.
    4. Least privilege means removal. Logging and confirmation presuppose that the capability stays.
    5. For a needed and consequential capability, the model emits a structured request and a separate service holding the credential validates and executes: "It proposes; the existing system decides."

    Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems

    Sheet
    D5-2
    Exam weight
    14%
    Domain
    Governance, Safety & Risk Management
    Corpus sections
    5.6 5.7 5.9
    Reading time
    ≈ 10 min
    Position
    2 of 5 in D5

    A claims workflow has ten steps. Tested on its own, each step is right 96% of the time, and every step passes its test. End to end, the workflow is right only about 66% of the time. No step is the culprit, and the team's reflex is to find a better model.

    That is one risk among several that this objective names. A second is an agent that follows an instruction hidden in a document it was asked to summarise. A third is a fluent figure that nobody can tell is invented. Each has a signature, a structural control and a wrong control that looks the same from a distance.

    Read the symptom's timing before blaming the model§5.6

    Reason from when and where the failure appears. A capability explanation that ignores the timing is almost always wrong. The corpus gives six signatures. Confidently wrong right after a content refresh points at retrieval and indexing, and not the model's reasoning. No memory of something said two turns earlier, in a short conversation, is the application not resending history, and not an exceeded window.

    Quality that degrades only on long inputs, on mid-document content, is uneven attention across position and not input length alone. Behaviour that changed with no code deployment is model version drift and not a prompt regression. An agent that took an unrequested action after processing an external document is an indirect prompt injection and not user error. A pipeline where every step passes its own test, with far lower end-to-end accuracy, is compounding across steps.

    For a ten-step agent at 96% per step delivering about 66% end to end, insert deterministic validation checkpoints mid-chain. They interrupt the compounding, and a better model shifts each step only marginally.

    If the same prompt and code behave differently this week, check the pinned model version and run the regression set, since, with the code unchanged, drift is the explanation the corpus gives, after any change in data or traffic has been ruled out. A RAG answer that turned confident and wrong the day the corpus was re-indexed points at chunking, embedding version and index freshness.

    In a risk register, rank by consequence and reversibility, and not by frequency alone. A rare irreversible action ranks above a frequent recoverable one.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Confidently wrong immediately after a content refreshRetrieval and indexing.Rules out: the model's reasoning ability.
    • No memory of something said two turns earlier, in a short conversationThe application is not resending history.Rules out: the context window being exceeded.
    • Quality degrades only on long inputs, on mid-document contentUneven attention across position.Rules out: input length alone.
    • Behaviour changed with no code deploymentModel version drift.Rules out: a prompt regression.
    • Every step passes its own test, and end-to-end accuracy is far lowerCompounding across steps (0.9610 is about 66%).Rules out: any single step.
    • An agent took an unrequested action after processing an external documentIndirect prompt injection.Rules out: user error.
    • RAG answers turned confident and wrong the day the corpus was re-indexedInvestigate chunking, embedding version and index freshness.The timing points at the pipeline change and not the model.
    • A ten-step agent at 96% per step delivers about 66% end to endInsert deterministic validation checkpoints mid-chain.It interrupts compounding, and a better model shifts each step marginally.
    • Same prompt, same code, different behaviour this weekCheck the pinned model version and run the regression set.Drift is the only explanation consistent with no code change.
    • Risk register ranking: a rare irreversible action against a frequent recoverable oneRank the irreversible one higher.Professional-tier risk ranking weights consequence and reversibility, not frequency alone.
    Go deeper: why a slightly better model does not rescue the chain

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule. Lift each step from 96% to 97% and the ten-step chain rises from 66% to 74%. A one-point gain per step still leaves about one task in four wrong.

    A deterministic checkpoint in the middle of the chain does something different: it stops an error from being carried into the later steps, where it can multiply. The corpus prefers it for that reason.

    Remove the privilege that an injection would hijack§5.7

    Instructions and data share one channel, so any text the model reads can try to act as an instruction. Indirect injection arrives through retrieved web pages, PDFs, support tickets, code comments, calendar invites and email bodies. The failure looks like a legitimate tool call that no user asked for. The structural control is to remove privilege from the model and to validate the requested action, not the text that requested it.

    If an agent summarises third-party documents and holds a tool that can send email, remove the send capability or require human approval on send. An injection then has no privileged action to hijack. A filter for known injection phrasings stays as a layer and is rejected as the control, because novel phrasings pass and the capability is untouched.

    When retrieved content must go into the context, wrap it in a delimited block that the system prompt declares to be data, and never let eligibility or authorisation decisions depend on its contents. That reduces the attack surface without pretending the channel is separated. For an agent that handles only internally authored, access-controlled content and holds no external tools, delimiting plus input validation is proportionate, since a human gate would cost more than the risk.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • An agent summarises third-party documents and holds a tool that can send emailRemove the send capability, or require human approval on send.Injection has no privileged action to hijack.
    • Same agent, and the proposal is a filter for known injection phrasingsKeep it as a layer, and reject it as the control.Novel phrasings pass, and the capability is untouched.
    • Retrieved content must be included in contextWrap it in a delimited block that the system prompt declares as data, and never let eligibility or authorisation decisions depend on its contents.It reduces the attack surface without pretending the channel is separated.
    • The agent processes only internally authored, access-controlled content and holds no external toolsDelimiting plus input validation is proportionate.Exposure is lower, and a human gate would cost more than the risk.

    Verify from outside the model§5.9

    Catching confident but wrong output needs verification that is independent of the model. A check is independent when it can fail while the model succeeds and succeed while the model fails. A check that draws on the same process cannot do that. Asking the same model to double-check, making a second call with the same context, and trusting a self-reported confidence score are all not independent.

    Verification pays most immediately after steps whose errors are cheap to detect and expensive to propagate. If extracted figures must match the source document, compare them deterministically against the structured source, which fails independently of the generation.

    If cited policy clauses must exist, look each citation up in the policy database before release. For free-text summary quality with no ground truth, use a second-model or rubric-based check and state its correlation limits. It is the best available and not a guarantee.

    A self-critique pass to catch hallucination is accepted as a quality improvement and rejected as the control, since it reduces the rate and shares the failure mode.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Extracted figures must match the source documentA deterministic comparison against the structured source.It fails independently of the generation.
    • Cited policy clauses must existLook each citation up in the policy database before release.Existence is checkable without the model.
    • Free-text summary quality with no ground truth availableA second-model or rubric-based check, with its correlation limits stated.It is the best available, not a guarantee, and the answer says so.
    • A team proposes a self-critique pass to catch hallucinationAccept it as a quality improvement, and reject it as the control.It reduces the rate and shares the failure mode.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's one Domain 4 sample is the first signature in §5.6: confident wrong answers after a document refresh, with the model unchanged, point at retrieval. O4.4 works through it.

    The guide gives no sample for injection or verification, and its Sample 1 shares the removal-first logic of §5.7. The shapes below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a symptom whose timing or channel names the layer, and options that patch downstream of it.

    An agent that summarises customer-submitted documents sent emails that no user requested.

    • CorrectRemove the email-send capability from the agent and route outbound messages through a service that requires human approval.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEAdd a filter that detects and strips instruction-like text from submitted documents. It is a useful layer that catches known phrasings and leaves the privileged capability in place.
    • WrongREPAIRStrengthen the system prompt to say that content inside documents is never to be followed as an instruction. It is a prompt-level tendency defending an architectural exposure.

    A system produces fluent, confident, occasionally fabricated figures, and the team proposes a second pass in which the model reviews its own output.

    • CorrectValidate every emitted figure deterministically against the structured source record and block release on a mismatch.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISAdd a self-critique pass in which the model checks its own output for errors. It has the right vocabulary and the wrong source, since the check comes from the process that produced the error.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEUse a second, different model as a checker and accept the output when both agree. It is more independent than a self-check and still correlated, since two models can agree and both be wrong.

    Design shapeA RAG assistant turns confident and wrong the week after a corpus refresh. The answer investigates retrieval and indexing: chunk boundaries, embedding model version, stale or duplicated index entries. A higher-capability model is DISCARD, because the timing points away from the model. Adding "only answer from the provided context" to the system prompt is REPAIR, since the model is already faithfully reporting wrong context.

    Say it backA ten-step agent passes every step test and fails one task in three. A summarising agent with an email tool sent mail nobody asked for. A system invents figures. What does each call for?

    The ten-step agent needs deterministic validation checkpoints mid-chain, because 96% per step compounds to about 66%. The summariser needs its send capability removed, or human approval on send, since an injection has nothing to hijack then. The figures need deterministic validation against the structured source record, because only a check from outside the model is independent of the error.

    Connections

    • O4.4, §4.10: the symptom-to-layer table is the same reasoning, and that chapter adds the diagnosis order and the three kinds of hallucination.
    • O5.1, §5.2: removing a capability or moving it behind a separate service is the structural control for injection.
    • O4.2, §4.6: a model grader from the same family shares the generator's blind spots, which is the reason a self-check is not independent.
    • O2.4, §2.6: uneven attention across position is the signature of long-input misses, and the fix there is structure.
    • O3.7, §3.13: a control that must always run is called by code and not offered as a tool. Inference: an injected instruction then cannot talk the model out of it.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 5, second objective, and section 8, Samples 1 and 3, summarised above. Course corpus §5.6, §5.7 and §5.9. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states risk-diagnosis and control rules and no product facts. The chain length and the per-step accuracies other than the corpus's 96% are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Reason from the symptom's timing and place: refresh points at retrieval, short-conversation amnesia at history, mid-document misses at position, no-code-change at version drift.
    2. Steps compound: 0.9610 is about 66%. Insert deterministic checkpoints mid-chain, since a better model shifts each step only slightly.
    3. Rank risks by consequence and reversibility, not frequency alone.
    4. Injection follows from one channel for instructions and data. Remove the privilege, or put a human gate on it. A filter is a layer, not the control.
    5. Wrap retrieved content as delimited data, and never base eligibility or authorisation on it.
    6. Verify from outside the model: source data, database lookups, schemas and citation existence. Where source data exists, a self-check or a second model is a quality gain and not the control. Where it does not, a second-model or rubric check is the best available, with its limits stated.

    Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies

    Sheet
    D5-3
    Exam weight
    14%
    Domain
    Governance, Safety & Risk Management
    Corpus sections
    5.8
    Reading time
    ≈ 6 min
    Position
    3 of 5 in D5

    A document pipeline processes 40,000 documents a day, and its extraction accuracy is 94%, so it gets about 2,400 of them wrong each day. A wrong formatting detail costs almost nothing. A wrong financial figure is expensive. The team proposes to have people review every output at first and to relax the review as confidence in the system grows. The figures are illustrative.

    At three minutes a review, 40,000 reviews is 2,000 hours of work a day, or 250 people on eight-hour shifts. Where should the scarce human attention go?

    Route by confidence and consequence together§5.8

    Route on two variables together: confidence and consequence. A strategy that names only one, or none, is incomplete by construction. The absolute rule is that above a consequence threshold the item goes to a human regardless of confidence. For any irreversible or externally visible action, such as a denial, a payment or a message to a customer, the human supplies accountability and not additional accuracy.

    The corpus lists the valid confidence signals: agreement from an independent verifier, a retrieval score, a schema validation result, a calibrated classifier, and business rules such as amount, tenure or jurisdiction. The business rules mark the consequence side of the routing as much as the confidence side. The invalid signal is the model's own statement of how sure it is.

    For high volume, high accuracy and mixed consequence, auto-approve the high-confidence, low-consequence items. Route the rest by threshold, and always route the high-consequence ones. That puts a scarce resource where being wrong is expensive.

    To check that the auto-approved threshold is still right, take a continuous small sample of the auto-approved stream and audit it on a schedule. That measures the unsupervised path, and it differs from routing by sample, which would send a random slice of everything to review. A random 10% would reach only 10% of the costly financial items.

    The cost is review percentage times volume times minutes per review, which equals headcount, and the answer should state it. A scenario that states a volume is there to make blanket review unstaffable, so reject 100% review. Where work is genuinely low in volume and uniformly high in consequence, such as a handful of regulatory filings a month, reviewing every item is correct, because blanket review is wrong because of scale and not on principle.

    The failure mode is automation bias: a reviewer who is shown a fluent conclusion without its evidence approves it. Inference: a reviewer needs the evidence set beside the conclusion, or the human gate adds a signature and no check.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • High volume, high accuracy, mixed consequenceAuto-approve high-confidence, low-consequence items. Route the rest by threshold, and always route high-consequence items.It allocates a scarce resource to where being wrong is expensive.
    • Any irreversible or externally visible action (denial, payment, message to a customer)A human, regardless of confidence.The human supplies accountability, not additional accuracy.
    • Monitoring whether the auto-approved threshold is still correctA continuous small sample of the auto-approved stream, audited on a schedule.It measures the unsupervised path, and it is distinct from routing by sample.
    • A volume figure is stated in the scenario, and 100% review is proposedReject.The volume figure is there to make blanket review unstaffable.
    • Genuinely low-volume, uniformly high-consequence work (a handful of regulatory filings a month)Human review of every item is correct.Blanket review is wrong because of scale, not on principle.
    Go deeper: the headcount sums behind the figure

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and every count is invented. Suppose 15% of the 40,000 documents carry financial figures, which is 6,000, and 10% of the other 34,000 are low-confidence, which is 3,400. Together that is 9,400 reviews a day, 23.5% of the volume.

    At three minutes each, 9,400 reviews take 470 hours, which is about 59 people. Reviewing everything takes 250. The sampled audit adds 306 reviews, or about 15.3 hours, and it is what tells the team whether the 30,600 auto-approved items are still accurate.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide gives no sample for human review, and its three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4. The scenario below comes from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a stem that states a volume and a cost asymmetry, with options that review everything, review a random slice, or route on one variable only.

    A pipeline processes 40,000 documents a day at 94% extraction accuracy. Errors on financial figures are costly, and errors on formatting are not.

    • CorrectRoute by consequence and confidence: auto-approve high-confidence non-financial extractions, send every financial-figure extraction and every low-confidence item to review, and continuously sample the auto-approved stream.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDReview 100% of outputs initially and relax as confidence grows. It reads as the prudent staged answer, it has no exit criterion or capacity plan, and 40,000 daily reviews is the reason the volume was stated.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISReview a random 10% sample of all outputs. Uniform sampling meets costly cases in proportion to their rarity, and sampling is a calibration mechanism for the automated path and not a routing policy.
    Say it backA system handles 40,000 items a day, a few of which authorise payments. A teammate proposes full review at first, and another proposes reviewing a random 10%. What routing do you propose, and what do you add to check it?

    Route on consequence and confidence together. Send every payment-related item to a human whatever the confidence, send low-confidence items by a calibrated threshold, and auto-approve the rest. Add a continuous small sample of the auto-approved stream, audited on a schedule, to check that the threshold still holds. Full review at 40,000 items a day cannot be staffed, and a random 10% meets the costly cases only as often as they occur.

    Connections

    • O5.1, §5.1: human approval is the fourth guardrail layer, and this chapter sets which actions reach it.
    • O4.2, §4.4: stratified sampling of the automated stream, and the rule that every segment clears the bar before oversight is reduced, are the audit side of this routing.
    • O4.1, §4.1: the routing threshold is a bar, and it is declared before results, not tuned afterwards.
    • O4.2, §4.6: a calibrated classifier as a confidence signal needs the same hand-labelled validation as a model grader.
    • O6.1, §6.3: error cost asymmetry as a design driver is the reason consequence is one of the two routing variables.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 5, third objective. Course corpus §5.8. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states routing rules and no product facts. The review time, the shares of financial and low-confidence items, the shift length and the 1% sample are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Route on confidence and consequence together. Above a consequence threshold, a human reviews whatever the confidence.
    2. Confidence comes from independent signals: a verifier, a retrieval score, schema validation, a calibrated classifier, business rules. The model's own statement of sureness is not one.
    3. Auto-approve high-confidence, low-consequence items, route the rest by threshold, and sample the auto-approved stream on a schedule.
    4. State the cost: review percentage times volume times minutes per review equals headcount. A stated volume rejects 100% review, and low volume with uniform high consequence accepts it.
    5. Automation bias means approving a fluent conclusion that arrives without its evidence.

    Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)

    Sheet
    D5-4
    Exam weight
    14%
    Domain
    Governance, Safety & Risk Management
    Corpus sections
    5.3 5.4 5.5
    Reading time
    ≈ 10 min
    Position
    4 of 5 in D5

    A healthcare client requires that patient identifiers never leave its network. The team adds a line to the system prompt: "do not repeat or store patient identifiers". Evaluation shows the assistant obeys it 99.4% of the time. At 50,000 requests a day, that leaves 300 replies a day that repeat an identifier. The figures are illustrative.

    The larger problem comes before the reply. All 50,000 requests have already carried the identifiers to the inference endpoint, and the instruction is read after they arrived. The requirement was that the data never leave, and no measured rate can turn that into a guarantee. What kind of control can?

    Fire the control before the data crosses the boundary§5.3

    A required control cannot depend on the model behaving correctly, because probabilistic behaviour does not produce a guarantee. The pattern is to classify, then de-identify or tokenise before the call, then re-associate locally and audit the crossing.

    The boundary is the edge of the system or network the data is permitted to stay in, such as the client's own network. The timing test is blunt: a control that acts after the request is assembled is too late, because the crossing has already happened.

    Inference: in free-text narratives, finding the identifiers can itself rely on a detector that can miss, so the design keeps the re-identification map and the audit inside the boundary. The corpus point stands: the control acts before the call and does not depend on the main model complying.

    Three things fail to turn a tendency into a guarantee: high measured accuracy, documented residual risk, and a larger model.

    If regulated identifiers must never reach the inference endpoint, de-identify or tokenise in the pipeline before the call. A system-prompt instruction to ignore identifiers is rejected, since it is evaluated after the identifiers are in the request and depends on compliance. Nightly redaction of stored logs is rejected as the control, because it fixes the record and not the transmission.

    The reverse case also exists. A strong preference, such as the tone wanted in redactions, is a tendency, and a prompt instruction is the fitting mechanism for it.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Regulated identifiers must never reach the inference endpointDe-identify or tokenise in the pipeline before the call.It is deterministic, fires before transmission and is independent of model behaviour.
    • Same requirement, and the proposal is a system-prompt instruction to ignore identifiersReject.It is evaluated after the identifiers are already in the request, and depends on compliance.
    • Same requirement, and the proposal is nightly redaction of stored logsReject as the control.It fixes the record and not the transmission.
    • The requirement is a strong preference rather than an absolute (for example, the preferred tone in redactions)A prompt instruction is appropriate.The requirement is a tendency, so a tendency-shaped mechanism fits.

    Ask which constraint binds: the payload or the environment§5.4

    The corpus names what each regime forces into the design. GDPR covers the personal data of people in the EU. HIPAA covers protected health information in the US. FedRAMP covers cloud services used by US federal agencies. GDPR and HIPAA mostly constrain what is in the request, and FedRAMP mostly constrains where the request may be processed. This is the course corpus's reading of each regime and not legal advice.

    Three further points from the corpus complete the picture. GDPR also requires being able to account for automated decisions that affect a person. HIPAA allows the processor to be brought inside the covered boundary under agreement, as an alternative to de-identifying. FedRAMP constrains deployment topology as well as the list of models, and it expects documented control implementation.

    For EU customer records feeding a support assistant, minimise the fields to what the task needs, declare the purpose, make sure the endpoint region is permitted, and list every store for erasure. For clinical narratives drafted by an assistant, strip direct identifiers before the call, send the narrative, reattach locally, and log access.

    For a federal agency whose preferred model is not in an authorised environment, the model is unavailable for that data: route through an authorised environment, or keep the data out. FedRAMP is a boundary and procurement fact and not a configuration setting.

    When a GDPR erasure request arrives for a customer whose tickets seeded an evaluation dataset and a vector index, deletion must reach the logs, the dataset and the index, since derived data is still that person's data.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • EU customer records feeding a support assistantMinimise fields to what the task needs, declare the purpose, make sure the endpoint region is permitted, and list every store for erasure.GDPR binds payload contents, purpose and location.
    • Clinical narratives drafted by an assistantStrip direct identifiers before the call, send the narrative, reattach locally, and log access.HIPAA binds what leaves the covered boundary.
    • A federal agency deployment where the preferred model is not in an authorised environmentThe model is unavailable for that data. Route through an authorised environment, or keep the data out.FedRAMP is a boundary and procurement fact, not a configuration setting.
    • A GDPR erasure request arrives for a customer whose support tickets seeded an evaluation dataset and a vector indexDeletion must reach the logs, the evaluation dataset and the index.Derived data is still that person's data.

    Retain with a purpose and a duration, and keep the audit record unalterable§5.5

    Retention requires a stated purpose and a bounded duration. Storage is a decision that creates obligations, and "it might be useful later" is not a purpose. Every retained interaction is erasure scope, breach surface and discoverable material. A team that proposes keeping every request and response indefinitely for future evaluation work is told to define the purpose and the duration, and to de-identify what is kept.

    The audit record holds what was sent, when, under what purpose, which model and prompt version, what returned and the outcome.

    It must be immutable, because an audit trail that can be edited is not evidence. Inference: immutability and erasure meet by de-identifying what the record holds and by deleting under a stated policy, a point to settle with counsel. If auditability is met only by application logs that the operations team can edit, reject it.

    An incident investigation that needs recent traffic gets a bounded window, for example 30 days, de-identified and purpose-coded. If a regulator may ask why a specific decision was made, retain the decision trace under its own policy. Explainability needs the trace, which is narrower and longer-lived than raw logs.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A team proposes retaining all requests and responses indefinitely for future evaluation workReject. Define the purpose and the duration, and de-identify what is kept.Indefinite retention of regulated content creates open-ended obligations.
    • Incident investigation needs recent trafficA bounded window (for example 30 days), de-identified and purpose-coded.Purpose and duration are both stated.
    • A regulator may ask why a specific decision was madeRetain the decision trace (inputs used, versions, thresholds, outcome) under its own policy.Explainability needs the trace, which is narrower and longer-lived than raw logs.
    • Auditability is met by application logs that the operations team can editReject.Mutable records are not evidence of a boundary crossing.
    Go deeper: what indefinite retention adds up to

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the volume is invented. At 50,000 requests a day, a 30-day window holds 1,500,000 interactions at any time. Kept indefinitely, the store reaches 18,250,000 after one year, and it keeps growing.

    Each of those interactions is something an erasure request has to find, something a breach exposes, and something a discovery process can demand. A scheduled redaction job over that store treats the problem after the decision to store the field has been made, which is why the corpus calls it a repair and not a control.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide gives no sample for compliance, and its three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4. The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect options that sound like governance and leave the data crossing, and one that fires first.

    A healthcare client requires that patient identifiers never leave its network, and the team proposes adding "do not repeat or store patient identifiers" to the system prompt.

    • CorrectDe-identify the record in the pipeline before the API call, hold the re-identification map inside the network, and re-associate locally on return.
    • WrongOVERSPECKeep the prompt instruction and support it with evaluation showing 99.4% compliance. The corpus tags this OVERSPEC in appearance, because it looks like extra rigour, and insufficient in fact: a measured rate is still a tendency, and the requirement is absolute.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDSign a data processing agreement with the provider and document the residual risk. It reads as the mature governance answer and allocates liability, and it does not stop the data crossing. The agreement may still be required, and it is insufficient alone.

    A federal agency wants the highest-capability model available, which is not offered in an authorised environment.

    • CorrectDeploy on an authorised environment using an available model, and state the capability trade-off explicitly to the sponsor.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDUse the preferred model and add compensating controls plus enhanced monitoring. It sounds rigorous, but authorisation is a property of the environment, and no control added on top confers it.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEUse the preferred model for non-sensitive requests and the authorised one for sensitive requests, routed by a model-side classification of the input. The routing decision is itself probabilistic, so regulated data reaches the unauthorised environment whenever the classifier is wrong.

    Design shapeA team wants to keep every interaction indefinitely to build evaluation datasets later. The answer defines a bounded window with a stated purpose, de-identifies what is kept, and holds a separate longer-lived decision trace for auditability. Restricting access to the team by role is HALF-MOVE, since it leaves the retention scope and the breach surface as they were. A scheduled redaction job over the store is REPAIR.

    Say it backA client says identifiers must never reach the model, and a teammate proposes a prompt instruction plus a compliance evaluation. Another team wants to keep all interactions for later evaluation work. What do you say to each?

    For the identifiers, reject the prompt instruction. It acts after the data has crossed, and a measured rate is a tendency. De-identify or tokenise in the pipeline before the call and re-associate locally. For the retention, reject indefinite storage and define a purpose and a bounded duration, de-identify what is kept, and hold a separate decision trace for audit under its own policy.

    Connections

    • O1.2, §1.10: redaction belongs at the input boundary, before the model sees anything, which is the same placement as the first row here.
    • O3.2, §3.3: a control that is deterministic and enforced at the point of access, as opposed to a prompt rule, is the shared logic.
    • O3.4, §3.6: the trace store holds regulated content and needs redaction, retention and access control designed with the pipeline.
    • O4.6, §4.12: the regulated overlay on logging is the monitoring side of this retention rule.
    • O5.1, §5.1: the guardrail layers are independent controls, and this chapter adds §5.3's timing test: a compliance control has to act before the data crosses.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 5, fourth objective. Course corpus §5.3 to §5.5. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states control-placement rules, and its account of each regime is the course corpus's reading and not legal advice or a statement of what any provider offers. The request volumes and the 99.4% rate are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. A required control cannot depend on the model. De-identify or tokenise before the call, re-associate locally, and audit the crossing. A control that acts after the request is assembled is too late.
    2. A prompt instruction is a tendency, and a high measured compliance rate, a documented risk or a larger model does not turn it into a guarantee. Absolute requirements need a deterministic control that fires first.
    3. GDPR and HIPAA bind the payload: purpose, minimisation, erasure that reaches derived stores, and what leaves the boundary. FedRAMP binds the environment, and no setting confers authorisation.
    4. Retain only with a stated purpose and a bounded duration, and de-identify what is kept. Keep a separate decision trace for explainability.
    5. An audit record must be immutable. Logs the operations team can edit are not evidence.

    Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)

    Sheet
    D5-5
    Exam weight
    14%
    Domain
    Governance, Safety & Risk Management
    Corpus sections
    5.10 5.11
    Reading time
    ≈ 8 min
    Position
    5 of 5 in D5

    A screening system reports 91% overall accuracy, and complaints come from one group of applicants. The applicants fall into three groups: 85% of them score 94% accuracy, 12% score 80%, and the last 3% score 50%. The team's reflex is to raise the overall target and retrain. The figures are illustrative.

    The 91% is a weighted average, and it can be pulled up by the 85% that works well while the 3% that does not is wrong half the time. The same averaging can hide the problem from the evaluation set as well as from the dashboard.

    Measure by subgroup, with enough cases in each§5.10

    Aggregate accuracy is a weighted average that hides subgroup failure. Evaluate on a set stratified by the subgroups the organisation is accountable for, with adequate N per group, meaning enough cases in each, and not a population-proportional sample. If the set holds 400 cases in proportion to the groups above, the 3% group has 12 of them, too few to measure a rate, against the working floor of about 30 per segment in §4.4.

    Measure by subgroup. Removing the protected attribute from the input does not remove the bias, since proxy variables carry the same signal: postal code, school name, employment gaps, name morphology and phrasing register.

    It also removes the ability to detect the disparity, so a proposal to drop the attribute is rejected as the fairness control. For a small subgroup under a proportional sample, rebalance to equal N per group, since proportional sampling gives the least power where the risk is highest.

    Fairness metrics can conflict. Equal selection rate, equal false-negative rate and equal calibration cannot generally hold together when base rates differ. The conflict is mathematical, and the resolution is a stated decision: choose by which harm is being controlled, and record the rationale. Declare which harm is controlled, and therefore which definition of fairness is in force.

    Three terms in that rule need a gloss. The false-negative rate is the share of people who qualify and are wrongly rejected. Calibration means that a given score carries the same chance of the outcome for every group. The base rate is how common the outcome is within a group.

    Fairness is a measurement that moves with the population and not a property measured once. If it was measured at launch and signed off, recompute it on live traffic on a schedule.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • 91% aggregate accuracy, with complaints concentrated in one groupDisaggregate the metric by subgroup on a stratified set.The aggregate cannot show what is being reported.
    • Proposal to drop the protected attribute from the inputReject as the fairness control.Proxies carry the signal, and measurement becomes impossible.
    • A small subgroup, and a population-proportional evaluation sampleRebalance to equal N per group.Proportional sampling gives the least power where the risk is highest.
    • Two fairness metrics cannot both be satisfiedChoose by which harm is being controlled, and record the rationale.The conflict is mathematical, and the resolution is a stated decision.
    • Fairness was measured once at launch and signed offRecompute on live traffic on a schedule.The applicant or customer population moves.
    Go deeper: why equal N costs fewer cases and shows more

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the shares are invented. A proportional sample of 400 cases gives groups of 340, 48 and 12. Equal N of 100 per group needs 300 cases in all, which is fewer, and it gives the weakest group 100 cases against 12.

    The aggregate from an equal-N set no longer mirrors the applicant population. That is acceptable, since the set exists to measure each group, and the corpus sets the threshold against the worst-performing group. The same reasoning appears in §4.4, where a rate needs about 30 cases per segment. The 100 per group here is this example's choice, comfortably above that floor.

    Keep a record of the decision, and tell people AI was involved§5.11

    Transparency has two distinct meanings, and a third need, contestability, sits beside them. Disclosure means the affected person knows AI was involved and how to reach a human. Explainability means a specific decision can be accounted for afterwards. The two need different mechanisms, and a design can meet one and miss the other.

    The explainability artefact is a logged, reconstructable trace: the inputs used, the evidence retrieved, the prompt and model version, the score, the threshold in force, the rule applied and any human decision. A model-generated rationale is not an explainability artefact. It is plausible text about the decision and not a record of what produced it, and it can be confidently wrong about its own causes.

    If a regulator asks why a specific applicant was declined, produce the stored trace. Attaching a model-written explanation to each decision is useful for the end user and does not serve as the audit record. Where the requirement is that people know they are interacting with an AI system, provide disclosure at the point of interaction plus a stated route to a human. That is disclosure and not explainability.

    A consequential automated decision with no challenge path needs a contestation route, with a queue and a status field. The trace is cheap at write time and expensive to reconstruct after the fact, and the same holds for a route to a human, which is cheap at design time and costly after the first complaint.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A regulator asks why a specific applicant was declinedProduce the stored trace: fields used, versions, score, threshold, rule.It reconstructs the actual decision path.
    • The team proposes attaching a model-written explanation to each decisionIt is useful for the end user and not for the audit record.A generated rationale can be confidently wrong about its own causes.
    • The requirement is that people know they are interacting with an AI systemDisclosure at the point of interaction, plus a stated route to a human.It is disclosure and not explainability, a different requirement with a different mechanism.
    • A consequential automated decision with no challenge pathAdd a contestation route with a queue and a status field.It is cheap at design time and expensive after the first complaint.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide gives no sample for bias or transparency, and its three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4. The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a stem with a headline number and a group, or an auditor and a decision, and options that fix the wrong artefact.

    A screening system reports 91% overall accuracy and is generating complaints from one demographic group.

    • CorrectRebuild the evaluation set stratified with equal N per group, report accuracy and false-negative rate per subgroup, and set the threshold against the worst-performing group.
    • WrongDISCARDRemove the demographic attribute from the model input. It discards the field and does not adjust the measurement, leaves the proxy signal untouched, and removes the ability to detect the disparity.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISRaise the overall accuracy target and retrain until it is met. It optimises the aggregate that was concealing the problem.

    An auditor asks the team to explain why a particular automated decision was made.

    • CorrectRetrieve the stored decision trace: the input fields used, the retrieved evidence, the prompt and model versions, the score and the threshold in force.
    • WrongREPAIRRe-run the case and ask the model to explain its reasoning. It reconstructs an explanation after the fact from a non-deterministic process, instead of recording what happened.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEProvide the system prompt and the model card as the account of the decision. It documents the system's general behaviour and says nothing about this decision.
    Say it backA system with 91% overall accuracy draws complaints from one group, and someone proposes dropping the demographic field. Separately, a regulator asks why one applicant was declined, and the team offers a model-written explanation. What do you do in each case?

    Keep the field and measure with it: build a set with equal N per group, report accuracy and false-negative rate per group, and set the threshold against the worst group, because dropping the field leaves the proxies and destroys the measurement. For the applicant, produce the stored decision trace of inputs, versions, score and threshold. The model-written explanation is for the user and is not the audit record.

    Connections

    • O4.2, §4.4: the aggregate mask and the per-segment case floor are the same reasoning, here applied to groups of people.
    • O3.4, §3.6: the decision trace is the trace that section says to capture, with the same correlation ID and the same redaction and retention duties.
    • O5.4, §5.5: the decision trace is the longer-lived record there, kept under its own policy, while the audit record is the immutable one.
    • O5.3, §5.8: the route to a human in disclosure and contestation is the human side of that routing.
    • O6.2, §6.6: explaining the limits of automation to a stakeholder uses the same disclosure.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 5, fifth objective. Course corpus §5.10 and §5.11. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states measurement and record-keeping rules and no product facts. The group shares, the group accuracies and the 400-case set are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Aggregate accuracy is a weighted average that hides subgroup failure. Stratify by the groups the organisation is accountable for, with equal N per group, and report accuracy and false-negative rate for each.
    2. Removing the protected attribute leaves the proxies and destroys the measurement. Reject it as the fairness control.
    3. Fairness definitions can conflict when base rates differ. State which harm is controlled and record the rationale.
    4. Recompute fairness on live traffic on a schedule, since the population moves.
    5. Disclosure and explainability are different requirements. Explainability is a stored trace of inputs, versions, score and threshold, and a model-written rationale is not one. A consequential decision needs a contestation route.

    Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management

    Domain
    D6

    14%

    v1.0, section 6

    Domain 6 carries 14% of the exam, about 9 of the 63 items, across five objectives. It follows an engagement from the first meeting to a system someone else runs: what to ask for, how to report, what to promise, what to write down, and what to hand over.

    Most items here describe a conversation or a document and offer an answer that is accurate, polite and too early or too general. Build the named pattern, quote the aggregate, promise the pilot number, hand over the repository. The test is usually whether the answer gives the stakeholder something they can decide with, or hold you to, or check. The table below is the course's reading of the domain, not the guide's wording.

    ObjectiveThe question it answers
    Discovery and requirement gatheringWhat decision does the system serve, and how will anyone verify it?

    Feedback loops and expectationsWhich metric fits this person's decision, and what can be promised?
    Documentation and implementation guidanceCan a reader who was not there tell why, and change it safely?
