    Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering

    Sheet
    D6-1
    Exam weight
    14%
    Domain
    Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management
    Corpus sections
    6.1 6.2 6.3
    Reading time
    ≈ 10 min
    Position
    1 of 5 in D6

    A sponsor opens the first meeting with three sentences. "We want a multi-agent system to handle our intake." "It has to be as accurate as possible." "Our board will accept 95% accuracy." Each sentence sounds like a requirement, and none of them can be designed against or checked. The first names a solution, the second sets no target, and the third gives a number that does not say what an error costs.

    An architect who builds what was named, or who pushes back that the request is vague, has skipped the work that discovery exists to do. The corpus puts it in three steps, and each one leaves the sponsor with something they can hold delivery to.

    Find the decision behind the request§6.1

    A stakeholder who arrives with a chosen solution has still not stated a problem. The corpus discriminator is whether the business decision the system serves has been stated, or only a solution the stakeholder has pre-selected. Discovery ends when that decision is written down. The architect's first output is the problem and the decision it feeds, and never a component list.

    If a sponsor asks for "a multi-agent system to handle our intake", elicit the intake problem and the decision it feeds, then assess whether the named pattern fits. The pattern may be right, and it cannot be assessed against a problem nobody has stated. If the elicited problem does not need the pattern, say so, offering the simpler design and what it gives up. The problem licenses the pattern, and the order matters.

    If a sponsor states a business outcome with no solution attached, the precondition is already met, and you can move to bounding the requirement. If the team proposes benchmarking candidate models before the problem is stated, defer it, since a benchmark number cannot be read without a target and an error cost.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A sponsor asks for "a multi-agent system to handle our intake"Elicit the intake problem and the decision it feeds, then assess whether the named pattern fits.The pattern may be right, and it cannot be assessed against a problem nobody has stated.
    • A sponsor names a pattern, and the elicited problem does not need itSay so, with the simpler design and what it gives up.Sequence matters: the problem licenses the pattern, and the pattern does not license the problem.
    • A sponsor states a business outcome with no solution attachedProceed to bounding the requirement (§6.2).The precondition is already met.
    • The team proposes benchmarking candidate models before the problem is statedDefer.A benchmark number is uninterpretable without a target and an error cost.

    Turn an aspiration into something verifiable§6.2

    The discriminator is whether the stated requirement can be verified: is there a number, a method and a set. Three phrasings are unbounded: "as accurate as possible", "reliable enough for production" and "at least as good as our team". A bounded requirement has four parts: a target number, a measurement method, an evaluation set and the cost of an error. The sponsor's answer is a signed acceptance criterion that they can hold delivery to.

    If a sponsor says "as accurate as possible", establish the accuracy the use case requires and what a wrong answer costs, before design. No design can be shown to have met or missed an unbounded target.

    If the requirement is bounded but the evaluation set is not specified, specify a held-out set stratified to the real input mix, meaning cases kept aside from tuning and sampled so that each type of input is represented. An unstratified set reports a number for a population that does not exist.

    If the sponsor cannot state the cost of an error, keep eliciting. The cost of an error is a design input for a probabilistic system and not a footnote, because it determines the threshold, where review sits and which direction errors lean. Once the requirement is bounded and measured and the mix is known, move to design.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A sponsor says "as accurate as possible"Establish the accuracy the use case requires and what a wrong answer costs, before design.No design can be shown to have met or missed an unbounded target.
    • The requirement is bounded but the evaluation set is unspecifiedSpecify a held-out set stratified to the real input mix.An unstratified set reports a number for a population that does not exist.
    • The sponsor cannot state the cost of an errorKeep eliciting.It determines threshold, review placement and error direction. Error cost is a design input for a probabilistic system and not a footnote.
    • The requirement is bounded and measured, and the mix is knownMove to design.The precondition is met.

    Let the cost of each kind of error set the threshold§6.3

    The discriminator is whether a false positive and a false negative cost the same. A false positive is an alert on something that was fine, and a false negative is a miss. The asymmetry decides three things: the confidence threshold, the direction in which the model is biased, and where human review sits. In regulated flows the expensive direction is usually the undetected miss, and the regulator defines it.

    If missed fraud costs 200 times a false alert, bias toward recall and route flagged cases to human review, since the cheap error is the one a human can dismiss in seconds. If a false rejection blocks a legitimate customer payment while a missed one is recoverable the next day, bias toward precision and set a higher action threshold, because the expensive error is the irreversible one.

    If a sponsor asks only for "95% accuracy" and neither direction is priced, return to discovery and price both directions, since one accuracy target cannot express an asymmetric cost. Where both directions cost roughly the same and are correctable, a single accuracy target is adequate, because there is nothing to trade off.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Missed fraud costs 200 times a false alertBias toward recall, and route flagged cases to human review.The cheap error is the one a human can dismiss in seconds.
    • A false rejection blocks a legitimate customer payment, and a missed one is recoverable next dayBias toward precision, and set a higher action threshold.The expensive error is the irreversible one.
    • A sponsor asks only for "95% accuracy", with both directions unpricedReturn to discovery and price both directions.A single accuracy target cannot express an asymmetric cost.
    • Both directions cost roughly the same and are correctableA single accuracy target is adequate.There is nothing to trade off.
    Go deeper: where a threshold comes from when the costs are known

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the costs are invented. Suppose a false alert costs $5 of review time and a missed fraud costs $1,000, which is 200 times as much. For a transaction with fraud probability p, leaving it alone costs p times $1,000 on average, and flagging it costs (1 minus p) times $5. Flagging is cheaper when p exceeds 5 over 1,005, which is 0.5%.

    The cost ratio puts the threshold close to 0.5%, and the large number of flags that follows is the reason human review sits behind them. A single accuracy target says nothing about this cost, which is why the cost ratio and not a default cutoff sets the threshold.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a stem in which the sponsor names a solution, a vague target or a single number, and options that start design or measurement too early.

    A sponsor opens the engagement by naming the architecture they want.

    • CorrectEstablish the business problem and the decision the system serves, then evaluate the proposed pattern against it.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEBegin design of the named pattern, since the stakeholder is the requirement owner. It honours the stakeholder and skips the step that makes the request buildable and verifiable.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISRun a model benchmark on sample data to ground the conversation in evidence. It produces a number before there is a target or an error cost to interpret it against.

    A triage system where a missed high-severity case is far costlier than a false alert.

    • CorrectBias the system toward flagging, set the confidence threshold from the cost ratio, and route flagged cases to human review.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISTune for the highest overall accuracy on the evaluation set. It optimises an aggregate that weights both error directions equally when the business does not.
    • WrongREPAIRAdd a post-hoc audit that samples missed cases weekly. It detects the expensive error after it has already been paid for, instead of biasing against it upstream.

    Design shapeA sponsor requests a document-processing system that is "as accurate as possible". The answer establishes the accuracy the use case requires, how it will be measured and what an error costs, before design.

    Selecting the highest-capability model and the most thorough pipeline is OVERSPEC, since it buys an unpriced guarantee against a target nobody has stated. Escalating to the sponsor's leadership that the requirement is too vague to work with is DISCARD, because it treats requirement definition as an obstacle to the architect's work and not as the work.

    Say it backA sponsor wants "a multi-agent system, as accurate as possible, at 95% accuracy". The product flags suspected fraud, where a miss costs far more than a false alert. How do you run the first conversations?

    Start with the decision the system feeds, and assess the multi-agent pattern against that problem. Bound "as accurate as possible" into a target number, a method, a stratified held-out set and the cost of an error. Price both error directions. Then bias toward flagging, set the threshold from the cost ratio, and put human review behind the flags, instead of tuning for one accuracy figure.

    Connections

    • O1.1, §1.1: translating a business outcome into an automatable decision is the same first move, and this chapter adds how to bound it.
    • O4.1, §4.1: a bounded requirement is where the pre-declared threshold of a metric comes from, since the bar is anchored in the success criterion.
    • O4.2, §4.4: the evaluation set stratified to the real input mix is the per-segment set built there.
    • O5.3, §5.8: where human review sits follows from consequence, which is the asymmetry here.
    • O6.2, §6.4 and §6.6: reporting performance to the sponsor and explaining the limits of automation come next. Inference: both are measured against the acceptance criterion agreed here.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 6, first objective. Course corpus §6.1 to §6.3. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states requirement-gathering rules and no product facts. The sponsor's sentences and the dollar figures in the fold, other than the corpus's 200 times ratio, are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. A stakeholder with a chosen solution has not stated a problem. Elicit the decision the system feeds, then assess the pattern. The first output is a problem and a decision, never a component list.
    2. Defer model benchmarks until there is a target and an error cost. Skipping to design is HALF-MOVE, and escalating that the requirement is vague is DISCARD.
    3. A bounded requirement has four parts: a target number, a measurement method, an evaluation set stratified to the real input mix, and the cost of an error. The sponsor gets a signed acceptance criterion.
    4. Error cost asymmetry sets the threshold, the direction of bias and the place of review. Missed fraud at 200 times means bias toward recall with human review. An irreversible false rejection means bias toward precision.
    5. A lone accuracy target cannot express an asymmetric cost, so price both directions first.

    Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs

    Sheet
    D6-2
    Exam weight
    14%
    Domain
    Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management
    Corpus sections
    6.4 6.6
    Reading time
    ≈ 7 min
    Position
    2 of 5 in D6

    In a steering meeting, the sponsor of a document-processing system asks two questions. "Give me one accuracy number I can take to the board." And, later, "why can't we automate the last 20%?" The system scores 94% on standard documents and 61% on complex ones. Neither question can be answered well with a single short sentence, and both can be answered badly in a few words.

    If 80% of the documents are standard, the headline is 87%. The sponsor will take that to the board. What happens to it next quarter?

    Report performance in the shape it actually has§6.4

    The corpus discriminator is whether performance varies sharply by input type. If it does, an aggregate misleads. The professional answer has three components: break performance out by case type, state the measurement method and the set it was measured on, and give the end-to-end outcome including human review. The sponsor is deciding a budget, and the end-to-end outcome is the number that decision needs.

    Both failure directions are real. A flattering aggregate misleads, and refusing to quantify fails the sponsor too, since a budget decision cannot be made on a qualitative answer. An architect who says "it depends on the case" is not acceptable. If the sponsor has been handed the model metric and is planning against it, supply the end-to-end outcome with the human steps included, because the sponsor is accountable for the process and not the component.

    If performance is genuinely uniform across input types, a single figure is honest, and the method and set are still stated. Segmentation without variance is noise.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • 94% on standard cases and 61% on complex ones, and the sponsor wants "one number"Give per-segment figures, the measurement basis, and the end-to-end outcome including human review.The aggregate is a weighted average over a mix that will change.
    • Performance is genuinely uniform across input typesA single figure is honest, and the method and set are still stated.Segmentation without variance is noise.
    • The architect declines to give any number because "it depends on the case"Not acceptable.The sponsor has a budget decision and cannot make it on a qualitative answer.
    • The sponsor has been given the model metric and is planning against itSupply the end-to-end outcome with human steps included.The sponsor is accountable for the process, not the component.
    Go deeper: what an end-to-end figure can look like

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its volumes are invented. Take 10,000 documents a month, with 8,000 standard and 2,000 complex. All complex documents go to a person. Then 2,000 documents a month get human review, and the standard stream gives 7,520 documents right without review and 480 wrong ones.

    That is a statement the sponsor can budget against: the number of reviews, the staff time they need, and the count of errors that remain. It says more than either 87% or 94%. The per-segment rates hold when the mix shifts, and the counts are recomputed from the new mix, assuming review corrects what it sees.

    Name the decisions that resist automation, and what automating them would risk§6.6

    The corpus discriminator is whether the specific decisions that resist automation can be named, along with what automating them would risk. Two classes resist it: decisions that carry accountability, which someone must attest to, and decisions the system cannot verify it got right. A general appeal to model imperfection, or to a human in the loop for safety, is the register that fails, because it gives the stakeholder nothing to decide with.

    If a stakeholder asks why the last 20% still needs people, name the decisions in that 20% that carry accountability or are unverifiable, and the risk of automating each. That hands the stakeholder a costed choice and not a caution.

    If the residual work is unverifiable and not regulated, say so: the system cannot check its own output on those cases against ground truth. That is a different limit with a different remedy, and better evaluation data may close it.

    If the residual work is small, low-risk and merely unbuilt, say so and price it, since not every human step is a principled limit. If a stakeholder proposes removing review from a regulated segment to hit a savings target, refuse on the named attestation requirement and quantify what the segment is worth. Where a regulator requires an accountable person, the constraint is the attestation and not the accuracy, and it cannot be traded against savings.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A stakeholder asks why the last 20% still needs peopleName the decisions in that 20% that carry accountability or are unverifiable, and the risk of automating each.It gives the stakeholder a costed choice and not a caution.
    • The residual work is unverifiable and not regulatedSay so: the system cannot check its own output on these cases against ground truth.It is a different limit with a different remedy, and better evaluation data may close it.
    • The residual work is small, low-risk and merely unbuiltSay so, and price it.Not every human step is a principled limit.
    • A stakeholder proposes removing review from a regulated segment to hit a savings targetRefuse on the named attestation requirement, where a named person must sign that the decision is correct, and quantify what the segment is worth.The constraint is external and cannot be traded against savings.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect options at both ends: an answer that gives the number requested and misleads, and one that refuses to give a number or to be specific.

    An executive demands a single accuracy figure for a system whose performance varies sharply by document type.

    • CorrectReport accuracy broken out by document type, state how it was measured and on what set, and give the end-to-end business outcome including the human review step.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEReport the weighted average across all document types as the headline figure. It answers the question asked with a number that is unstable and conceals the weak segment.
    • WrongDISCARDExplain that accuracy varies too much by case for a single figure to be meaningful. It is technically defensible and it abandons the quantification the sponsor's decision requires.

    A stakeholder asks why the system cannot be fully automated.

    • CorrectIdentify the specific decisions that require human accountability or cannot be verified by the system, and state what automating each would risk.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEExplain that AI systems are probabilistic and that a human in the loop is a safety practice. It is true and unspecific, and the stakeholder still cannot tell which work could be automated and which cannot.
    • WrongOVERSPECCommit to full automation once accuracy improves past a threshold. It promises a future guarantee on decisions whose obstacle is accountability, which accuracy does not remove.
    Say it backA sponsor wants one accuracy figure for a system that scores 94% on standard documents and 61% on complex ones, and asks why the last 20% still needs staff. What do you give, and what do you name?

    Give the two segment figures, say how and on what set they were measured, and add the end-to-end outcome with the human review step, so the sponsor can budget. For the last 20%, name the decisions that need a named person to attest or that the system cannot verify, and say what automating each would risk. Do not cite model imperfection in general.

    Connections

    • O4.2, §4.4: the aggregate mask in an evaluation set and the misleading headline for a sponsor are the same arithmetic.
    • O6.1, §6.2: Inference: the signed acceptance criterion from discovery is what these reports are measured against.
    • O5.3, §5.8: the human step that this chapter says to include in the end-to-end figure is the routed review of that chapter.
    • O1.6, §1.12: stating a design in the unit the listener measures is the end-to-end outcome here, in minutes, errors and cost.
    • O6.3, §6.5, §6.9 and §6.10: the next objective turns these reports into commitments and feedback loops.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 6, second objective. Course corpus §6.4 and §6.6. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states communication rules and no product facts. The mixes, the document counts and the 80/20 and 60/40 splits are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Where performance varies by case type, an aggregate misleads and moves when the mix does. Report per segment, state the method and set, and give the end-to-end outcome including human review.
    2. Do not refuse to quantify. The sponsor has a budget decision, and "it depends on the case" does not serve it.
    3. Where performance is uniform, one figure is honest, and the method and set are still stated.
    4. Name the specific decisions that resist automation: those carrying accountability someone must attest to, and those the system cannot verify. Say what automating each would risk.
    5. Price work that is merely unbuilt. Refuse to drop review in a regulated segment for a savings target, since the constraint is the attestation and not the accuracy.

    Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)

    Sheet
    D6-3
    Exam weight
    14%
    Domain
    Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management
    Corpus sections
    6.5 6.9 6.10
    Reading time
    ≈ 9 min
    Position
    3 of 5 in D6

    In one week, four people ask about the performance of the same document-classification service, which handles 40,000 items a month and routes 12% of them to human review, or 4,800 reviews. The operations lead is staffing the review queue. The finance director is deciding a renewal. The compliance owner is about to sign off. The engineering lead is tuning the system. The figures are illustrative.

    An architect who sends all four the same dashboard has given each of them a pile of true numbers and left each to find the one that bears on their decision. What should each person see, and what should the contract with the client promise?

    Choose the metric from the decision in front of the person§6.5

    The corpus discriminator is which decision this particular stakeholder is about to make. A useful metric is tied to that decision and is stated together with what it does not cover. The failure mode is a set of metrics that are real, measurable and irrelevant to the decision in front of that person. Pick the metric from the pending decision, and not from what the monitoring stack already emits.

    For the operations lead, report the volume reaching human review and its variance. The finance director gets cost per processed item and its trajectory at projected volume, since model accuracy in isolation does not price a renewal. The compliance owner gets the override rate and audit-trail completeness on the regulated segment. The engineering lead gets per-segment accuracy, latency percentiles and a failure taxonomy.

    Handing a stakeholder the full monitoring dashboard to select from looks thorough and transparent. It transfers the architect's interpretation job to someone without the context to do it. More metrics is not a fuller picture, because a figure that does not inform the decision in front of the person is noise. State the blind spot of each metric alongside it.

    Qualify an accuracy commitment, and commit only what the provider controls§6.9

    The discriminator is whether the commitment depends on inputs the provider does not control. Availability and latency are provider-controlled and are committed normally. An accuracy commitment has four parts: what is committed, on what population, how and how often it is measured, and what is excluded. A stated metric with no stated exclusions is read as covering everything.

    If a client wants "95% accuracy" in the contract, commit per segment, with the scoring method, the cadence and the excluded segments named. Accuracy depends on the client's future input mix, which the provider does not control. A provider that offers only availability and latency and no accuracy commitment is insufficient, because it pushes all performance risk to the client and leaves them unable to plan.

    If the client's input mix is contractually fixed and monitored, a tighter accuracy commitment is defensible, since the uncontrolled variable has been controlled. For latency on a provider-hosted endpoint, commit a percentile and not a maximum, because tail latency on a shared service is not fully controllable.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A client wants "95% accuracy" in the contractCommit per segment, with the scoring method, the cadence and the excluded segments named.Accuracy depends on the client's future input mix, which the provider does not control.
    • The provider offers only availability and latency, with no accuracy commitmentInsufficient.It pushes all performance risk to the client and leaves them unable to plan.
    • The client's input mix is contractually fixed and monitoredA tighter accuracy commitment is defensible.The uncontrolled variable has been controlled.
    • A latency commitment on a provider-hosted endpointCommit a percentile, not a maximum.Tail latency on a shared service is not fully controllable.
    Go deeper: how a flat number can fail with no change in the system

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its figures are invented. In the pilot, 70% of the documents were standard and scored 98%, and 30% were scanned forms that scored 88%. The pilot's overall accuracy was 95%, and a team that commits that number flat is promising it for every future mix.

    If the client later sends 40% standard and 60% scanned forms, the same system scores 92%. The system did not change, and the contract was missed. A per-segment commitment of 98% on standard documents and 88% on scanned forms would have been kept in both mixes.

    Make feedback a recurring loop that grows the evaluation set§6.10

    The discriminator is whether the mechanism recurs and whether each item becomes an evaluation case. A structured loop captures four things: the input, the system output, the expected output and the reviewer. Expectations drift in one direction, toward believing the system is more capable and more finished than it is. They re-inflate at every demonstration, so keeping expectations in line is a routine and not a single event.

    If a sponsor's expectations inflate after a successful demo, establish a recurring review that shows real performance on real inputs against the agreed criteria. A single correction does not hold against continuous drift. A single well-argued memo is necessary and not sufficient, since it fixes today's gap and none of next quarter's.

    If users report failures in a shared chat channel, restructure the intake so that it captures input, output, expected output and reviewer, and feeds the evaluation set. Anecdotes have no frequency and cannot be prioritised. If feedback is collected and the evaluation set never grows, the loop is broken, because the system is measured against a set that diverges from what it processes.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A sponsor's expectations are inflated after a successful demoEstablish a recurring review showing real performance on real inputs against the agreed criteria.A single correction does not hold against continuous drift.
    • Users report failures in a shared chat channelRestructure: capture input, output, expected output and reviewer, and feed the evaluation set.Anecdotes have no frequency and cannot be prioritised.
    • Feedback is collected but the evaluation set never growsThe loop is broken.The system is measured against a set that diverges from what it processes.
    • A single well-argued memo resets the sponsor's understandingNecessary, not sufficient.It fixes today's gap and none of next quarter's.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect options that give a stakeholder something true and unhelpful, a guarantee that is too broad, or a correction that does not recur.

    A client asks for a contractual accuracy guarantee on a document-classification service.

    • CorrectCommit an accuracy figure scoped to a named document population, with the evaluation set, the scoring method, the review cadence and the excluded document types stated.
    • WrongOVERSPECCommit to the aggregate accuracy measured during the pilot. It converts a measurement taken on one input mix into a guarantee about every future input mix.
    • WrongDISCARDCommit to availability and latency only, and state that accuracy cannot be contractually guaranteed. It drops the commitment the client needs, instead of qualifying it into something keepable.

    A sponsor's expectations have inflated after an early period on clean data.

    • CorrectEstablish a recurring review that reports real performance on real production inputs against the agreed acceptance criteria.
    • WrongHALF-MOVESend a detailed written correction setting out the system's actual limitations. It is accurate and one-time, against a drift that is continuous.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISOpen a feedback channel where users raise issues as they encounter them. It collects reactions and not measurements, and produces anecdotes with no frequency.

    Design shapeAn operations director is planning next quarter's staffing. The answer reports the proportion of volume routed to human review, its variance, and what that metric does not cover. Reporting overall system accuracy is WRONG-AXIS, because it does not answer the staffing decision. Handing over the full monitoring dashboard is ARCHITECTED: it looks transparent and passes the architect's interpretation job to someone without the context.

    Say it backA client wants "95% accuracy" in the contract. Separately, a sponsor believes the system is nearly finished after a good demo, and the operations lead asks what to tell the review team. What do you commit, set up and report?

    Commit accuracy per segment, with the scoring method, the cadence and the excluded segments named, because the client's future mix is outside the provider's control. Set up a recurring review of real performance on real inputs against the agreed criteria, with a loop that turns each failure into an evaluation case. Give the operations lead the review volume and its variance, with what it does not cover.

    Connections

    • O6.2, §6.4: segmented reporting is the base for a per-segment commitment, since both name the case types where performance differs.
    • O3.3, §3.5: a percentile and not a maximum is the same latency discipline, and the SLA is written against the tail.
    • O4.2, §4.3: the evaluation set that the loop feeds should be rebuilt from real production failures, which is what a structured loop collects.
    • O4.6, §4.12: the logs that attribute a metric to a release are what a recurring review is read from.
    • O6.4, §6.7 and §6.8: the next objective records the decisions and hands the system over, and the review routine goes with it.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 6, third objective. Course corpus §6.5, §6.9 and §6.10. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states expectation and commitment rules and no product facts. The item volumes, the review rate, the pilot mix and the segment accuracies are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Choose each stakeholder's metric from the decision they face, and state what it does not cover. A dashboard is not an answer, and more metrics is not a fuller picture.
    2. Commit availability and latency normally, with latency as a percentile. Qualify an accuracy commitment with its population, method and cadence, and exclusions, and commit per segment.
    3. Do not commit the pilot aggregate flat, and do not refuse to commit accuracy at all. A fixed and monitored input mix permits a tighter figure.
    4. Expectations drift upward, so keeping expectations in line is a routine: a recurring review of real performance on real inputs against the agreed criteria.
    5. A loop captures input, output, expected output and reviewer and feeds the evaluation set. A channel of anecdotes cannot be prioritised.

    Document architectures and provide implementation guidance

    Sheet
    D6-4
    Exam weight
    14%
    Domain
    Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management
    Corpus sections
    6.7 6.8
    Reading time
    ≈ 7 min
    Position
    4 of 5 in D6

    A year after a claims system went live, a new engineer asks why the routing step runs on the smaller model. The latency ceiling has just been raised from 3 seconds to 6, and the bigger model is tempting. The original team has moved on. The code shows which model is used, and it does not show why, or whether the reason still holds.

    The reader who asks that question is the person documentation exists for. They are not asking what the system does, since the code says that. They are asking why it is like this and whether they may change it. What would the record have to contain to answer?

    Record why, so the decision can be reopened§6.7

    The corpus discriminator is whether a reader who was not present can tell a constraint that mattered from a preference. An architecture decision record has four parts: the decision, the alternatives considered, the trade-offs, and the constraints that drove the choice. For an AI system, also record the evaluation numbers the decision rested on and the condition that reopens it.

    A record of the chosen design answers "what". Only the alternatives, the trade-offs and the driving constraints answer "why, and may I change it". When a model-tier choice is made under a latency ceiling, record the decision, the rejected options with their numbers, the trade-off and the ceiling. When the ceiling moves, the decision can be reopened on evidence. Constraints expire, and an unrecorded one makes the decision impossible to reopen.

    If a year-old decision is questioned after a constraint changed, check the recorded constraint and re-evaluate against it, which is the moment the record exists for. A detailed component diagram and inventory is insufficient alone, since diagrams answer "what" and carry no reasoning. A recorded walkthrough is insufficient alone as well. It transfers knowledge once, and it goes stale on the first change.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Documenting a model-tier choice made under a latency ceilingRecord the decision, the rejected options with their numbers, the trade-off and the ceiling.When the ceiling moves, the decision can be reopened on evidence.
    • A year-old decision is questioned after a constraint changedCheck the recorded constraint and re-evaluate against it.The record exists for exactly this moment.
    • The team proposes a detailed component diagram and inventory as the documentationInsufficient alone.Diagrams answer "what", and they carry no reasoning.
    • The team proposes a recorded architecture walkthroughInsufficient alone.It transfers knowledge once and goes stale on the first change.
    Go deeper: why the numbers belong in the record

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the figures are invented. The larger model scored 1.3 points higher on a 400-claim set, which is 5.2 claims. A successor who knows that can judge whether the gap is real, and a record that says only "the larger model was better" cannot be re-run.

    The 2.1 seconds also has a price. At 40,000 requests a day it adds 84,000 seconds of waiting, about 23.3 hours a day. With the ceiling raised to 6 seconds the cost may now be affordable, and the record tells the successor which two numbers to measure again.

    Give the receiving team what lets them change it safely§6.8

    The corpus discriminator is whether the receiving team can build and change the system without reconstructing the architect's reasoning. Implementation guidance holds four things: interface contracts, the rationale behind configuration values, the failure modes with the response to each, and the tests that must pass before a change ships. It is distinct from the decision record, which explains why the design is as it is.

    If another team will extend the pipeline, give them interface contracts, configuration rationale, failure modes and gating tests, so that they can change it safely without the original team. If a prompt or model change is proposed after handover, name the regression tests that must pass first in the guidance. That prevents a silent behavioural regression from shipping.

    An onboarding overview document is a supplement and not a substitute, since it orients a reader and does not gate a change. Configuration values documented without their rationale are insufficient, because a value without its reason is changed by the next person who finds it inconvenient.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Another team will extend the pipelineInterface contracts, configuration rationale, failure modes and gating tests.They can change it safely without the original team.
    • A prompt or model change is proposed after handoverRegression tests that must pass first, named in the guidance.It prevents a silent behavioural regression from shipping.
    • The team asks for an onboarding overview document insteadA supplement and not a substitute.It orients a reader, and does not gate a change.
    • Configuration values are documented without their rationaleInsufficient.A value without its reason is changed by the next person who finds it inconvenient.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect options that look thorough and describe the system, and one that records reasoning or gates change.

    The documentation for a design that another team will maintain has to be specified.

    • CorrectRecord the decision, the alternatives considered, the trade-offs accepted and the constraints that drove the choice.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDProduce a full description of the chosen architecture with detailed component diagrams. It is more effort and more pages, and it misses the content that makes the design safe to change.
    • WrongHALF-MOVERecord a walkthrough session with the original architects. It is a one-time transfer to whoever watches it, and it is stale the first time the system changes.

    An internal team will take over extending a delivered Claude system.

    • CorrectProvide interface contracts, the rationale behind each configuration value, the known failure modes with the response to each, and the tests that must pass before any change ships.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDProvide a thorough narrative overview of how the system works end to end. It reads as complete documentation and gates nothing.
    • WrongREPAIRProvide the repository with well-commented code, and offer to answer questions in a shared channel. It is reactive support in place of a durable artifact, and it evaporates when the original team is reassigned.
    Say it backA year on, someone asks why the smaller model was chosen, and a second team is about to extend the pipeline. What does each of them need from the documentation?

    The questioner needs a decision record: the decision, the alternatives with their numbers, the trade-offs and the constraint, here the latency ceiling, so the choice can be reopened when the ceiling moves. The second team needs implementation guidance: interface contracts, the reason for each configuration value, the failure modes with responses, and named tests that must pass before any prompt or model change ships.

    Connections

    • O4.3, §4.9: the regression set and the release path are the tests that the guidance names as gating a change.
    • O4.6, §4.12: the prompt version and model identifier on every request are what let a metric be tied to a recorded decision.
    • O3.3, §3.4: a latency ceiling and a stage table are the kind of constraint and numbers the record holds.
    • O6.1, §6.2: the signed acceptance criterion is one of the constraints the record cites.
    • O6.5, §6.11 and §6.12: handoff, monitoring and iteration come next. Inference: both artifacts travel with the handover.

    Remember

    1. A decision record has four parts: the decision, the alternatives, the trade-offs and the constraints that drove it. For an AI system, add the evaluation numbers and the condition that reopens the decision.
    2. Constraints expire, and an unrecorded one makes the decision impossible to reopen. When a constraint changes, check the record and re-evaluate against it.
    3. A component diagram answers "what" and a recorded walkthrough goes stale. Neither is sufficient alone.
    4. Implementation guidance holds interface contracts, configuration rationale, failure modes with responses, and tests that must pass before a change ships.
    5. An onboarding overview is a supplement. Code and a question channel are not a handover.

    A claims assistant has had a successful pilot with 40 users, and the plan is to roll it out to 800, which is twenty times as many. The pilot's failure rate was low, its users were happy, and the build team sat next to them. A manager asks for a capacity plan: how many requests a day, what rate limits, what the bill will be.

    The capacity plan is a fair request, and it is not the first thing to produce. Scaling changes who sends requests and what they send, as well as how many. What has the pilot been quietly assuming?

    List the assumptions the pilot relied on before planning capacity§6.11

    The corpus discriminator is which small-scale assumptions stop holding at large scale. There are three classes. The input distribution widens, the support and human-review load grows, and rare failures become routine. The sequence is to surface the assumptions first, and the cost model and model choice follow from them. The failure mode is to extrapolate pilot cost and pilot accuracy linearly onto a wider population.

    For a successful 40-user pilot going to 800 users, list which input, support-load and edge-case assumptions may not hold, then rebuild the cost model. The wider population brings input types the pilot never sampled. A 1-in-500 failure seen twice in a 200-case pilot is a routine event at scale: rare is relative to volume, and at that volume it is several events a day.

    If human review absorbed 12% of pilot volume, convert it into a staffing line at projected volume before rollout. The pilot review was done by the build team and is invisible in the pilot cost. Rate limits and infrastructure capacity for the new volume are necessary, and they are not the binding constraint. They are the visible constraint, and the input distribution is the one that bites.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A successful 40-user pilot is going to 800 usersList which input, support-load and edge-case assumptions may not hold, then rebuild the cost model.The wider population brings input types the pilot never sampled.
    • A 1-in-500 failure seen twice in a 200-case pilotPlan for it as a routine event.Rare is relative to volume, and at scale it is several events a day.
    • Human review absorbed 12% of pilot volumeConvert it to a staffing line at projected volume before rollout.Pilot review was done by the build team and is invisible in the pilot cost.
    • Rate limits and infrastructure capacity for the new volumeNecessary, and not the binding constraint.It is the visible constraint, and the input distribution is the one that bites.
    Go deeper: the staffing and failure sums

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the volumes are invented. Suppose 800 users send 50 requests a day each, which is 40,000 requests. A failure at 1 in 500 happens 80 times a day. The pilot saw it twice in 200 cases, which looked like a footnote, and at this volume it is daily work.

    At 12% review, 4,800 items a day need a person. At three minutes each that is 240 hours, or 30 people on eight-hour shifts, a line that appeared in no pilot budget.

    Hand over the means to detect degradation, and not only the code§6.12

    The corpus discriminator is whether the receiving team can answer "is it still working?" without the original team. A handover has four items: the evaluation suite, the acceptance criteria, a named owner who is a person with a deputy, and the re-check routine.

    Monitoring has two layers. Operational telemetry covers latency, errors, cost and volume. Quality telemetry covers evaluation scores, the human-override rate and the confidence distribution, which is how often the system reports high or low confidence.

    If a system is transferring to an internal operations team, hand over the evaluation suite, the thresholds, a named owner and a deputy, the re-check cadence and the implementation guidance. Then the receiving team can detect and act without the original team.

    A handover of repository access, documentation and training sessions is insufficient, since nothing in it detects a change in behaviour. Ownership assigned to a team and not to a person is insufficient too, because a distributed owner is no owner.

    If complaints rise after launch while error rates stay flat, check for a shift in the input distribution and re-run the evaluation suite, since silent quality degradation does not show in operational telemetry. If the evaluation set is unchanged twelve months after launch, iteration is broken, because the set has drifted away from what the system actually processes.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A system is transferring to an internal operations teamThe evaluation suite, thresholds, a named owner and deputy, the re-check cadence, plus the implementation guidance.The receiving team can detect and act without the original team.
    • The handover consists of repository access, documentation and training sessionsInsufficient.Nothing in it detects a change in behaviour.
    • Ownership is assigned to a team rather than a personInsufficient.A distributed owner is no owner.
    • Complaints rise after launch while error rates are flatCheck input-distribution shift and re-run the evaluation suite.Silent quality degradation does not show in operational telemetry.
    • The evaluation set is unchanged twelve months after launchBroken iteration.The set has drifted away from what the system actually processes.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect options that do a real and necessary task in the wrong order, or that transfer capability without the means to detect failure.

    A successful pilot is to be rolled out to twenty times the user base.

    • CorrectIdentify which assumptions held at pilot scale and may not hold at full scale (input variety, support and review load, edge-case frequency), and rebuild the cost and model-tier decisions on those findings.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEProject infrastructure capacity and rate limits for the new request volume. It is a real and necessary step that skips the assumptions which determine what to project.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDMove to a higher-capability model ahead of rollout to absorb the wider variety of inputs. It sounds prudent and spends money before anyone has characterised the inputs it is meant to handle.

    A delivered system is being handed to the client's internal team.

    • CorrectTransfer the evaluation suite, the acceptance thresholds and the trigger for action, a named owner with a deputy, and the routine for re-running the suite on a stated cadence and after any model or input-format change.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDTransfer the repository, full architecture documentation and training sessions. It is thorough and effortful, and silent on how the team detects that the system has stopped working.
    • WrongREPAIRRetain a support arrangement with the delivery team for the first year. It keeps the capability with the wrong party and defers the handover instead of completing it.
    Say it backA 40-user pilot is going to 800 users, and the delivery team will hand the system to operations after launch. What do you produce before the rollout, and what do you hand over?

    Before the rollout, an assumption audit: which input, support-load and edge-case assumptions may not hold, then the cost model rebuilt on that list, with review converted to a staffing line. At handover, the evaluation suite, the acceptance thresholds, a named owner with a deputy, and the re-check routine, plus the implementation guidance, so that the operations team can tell when quality drifts.

    Connections

    • O6.4, §6.8: the implementation guidance is part of the handover, and Inference: the decision record travels with it.
    • O4.6, §4.12: the two telemetry layers here are the monitoring and the quality sampling there.
    • O4.2, §4.3: an evaluation set that has not grown is the set drifting from production, and rebuilding it from real failures is the iteration step.
    • O6.3, §6.10: the recurring review and the feedback loop are a routine. Inference: the named owner is who runs it.
    • O5.3, §5.8: review percentage times volume times minutes is the headcount sum behind the staffing line.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 6, fifth objective. Course corpus §6.11 and §6.12. No live-document check was needed: the chapter states lifecycle rules and no product facts. The user counts, the request volume, the review time and the shift length are invented for illustration, apart from the corpus's 12% and 1-in-500 figures.

    Remember

    1. Scaling changes the inputs and not only the volume. List the assumptions at risk before the capacity plan: input distribution, support and review load, rare failures.
    2. A rare failure is routine at volume. Convert pilot review into a staffing line, and do not extrapolate pilot cost or accuracy linearly.
    3. Rate limits and capacity are necessary, and the input distribution is the constraint that bites.
    4. A handover that can detect degradation holds the evaluation suite, the acceptance criteria, a named person as owner with a deputy, and the re-check routine.
    5. Degradation is silent. When complaints rise and errors are flat, check input shift and re-run the suite. An evaluation set that never grows is a broken iteration.

    Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement

    7%

    v1.0, section 6

    Domain 7 carries 7% of the exam, about 4 of the 63 items, across three objectives. It is the smallest domain, and it is also the one with the most product detail: where Claude Code reads its configuration, which settings win, and which mechanism can enforce a rule.

    The items turn on one distinction. An instruction shapes what Claude tries to do, and a setting changes what Claude Code allows. Most wrong answers fix a configuration problem with more prose. The table below is the course's reading of the domain, not the guide's wording.

    ObjectiveThe question it answers
    Configure tools and environments for teamsWhere does a rule live so that a clone inherits it, and how hard does it hold?
    Improve developer workflowsPlan or execute, which technique fits the failure, and what proves the value?
    Debugging and operational issuesWhich layer owns the symptom?

    The guide's three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4, so Domain 7 has none of its own. Claude Code changes quickly, and the chapters mark each point taken from its documentation with the date it was read.

    • O7.1Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)Not written yet
