    Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)

    Sheet
    D7-1
    Exam weight
    7%
    Domain
    Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement
    Corpus sections
    7.1 7.2 7.8
    Reading time
    ≈ 14 min
    Position
    1 of 3 in D7

    Four engineers work in one repository. Three of them get generated code that follows the team's naming convention. The fourth joined last week and gets code that does not. Nobody changed the model, the prompt or the code, and the new engineer's pull requests keep failing review on the same point.

    The convention sits in the other three engineers' personal configuration files, on their laptops. It never reached the repository, so a fresh clone inherits none of it. Which configuration belongs where, and which of it is a request and which is a rule?

    Put shared standards where a clone inherits them§7.1

    The corpus lists four levels of instruction file: user (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project (CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md in the repository), directory-level files, and .claude/rules/*.md. They are concatenated from the root down to the working directory. The live documentation (read 2026-10-27) adds that files above the working directory load at launch, and files in subdirectories load when Claude works with files there. Every discovered file contributes, and the corpus documents no override precedence between CLAUDE.md levels.

    Project-level files are version-controlled and reach everyone who clones. User-level files reach one person and are invisible in code review. The test is whether a thing survives a clone and reaches someone who was not present: if it does not, it is not enablement. When three engineers apply a convention and a new fourth does not, move the convention from their user-level files into the project file and commit it.

    The command /context shows what actually loaded into the current session, and /memory answers a different question, which is where the memory files are.

    A partner team that wants your Claude Code setup needs version-controlled shared configuration, skills and commands, plus an onboarding path to follow, because the artifact is inherited and nothing depends on who attended what. A recorded walkthrough is rejected: it is durable and frozen, and teaches the old setup with full confidence on the day it changes. A shared chat channel for questions is rejected as reactive support and not an inherited artifact.

    Poor results on a large legacy codebase, blamed on repo size and contributor count, point to missing committed context: write the conventions and structure into the project files.

    A personal override is available too. One engineer who wants a private /commit behaviour places ~/.claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md, and a personal skill overrides a project skill of the same name, so teammates are unaffected. A subdirectory file added to "override" the project file is rejected, since files concatenate and a conflict leaves the model with two contradictory instructions.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Three engineers apply a convention, a fourth (new) does not, same repoThe convention lives in the originals' ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Move it to project level and commit it.User-level config is not in version control, so a clone inherits none of it.
    • A partner team wants to adopt your Claude Code setupVersion-controlled shared configuration, skills and commands, plus an onboarding path they follow.The artifact is inherited, and nothing depends on who attended what.
    • Same situation, offered as a recorded walkthroughReject.It is durable and frozen, and teaches the old setup with full confidence the day it changes.
    • Same situation, offered as a shared chat channel for questionsReject.It is reactive support and not an inherited artifact.
    • Results on a large legacy codebase are poor, and the team blames repo size and contributor countWrite the conventions and structure into committed project context.Missing committed context is the blocker. Size, language and contributor count are not.
    • One engineer wants their own /commit behaviour without affecting the team~/.claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md, with the same name, as a personal override.Personal skills override project skills of the same name, and teammates are unaffected.
    • A subdirectory file is added to "override" the project file for that directoryReject.Files concatenate, so both load, and a conflict leaves the model with two contradictory instructions.

    Ask when it must apply, then how hard it must hold§7.2

    Choose a mechanism with two questions, in order. First, when must this be in effect: always, on matching paths, or on invocation. Second, how hard must it hold: as guidance, as a capability boundary, as isolation, or as unconditional enforcement. A behaviour that a configuration mechanism governs is corrected at that mechanism, and not by prose placed beside it.

    Universal coding standards belong in the project CLAUDE.md, since they are needed every session and on-demand invocation would depend on memory.

    A convention that applies only to test files and bleeds elsewhere belongs in a .claude/rules/ entry with a glob for the test paths, which is deterministic path matching and not the model's inference from headings.

    A 500-line CLAUDE.md that mixes standards, pull-request checklists and deploy steps should keep the universal standards, move workflow procedures to skills and file-scoped conventions to rules. Always-loaded tokens are paid every session, and occasional procedures should cost nothing when unused. Moving everything into skills is rejected, because universal standards would then need explicit invocation every time.

    When a skill uses a tool it should not touch, scope allowed-tools in that skill's frontmatter. Adding "do not use that tool" to the skill body is rejected, since advisory prose competes with context and does not set the condition.

    When a skill's exploratory output crowds the main task out of context, set context: fork, which runs the skill in an isolated subagent context and returns only the result. "Be concise" is rejected because it asks the model to simulate isolation instead of imposing it.

    A rule that must hold every time, whatever any prompt says, needs deterministic enforcement: a hook, or a deny rule in the settings permissions (§7.8). Instruction prose is weighed against other context, and enforcement is not. A style preference proposed for deterministic enforcement is rejected, since it turns a suggestion into a hard failure that someone must merge a config change to undo.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A skill uses a tool it should not touchScope allowed-tools in that skill's frontmatter.The frontmatter key is the mechanism that governs the behaviour.
    • Same situation, fixed by adding "do not use that tool" to the skill bodyReject.Advisory prose competes with context and does not set the condition.
    • A skill's exploratory output crowds the main task out of contextSet context: fork.It runs the skill in an isolated subagent context, and only the result returns.
    • Same situation, fixed by adding "be concise" to the skillReject.It asks the model to simulate isolation instead of imposing it.
    • A convention applies only to test files but bleeds elsewhereA .claude/rules/ entry with a glob for the test paths.It is deterministic path matching and not model inference from headings.
    • Universal coding standardsProject CLAUDE.md.They are needed every session, and on-demand invocation would depend on memory.
    • A 500-line CLAUDE.md mixing standards, PR checklists and deploy stepsKeep the universal standards. Move workflow procedures to skills and file-scoped conventions to .claude/rules/.Always-loaded tokens are paid every session, and occasional procedures should cost nothing when unused.
    • Same situation, fixed by moving everything into skillsReject.Universal standards would then need explicit invocation every time.
    • A rule must hold every time regardless of what any prompt saysDeterministic enforcement: a hook, or a deny rule in settings.json permissions (§7.8).Instruction prose is weighed against other context, and enforcement is not.
    • A style preference is proposed for deterministic enforcementReject.It converts a suggestion into a hard failure that someone must merge a config change to undo.
    Go deeper: the token cost of a long file, and what the documentation says

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and the sizes are assumptions. Suppose a line costs about 12 tokens, so a 500-line CLAUDE.md is 6,000 tokens at the start of every session. With 1,000 sessions a day across a team, that is 6,000,000 tokens a day. Cutting the file to 120 lines of universal standards gives 1,440,000, and the moved procedures cost nothing until invoked.

    Anthropic's Claude Code documentation (live docs, read 2026-10-27) agrees with the direction. It says CLAUDE.md files are concatenated and not overridden, and it advises under 200 lines per file, because longer files consume more context and reduce adherence. It describes path-scoped rules as loading when matching files are opened, and it says instructions are context and not enforced configuration.

    Its import syntax allows a depth of four hops. The corpus warns that sources disagree on that number, so never key an answer on it.

    One point in the documentation differs from the corpus row. It describes allowed-tools as tools Claude may use without asking permission while the skill runs, and disallowed-tools as tools removed from the pool. The exam rule stays as the corpus states it, and a real design should test which key does what on the version in use.

    Enforce in settings and hooks, since instructions only shape what Claude tries§7.8

    Permission rules sit in settings.json under permissions, in three arrays: allow, ask and deny. Entries name a tool and optionally a pattern, such as Bash(git push *). Claude Code enforces them, and the model does not. Instructions in a prompt or CLAUDE.md shape what Claude tries to do, and they do not change what Claude Code allows.

    If a capability must never be exercised, whatever any prompt says, add a deny rule in the settings permissions. A strongly worded CLAUDE.md instruction is rejected, since it shapes what Claude tries and does not change what is allowed.

    If an action must happen every time a tool runs, such as a format, a test or an audit entry, use a hook on the relevant event, scoped by a matcher. A reminder to run the formatter in the project file is rejected, because it competes with everything else in context.

    If a tool call must be stopped before it executes, use a PreToolUse hook or a deny permission rule, since both act before execution and a log acts after. When a narrow allow exists and a broad deny also matches, the call is denied: the first match in the deny, ask, allow order wins. A team style preference proposed for a hook or a deny rule is rejected as over-specification.

    Settings precedence runs from managed enterprise policy, then the command line, then .claude/settings.local.json, then .claude/settings.json, then ~/.claude/settings.json. Nothing below managed policy overrides it. If an organisation must guarantee a rule survives every local override, use managed policy settings. The shared project file is .claude/settings.json, which everyone who clones receives, and the local file is one developer's personal override.

    Instruction files and settings files behave in opposite ways. Instruction files concatenate, and none overrides another. Settings files have a winner: a single-value key takes its value from the highest scope, while list keys such as permissions.allow, ask and deny merge across every scope, and the merged rules run deny, ask, allow. A deny in any scope beats an allow in any scope. Inference: a managed-policy value on a single-value key still outranks every lower scope.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A capability must never be exercised, regardless of any promptA deny rule in settings.json permissions.It is enforced by Claude Code, outside the model's discretion.
    • Same situation, addressed by a strongly worded CLAUDE.md instructionReject.It shapes what Claude tries to do and does not change what is allowed.
    • An action must happen every time a tool runs (format, test, audit entry)A hook on the relevant event, scoped by matcher.The action always happens, rather than depending on the model choosing it.
    • Same situation, addressed by "remember to run the formatter" in the project fileReject.A reminder competes with everything else in context.
    • A tool call must be stopped before it executesA PreToolUse hook, or a deny permission rule.Both act before execution, and a log acts after.
    • A narrow allow exists and a broad deny also matchesDenied.The first match in the deny, ask, allow order wins, and specificity is irrelevant.
    • An organisation must guarantee a rule survives every local overrideManaged policy settings.Nothing below it in the precedence order can override it.
    • A team style preference is proposed for a hook or a deny ruleReject.It is over-specification: a suggestion converted into a hard failure that someone must merge a config change to undo.
    Go deeper: what the hooks documentation says

    These are dated notes, not corpus rules (live docs, read 2026-10-27). Anthropic's hooks guide describes hooks as user-defined shell commands run at lifecycle points, which gives deterministic control, so that certain actions always happen instead of relying on the model. It configures them in the settings files, under the user and project settings.json.

    A PreToolUse hook runs before a tool call and can block it: a script that exits with code 2 blocks the action and passes its message to Claude as feedback, and a hook that exits 0 can print JSON with a permissionDecision of deny.

    When several hooks match, the most restrictive answer applies, in the order deny, defer, ask, allow. The memory documentation adds that CLAUDE.md is context and not enforced configuration, and that blocking a tool or path is done with a permissions deny rule in managed settings or with a hook.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4, so none of them is a sample for this domain. Its Sample 1, on removing capabilities, is a Domain 3 item. Inference: a deny rule applies the same removal-first logic.

    The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect options that fix the symptom with a prompt, a reminder or a wiki page, and one that changes the mechanism.

    A newly hired engineer's generated code omits a convention the other three engineers always get.

    • CorrectThe convention is in the other engineers' user-level configuration and not at project level. Move it into the version-controlled project configuration and confirm with /context.
    • WrongREPAIRHave the new engineer prefix every prompt with the convention. It patches each session downstream of a configuration gap that a committed file closes once, and it fails silently the first time they forget.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEAdd the convention to a team wiki page and link it in the onboarding email. It transfers the knowledge to a human and never reaches the model's request at all.

    A skill must be prevented from performing destructive operations.

    • CorrectSet allowed-tools in the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter to the minimal set it needs.
    • WrongREPAIRAdd an instruction inside the skill body telling it not to perform destructive operations. It asks the model to honour a boundary that the frontmatter can impose, and it competes with everything else in context.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISConfigure the restriction in .mcp.json or the project CLAUDE.md. The intent is right and the mechanism is wrong, since skill tool scoping lives in SKILL.md frontmatter.

    An agent must never be able to force-push, and a CLAUDE.md instruction saying so has not held.

    • CorrectAdd a deny rule for the force-push command pattern to the settings.json permissions.
    • WrongREPAIRRestate the prohibition more forcefully and in more places in CLAUDE.md. Instructions shape what Claude tries and do not change what Claude Code allows, so more prose is more of what already failed.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEAdd an allow rule listing every git command the agent may run, on the grounds that an allow-list is stricter. It narrows the default path and does not stop a matching call the way an explicit deny does, and it breaks every legitimate command nobody thought to list.

    Design shapeA rule must hold on every developer machine and cannot be overridden locally. The answer is managed policy settings. Putting it in the project .claude/settings.json and requiring review is HALF-MOVE, since review controls what is committed and not what runs. Putting it in the project CLAUDE.md is WRONG-AXIS, because instruction files concatenate and cannot produce a rule that wins a conflict.

    Say it backA new hire's code misses a convention the others get. Separately, an agent keeps running a command that a CLAUDE.md line forbids, and a coding standard sits in a 500-line CLAUDE.md beside deploy steps. What do you change in each case?

    Move the convention from the others' user-level files into the committed project file and check with /context. For the forbidden command, add a deny permission rule, because instructions shape what Claude tries and do not change what is allowed. In the long file, keep the universal standards, move procedures to skills and file-scoped conventions to .claude/rules/, and leave the always-loaded part short.

    Connections

    • O3.2, §3.2: a deny rule is least privilege in configuration, since the capability is refused and not merely logged.
    • O5.1, §5.2: removing a capability or moving it behind a separate service is the same principle, applied to an agent's tools.
    • O6.4, §6.8: committed shared configuration is a handover artifact, and a recorded walkthrough or a chat channel fails there for the same reasons.
    • O2.5, §2.9: shared, versioned skills are the reuse strategy, and a personal override is the sanctioned exception.
    • O7.3, §7.7 and §7.8: the last objective in the domain uses the same layers to find which one owns a symptom.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 7, first objective. Course corpus §7.1, §7.2 and §7.8. Live checks, read 2026-10-27: Anthropic, "How Claude remembers your project" (code.claude.com/docs/en/memory); "Extend Claude with skills" (code.claude.com/docs/en/skills), first 100,000 of 118,114 characters; "Automate actions with hooks" (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide). The engineers, the 12 tokens a line and the session counts are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Shared standards go in committed project files, since user-level files are not in version control and a clone inherits none of them. Verify with /context.
    2. Instruction files concatenate, and none overrides another. A personal skill overrides a project skill of the same name. A recorded walkthrough and a chat channel are not inherited artifacts.
    3. Pick a mechanism by two questions: when it applies (always, on paths, on invocation) and how hard it holds (guidance, boundary, isolation, enforcement). Fix a behaviour at its mechanism and not with prose beside it.
    4. Keep always-loaded files to universal standards. Procedures go to skills, and path-specific conventions go to .claude/rules/ with globs.
    5. Instructions shape what Claude tries. A deny rule or a hook changes what happens. Permissions resolve deny, ask, allow, first match wins, and specificity never counts.
    6. Managed policy sits above every local override. Do not convert a style preference into a hook or a deny rule.

    Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling

    Sheet
    D7-2
    Exam weight
    7%
    Domain
    Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement
    Corpus sections
    7.3 7.4 7.5 7.6
    Reading time
    ≈ 12 min
    Position
    2 of 3 in D7

    On Monday a team has two tasks for its AI coding tool. One is a library migration across 45 files, with three plausible ways to sequence it. The other is a single-file bug with a clear stack trace. Starting both in the same way is the mistake, and the difference between them has nothing to do with how hard each one looks.

    Six months after adoption, an executive asks whether the investment paid off. The team's answer is that invocations have grown every month. This objective covers the choices in between: how to start a task, how to correct one that went wrong, how to run the tool in a pipeline, and what to measure afterwards.

    Plan when the approach is undetermined, and execute when it is fixed§7.3

    Plan mode explores, understands and designs, then presents a plan before executing. It uses read-only operations, so it has no side effects. Direct execution implements immediately. The combined pattern is to plan for investigation and design, have a human approve, then execute directly against the approved plan. The documented trap is to start directly and switch to planning when the task gets hard.

    The discriminator is whether the approach is already determined, and not the size or difficulty of the task. If several valid approaches exist and choosing wrong means expensive rework, plan first. If the spec fixes the approach, execute. A plan is also a reviewable artifact, which satisfies approval and audit requirements that a finished diff does not.

    Restructuring a monolith into services across dozens of files has many valid approaches, and a wrong one is expensive to unwind. Adding an integration with several valid approaches makes the approach the decision. A migration touching 45 or more files has blast radius, and a reversal halfway is costly. In a change-controlled environment, a multi-approach refactor needs a plan, because the plan is the artifact the approval process attaches to.

    Implementing a function against a well-defined input and output spec needs direct execution, since a planning round would be pure overhead. So does a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace, where there is nothing to decide. A large task whose approach was settled in an approved design also executes directly, since size is not the discriminator.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Restructure a monolith into services across dozens of filesPlan mode.There are many valid approaches, and a wrong one is expensive to unwind.
    • Add a new integration with multiple valid approachesPlan mode.The approach is the decision being made.
    • A library migration touching 45+ filesPlan mode.Blast radius, and a mid-migration reversal is costly.
    • Implement a function against a well-defined input and output specDirect execution.The spec determines the approach, and a planning round is pure overhead.
    • A single-file bug fix with a clear stack traceDirect execution.There is nothing to decide.
    • A large task, but the approach was settled in an approved designDirect execution.Size is not the discriminator.
    • A multi-approach refactor in a change-controlled environmentPlan mode.The plan doubles as the artifact the approval process attaches to.

    Match the technique to the failure you can see§7.4

    When a first attempt goes wrong, the stem usually shows the signature of the failure, and the signature selects the technique. The corpus names five: the interview pattern, test-driven iteration, concrete examples, feedback batching and review isolation. Batching covers two cases, so the figure has six rows.

    If each generated version misses a different requirement, the brief is incomplete, and iterating on the output never completes a brief. Use the interview pattern: have the model ask its clarifying questions before it implements. If correctness can be checked as an assertion and prose bug reports get partial fixes, write the test suite first and iterate by feeding concrete failures back.

    Tests are a machine-checkable definition of done, and prose edge cases are read inconsistently.

    If the shape of the output varies from run to run under an unchanged instruction, add 2 to 3 concrete input and output pairs, since examples show the format and the decision logic unambiguously. Lengthening the prose description is rejected, because it is still ambiguous and only longer.

    For review feedback, put interacting issues in one detailed message, because separate fixes to interacting issues contradict each other. Independent issues go one at a time, so that each change stays easy to verify. A session that generated code is less effective at reviewing it, because it retains its reasoning context and is unlikely to challenge its own decisions, so use an independent instance.

    Make the output machine-readable at the source§7.5

    To run Claude Code in a pipeline, use claude -p "<prompt>", equivalently --print. It processes the prompt, prints to stdout and exits. Without it, the pipeline hangs waiting for input. The corpus lists options that do not exist and must be rejected: --batch and CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true. Redirecting stdin from /dev/null is a workaround and not the mechanism.

    A person reading prose tolerates variation, and a program parsing fields does not. For structured output, --output-format json forces JSON and --json-schema enforces a schema for safe downstream parsing.

    The project instruction file can supply testing standards, fixture conventions and review criteria to the CI run, and existing test files in context prevent duplicate test generation. A review that posts near-duplicate comments on every push needs the prior run's findings fed in, with an instruction to report only new or still-unaddressed issues.

    The Batch API is 50% cheaper and allows up to 24 hours, with no latency guarantee. A custom_id matches outputs to inputs. It cannot execute a tool mid-request and return the result.

    An overnight tech-debt report that nobody is blocked on suits it. A blocking pre-merge check does not, because a developer is waiting. Non-urgent analysis that fetches related files mid-analysis also stays synchronous, since batch cannot execute tools during a request and the flexible deadline is irrelevant.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • Each finding must be posted as an inline PR comment (path, line, severity, fix)--output-format json with --json-schema.It guarantees a well-formed, parseable shape every run.
    • Same situation, addressed by an "Output Format" section in CLAUDE.mdReject.Instruction context makes the format likely and not guaranteed.
    • A CI job hangs indefinitely instead of completingAdd -p or --print.Without it the tool waits for interactive input.
    • A review posts near-duplicate comments on every pushInclude the prior run's findings in the re-run prompt.A blank-slate re-run re-litigates settled findings.
    • An overnight tech-debt report, and nobody is blockedThe Batch API.The deadline is flexible, and it saves 50% of the cost.
    • A blocking pre-merge checkSynchronous.A developer is waiting on it.
    • Non-urgent analysis that fetches related files mid-analysisSynchronous.Batch cannot execute tools during a request, and the deadline is irrelevant.
    Go deeper: what the CLI documentation confirms, and a batch saving

    These are dated notes, not corpus rules (live docs, read 2026-10-27). Anthropic's CLI reference describes claude -p "query" as a query through the SDK that then exits. It can take piped input. --output-format accepts text, json and stream-json, and applies in print mode. --json-schema returns validated JSON matching a schema, also in print mode only. --permission-mode accepts plan among its values, which is how a session can start in plan mode.

    A worked example, not a corpus rule, with invented costs. A nightly report that costs $200 run synchronously costs $100 as a batch, using the 50% discount in Anthropic's model documentation (live docs, read 2026-10-25). The saving applies only if the report needs no tool call partway through and can wait, since batch allows up to 24 hours and gives no latency guarantee.

    Measure the delivery outcome, against a baseline set before adoption§7.6

    The value of AI tooling is the change in the delivery outcome it was adopted to improve. Invocation counts, seats onboarded, hours in the tool and lines of generated code accepted are not value. The discipline has three parts: name the metric before adoption, establish a baseline, and state the confound, the other change in the period that could explain the result.

    Activity data has one legitimate use, as a leading indicator during rollout, since low adoption explains a flat outcome metric.

    Match the metric to the adoption rationale. To shorten delivery cycles, use cycle time from first commit to merge. To reduce defect escape, use defects found in production per release. To cut review latency, use the time from review requested to review completed. To accelerate onboarding, use the time from a new engineer's start date to their first merged non-trivial change.

    Reject any metric chosen after the data was collected, because a metric selected because it moved is not evidence. Reject any with no pre-adoption baseline, because a figure with nothing to compare against is a number and not evidence. State the confound yourself: the team size changed, the release process changed, or a large refactor landed mid-quarter. Naming it is the difference between a measurement and a pitch.

    Go deeper: a baseline and a confound in numbers

    This is a worked example, not a corpus rule, and its numbers are invented. In the quarter before adoption, cycle time from first commit to merge averaged 5.2 days. Six months later it averages 4.1 days, a fall of 21.2%.

    That is a result worth reporting, and only with its confound beside it. If the release process also changed in the period, say so, and say how much of the change you cannot separate. Invocations that grew every month would have been equally true if cycle time had not moved at all.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect the signature in the stem to name the technique, and options that act on the symptom or measure the wrong thing.

    A migration touches 45 or more files, with several viable sequencing strategies.

    • CorrectUse plan mode to explore and present a sequencing plan for approval, then execute directly against the approved plan.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEBegin executing and switch to planning once the task proves complex. By then structural decisions are sunk on a path chosen without deliberation, and reactive switching costs more than planning upfront.
    • WrongOVERSPECAdopt a standing rule that every change goes through plan mode and written approval, single-file fixes included. It is a stronger guarantee than the requirement asks for, and it taxes every routine change to control a risk that exists only where the approach is undetermined.

    An automated review's findings must be posted as inline PR comments by a downstream script.

    • CorrectRun non-interactively with --output-format json and --json-schema, so every finding carries path, line, severity and suggested fix in a guaranteed shape.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEAdd a detailed "Output Format" section to the project CLAUDE.md. It raises compliance without guaranteeing it, and the parser fails on the run that deviates.
    • WrongREPAIRHave the downstream script parse the prose output with regular expressions. It builds tolerance for malformed output downstream instead of enforcing well-formed output at the source.

    An executive asks whether six months of AI tooling investment paid off.

    • CorrectReport the delivery outcome the tooling was adopted to improve, against its pre-adoption baseline, with the confounding changes in the period named.
    • WrongWRONG-AXISReport that invocations grew every month and 90% of engineers are now active users. It measures adoption, which is a rollout indicator, and says nothing about delivery outcomes.
    • WrongARCHITECTEDCommission a developer satisfaction survey and report the sentiment score. It sounds rigorous and produces a number, and it substitutes perception for the delivery outcome the investment was justified on.

    Design shapeThree attempts at a caching layer in an unfamiliar domain each miss a different requirement. The answer restarts with the interview pattern, asking about invalidation strategy, tolerance for stale reads, scoping and volume before implementing.

    Continuing to correct one missed requirement per round is HALF-MOVE, since the incomplete brief is never addressed. Moving to a more capable model is DISCARD, because it replaces a working tool instead of supplying the requirements it was never given.

    Say it backA team has a 45-file migration with several sequencing options, a nightly report that needs no human, a review job whose output a script must parse, and an executive who asks if the tooling paid off. What do you choose for each?

    Plan the migration, get the plan approved, then execute directly. Run the nightly report through the Batch API if it needs no tool mid-request. Run the review job with -p, --output-format json and --json-schema, so the shape is guaranteed. For the executive, report a delivery outcome such as cycle time against its pre-adoption baseline, and name the confounds.

    Connections

    • O7.1, §7.1: the project instruction file that supplies CI context is the committed configuration of that chapter. Inference: a non-interactive run draws on the same files.
    • O4.2, §4.5: schema validation is a deterministic check, and enforcing the schema at the source is the same code-first rule.
    • O4.5, §4.11: batch and async processing is the lever for a non-urgent job there, and its limit is the same.
    • O4.1, §4.1: a metric named before adoption, with a baseline, is the same pre-declared bar applied to a tooling investment.
    • O7.3, §7.7 and §7.8: the next objective turns to finding which layer owns a symptom when the tooling misbehaves.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 7, second objective. Course corpus §7.3 to §7.6. Live checks: Anthropic, "CLI reference" (code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference), read 2026-10-27, and the model overview (platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview), read 2026-10-25, for the batch discount. The costs and the cycle-time figures in the folds are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Plan when the approach is undetermined and a wrong one is expensive. Execute when the spec or an approved design fixes it. Size is not the test, and switching to planning after a bad start is the documented trap.
    2. A plan is a reviewable artifact, which is what approval and audit processes attach to.
    3. Read the failure signature: a different miss each time means the interview pattern, a checkable assertion means tests first, a varying shape means 2 to 3 examples, interacting findings go together, independent ones go one at a time, and an author does not review its own code.
    4. In a pipeline, use claude -p. Get a parseable shape with --output-format json and --json-schema, and feed prior findings into a re-run. --batch and CLAUDE_HEADLESS do not exist.
    5. Batch is 50% cheaper and slow, and it cannot run a tool mid-request. Blocking checks are synchronous.
    6. Value is a delivery outcome against a baseline, with the confound named. Invocations, seats, hours and accepted lines are activity.

    Support debugging and operational issue resolution

    Sheet
    D7-3
    Exam weight
    7%
    Domain
    Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement
    Corpus sections
    7.7 7.8
    Reading time
    ≈ 9 min
    Position
    3 of 3 in D7

    A team convention holds in some Claude Code sessions and fails in others. Same repository, same week, same machine. A teammate finds that writing the convention at the top of every prompt in capitals makes it hold in four sessions out of five. Of 50 sessions a week, that leaves 10 failures. The failures are now occasional enough that the team stops investigating them.

    The workaround has done something worse than leave a gap. It has hidden the pattern that would have located the cause. A symptom that appears in some sessions and not others is usually conditional and not random, and the first job is to find the condition.

    Find the layer that owns the symptom§7.7

    The method is to identify the layer that owns the symptom. Bisection, halving the change set until the culprit appears, assumes determinism that an agentic system does not have. The corpus gives a ladder of six rungs, taken in order. Inference: each rung is usually a cheaper question than the one below it.

    Rung 1 asks whether the content is loaded, and /context shows what actually loaded into the session. Rung 2 asks whether it sits in the right layer for the strength required: guidance, tool scope, isolation or enforcement (§7.2). Rung 3 asks whether context is polluted or stale. Use context: fork to isolate verbose work. /compact risks losing exact values, dates and specifics, and mid-task it is rejected, because the loss lands on exactly the values the implementation still needs.

    Rung 4 asks whether the tooling is wired and scoped, and least privilege means removing the unneeded capability and not logging or confirming its use. Rung 5 is retrieval and indexing, the first suspect when accuracy drops after a data change. Rung 6, the prompt or the model, comes last. The evidence rule is that output varies between runs, so a fix is demonstrated against a test set and not one clean run.

    Read the stem for what it excludes. Behaviour that differs between engineers on the same repository points at configuration scope, user level against project level, and rules out the model and tool versions. Behaviour that works in some sessions and not others on the same machine points at conditional loading, so check what /context reports, since conditional is not intermittent.

    A fact from two turns ago missing in a short conversation means the application (an API-based one, as in §2.5) is not sending the history, and rules out an exhausted window. Accuracy that collapsed right after a document refresh, with confident answers, is retrieval and indexing, since confident and wrong is correct reasoning over wrong retrieved content.

    A subagent that holds a tool and never uses it correctly is a wiring and permissions problem and not prompt wording. Exploratory output that pushed the original task out of focus is context pollution, and the verbose step is forked.

    When a rule did not hold, move it to enforcement§7.8

    The ladder's second rung asks how hard a rule must hold. When the answer is "every time, whatever any prompt says", the symptom's owner is the wrong layer: the rule sits in guidance and needs enforcement. Instructions in a prompt or CLAUDE.md shape what Claude tries to do, and permission rules are enforced by Claude Code and decide what is allowed.

    These are the eight §7.8 rules, seen from the debugging side, and O7.1 lays out the settings and precedence in detail.

    If a capability must never be exercised, add a deny rule in the settings permissions, and reject a more strongly worded CLAUDE.md line. If an action must happen every time a tool runs, such as a format, a test or an audit entry, use a hook scoped by a matcher, and reject a reminder in the project file.

    If a call must be stopped before it executes, use a PreToolUse hook or a deny rule, since a log acts after.

    A narrow allow and a broad deny that both match give a denial, because the first match in the deny, ask, allow order wins and specificity is irrelevant. To guarantee that a rule survives every local override, use managed policy settings, since nothing below it in the precedence order can override it. A team style preference proposed for a hook or a deny rule is rejected as over-specification.

    • If the scenario saysThen
    • A capability must never be exercised, regardless of any promptA deny rule in settings.json permissions.It is enforced by Claude Code, outside the model's discretion.
    • Same situation, addressed by a strongly worded CLAUDE.md instructionReject.It shapes what Claude tries to do and does not change what is allowed.
    • An action must happen every time a tool runs (format, test, audit entry)A hook on the relevant event, scoped by matcher.The action always happens, rather than depending on the model choosing it.
    • Same situation, addressed by "remember to run the formatter" in the project fileReject.A reminder competes with everything else in context.
    • A tool call must be stopped before it executesA PreToolUse hook, or a deny permission rule.Both act before execution, and a log acts after.
    • A narrow allow exists and a broad deny also matchesDenied.The first match in the deny, ask, allow order wins, and specificity is irrelevant.
    • An organisation must guarantee a rule survives every local overrideManaged policy settings.Nothing below it in the precedence order can override it.
    • A team style preference is proposed for a hook or a deny ruleReject.It is over-specification: a suggestion converted into a hard failure that someone must merge a config change to undo.

    Where the exam bites

    KnownThe guide's three samples sit in Domains 2, 3 and 4, so none of them is a sample for this domain. The scenarios below come from this project's own set, and the Trap families page defines each label. InferenceExpect a stem full of environmental detail where each detail eliminates a layer, and options that patch the symptom or swap the model.

    A convention holds in some Claude Code sessions and not others, in the same repository during the same week.

    • CorrectRun /context in a working session and a failing one and compare what loaded. The rule is in a file that is not consistently discovered: the wrong level, the wrong directory, or a path-scoped glob that does not match.
    • WrongREPAIRRestate the convention at the top of every prompt in capitals. It patches each session downstream of a loading problem, and mostly-working suppresses the diagnostic signal.
    • WrongDISCARDMove to a more capable model on the grounds that instruction-following is inconsistent. It replaces a working component to explain a symptom the configuration layer already accounts for.

    An agent must never be able to force-push, and a CLAUDE.md instruction saying so has not held.

    • CorrectAdd a deny rule for the force-push command pattern to the settings.json permissions.
    • WrongREPAIRRestate the prohibition more forcefully and in more places in CLAUDE.md. Instructions shape what Claude tries and do not change what Claude Code allows, so more prose is more of what already failed.
    • WrongHALF-MOVEAdd an allow rule listing every git command the agent may run, because an allow-list is stricter. It narrows the default path and does not stop a matching call the way an explicit deny does, and it breaks every legitimate command nobody listed.

    Design shapeA rule must hold on every developer machine and cannot be overridden locally. The answer is managed policy settings. Putting it in the project .claude/settings.json and requiring review is HALF-MOVE, since review controls what is committed and not what runs. Putting it in the project CLAUDE.md is WRONG-AXIS, because instruction files concatenate and cannot produce a rule that wins a conflict.

    Say it backA convention holds in some sessions only, and separately an agent ignores a "never force-push" line in CLAUDE.md. Where does each investigation start, and what is the fix?

    For the convention, run /context in a working session and a failing one and compare what loaded, since conditional behaviour has a condition and the model is the last suspect. For the force-push, the rule needs enforcement: add a deny permission rule, because the CLAUDE.md line shapes what Claude tries and does not change what is allowed.

    Connections

    • O7.1, §7.2: rung 2 of the ladder is the mechanism choice there, and the strength of the rule decides the layer.
    • O4.4, §4.10: the diagnosis order there, data and retrieval before the prompt and the model, is the same shape as the ladder.
    • O5.2, §5.6: reading when a symptom appears and where, before blaming the model, is the discipline of both chapters.
    • O2.4, §2.7: compaction risks the exact values that the hybrid pattern there extracts and keeps verbatim.
    • O3.4, §3.6: a trace is the evidence that shows which layer produced a symptom.

    Sources. Exam guide v1.0, section 6, Domain 7, third objective. Course corpus §7.7 and §7.8. No live-document check was needed for this chapter: it applies rules and a method from the corpus, and the Claude Code documentation read for O7.1 on 2026-10-27 covers the settings and hooks facts. The session counts in the opening are invented for illustration.

    Remember

    1. Find the layer that owns the symptom, in order: is it loaded (/context), is it in the right layer, is context polluted, is the tooling wired and scoped, retrieval and indexing, and the prompt or model last.
    2. Read the stem for what it excludes. Differences between engineers point at scope, some sessions and not others at conditional loading, confident wrong answers after a refresh at retrieval.
    3. Behaviour that works sometimes is conditional and not random. A workaround that works four times in five hides the signal.
    4. Do not /compact mid-task when exact values are needed. Fork verbose work with context: fork.
    5. A rule that must always hold moves to enforcement: a deny rule, a hook, or managed policy. Permissions resolve deny, ask, allow with the first match winning, and a style preference is not converted into a hard failure.

    Trap families

    Eight shapes that wrong options take, with the question to ask against each one.

    These labels are this project's. They come from tagging the wrong options in the practice corpus and in the guide's three samples. The guide gives a rationale for each of its three samples but no taxonomy of wrong answers, so treat the names as a study aid and the questions as the useful part. A wrong option can fit more than one family.

    HALF-MOVE

    Correct as far as it goes, but it leaves a stated requirement untouched. Showing the heading path to the model after retrieval helps it read what it got and does nothing for which chunks come back (§3.9).

    Ask: does this option still leave any requirement in the stem unmet?

    WRONG-AXIS

    A real technique applied to the wrong dimension of the problem. Doubling chunk size when the chunks lack context, or lowering the temperature when the fault is in retrieval (§3.9, §3.10).

    Ask: what is the stem actually about, and does this option act on that?

    REPAIR

    Rebuilds downstream what an earlier step should have done cleanly. A firmer system prompt for a sequence that needs a programmatic precondition is the standard case (§1.10).

    Ask: which earlier stage could have prevented this, and does the option use it?

    DISCARD

    Solves the problem by replacing or throwing away something the scenario still needs. A more capable model when the missing piece is the feedback path (§1.9), or truncating a policy the answer depends on (guide Sample 2).

    Ask: what working part does this option throw away?

    ARCHITECTED

    Sounds like the mature, professional design, more thorough or more unified than the stem asks for, but does not solve the problem the stem states. A monitoring dashboard as the improvement mechanism is the standard case (§1.9), and so is one unified index that embeds a table meant for filtering (§3.8).

    Ask: does this solve the stated problem, or does it only sound more complete?

    OVERSPEC

    The strength of the guarantee does not match the requirement. It is either stronger than asked, such as a blocking control for a mere preference, or only statistical where the requirement is absolute, such as a 99.4% compliance rate standing in for a rule that must never break (§5.3).

    Ask: is the requirement "always" or "prefer", and does the mechanism match?

    EVIDENCE-MISMATCH

    Offers a cause that the evidence in the stem does not support or already rules out. Sample 3's "the model weights silently changed" when the stem says the model version is unchanged, and its "the temperature is too low", which nothing about a document refresh would trigger.

    Ask: which facts does the stem state, and which options contradict them?

    DETECTIVE-FOR-PREVENTIVE

    Detects or confirms a misuse where the requirement is to remove the capability. Sample 1's audit logging and confirmation prompt, when the role never needs the refund or delete tools.

    Ask: does the stem say the capability is unneeded? Then removal is the answer.

    Glossary

    Each term is defined once, where it first matters. 80 so far.

    accuracy bar
    The minimum accuracy a task needs, set in advance and measured on representative inputs. O2.1
    agent
    A design in which the model chooses its own next step, one action at a time, instead of following a path written in advance. O1.3
    attention
    How strongly the model weighs each part of its input when it produces the next word. O2.4
    attention dilution
    The tendency of one pass over many inputs to go deep on some and shallow on others, in a way you cannot predict. O1.5
    augmented LLM
    A large language model (LLM) given retrieval, tools or memory. It can fetch documents at request time, call functions or use information kept from earlier interactions. O1.3
    baseline
    The current cost of a process, stated in a value unit and measured before design begins. Every later claim of improvement is compared with it. O1.1
    benchmark
    A test of candidate models on representative inputs, scored against the accuracy bar, run before a choice is committed. O2.1
    binding constraint
    The factor that actually limits a result. Improving any other factor leaves the result where it is. O1.1
    blast radius
    How far the effects of one wrong action reach. O1.3
    blast radius
    How much damage a wrong action can do, and whether the damage can be undone. O1.5
    blast radius
    How far the effects of one wrong or hostile action reach. Each tool an agent holds adds to the damage possible if it is misused. O3.1
    chain-of-thought cue
    A line in the prompt, such as think step by step, that asks the model to write out its reasoning before it answers. O2.3
    chunk
    The smallest span of a document that still makes sense when read completely out of context. O3.5
    closed
    A feedback loop is closed when a correctness signal reaches something that changes the system's behaviour: the evaluation set, the prompt or examples, the retrieval layer, routing thresholds or the choice of model. O1.2
    Compensating controls
    A control wrapped around a privilege you have decided to keep, such as logging, a confirmation prompt, a time-window restriction or a rate limit. O3.2
    confidence-tier split
    A split by how hard a case is: a cheap path for the routine majority and an expensive path for the hard minority. It is the main architectural lever on cost. O1.5
    context isolation
    Giving each thread of work its own context window, so a long task does not overflow one window and one thread's material cannot contaminate another's reasoning. O1.4
    coordinator
    The agent that splits the task, delegates the parts, passes each subagent its context, handles failures and decides when the work is done. O1.4
    coupled unit
    Three things that must stay consistent: the chunking scheme that produced the chunks, the embedding model version that turned them into vectors, and the vector index that stores them. Change one without the others and the space becomes inconsistent. O3.5
    decision
    A recurring point in a workflow where someone reads inputs and forms a judgment. It is the unit of automation; an outcome and a task are not. O1.1
    Decomposition
    Splitting a task into units of work, each handled by its own call or step. O1.5
    Dense retrieval
    Search by embeddings, numeric summaries of meaning. It finds text that means the same thing in different words. O3.6
    Dynamic adaptive decomposition
    A plan whose subtasks are generated from what earlier steps discover. It suits a scope that is unknown up front. O1.5
    enumerable
    A set of paths is enumerable when every route a request may take can be written down before any request runs. O1.3
    evaluation criterion
    The single question a unit's output is judged against, such as local correctness or cross-file consistency. O1.5
    extended thinking
    A setting in which the model reasons at length before it gives its answer. O2.1
    failure mode
    The one way a unit can go wrong. With a single failure mode, a drop in quality points at its own fix. O1.5
    Few-shot prompting
    A prompt that includes worked examples, each pairing an input with the output wanted. The model matches the pattern the examples show. O2.3
    fit signals
    Four properties that favour automating a step: scale beyond human capacity, a repeatable pattern with observable feedback, machine-readable context, and volume that repays the cost of building. O1.1
    fixed pipeline
    A sequence of steps fixed in advance, also called prompt chaining. It suits a known scope where reproducibility matters. O1.5
    graceful degradation
    When part of the input is missing, the system still produces a result and says where the gap is, instead of failing the whole run. O1.4
    guardrail
    A boundary on what the model will do, such as a refusal boundary or an escalation trigger. O2.2
    handoff
    A point where work and context pass from one agent to another, or from an agent to a person. O1.4
    Headroom
    Capability beyond what the task needs. It has a price and, with no stated requirement behind it, buys nothing the task uses. O2.1
    hub-and-spoke
    An arrangement with one coordinator at the centre and subagents on the spokes. Subagents never communicate directly with each other. O1.4
    ingest
    The moment a document or record enters the system. Work done then is done once, before any request needs it. O1.6
    input boundary
    The place where outside data enters the system. It acquires the data, validates and normalises it, and decides how far to trust it. O1.2
    integration pass
    A final unit that combines the outputs of earlier passes and judges what only the whole shows, such as cross-file consistency. O1.5
    Iterative refinement
    A loop in which the coordinator delegates, synthesises, evaluates the result for gaps, re-delegates targeted queries and synthesises again, until stated criteria are met. O1.4
    Lexical retrieval
    Search that scores documents by the exact terms they share with the query, the best-known scorer being BM25. O3.6
    MCP
    Model Context Protocol: an open standard for how a server offers actions, readable content and templates to an AI application. O3.7
    messages array
    The list of earlier turns, user and assistant, that the application sends with each call so the model can see the conversation so far. O2.4
    metadata
    The facts about where a finding came from: source URL, document name, page and date. Also called provenance. O1.4
    modular prompt
    A prompt built from shared components that many prompts reuse, instead of one long block rewritten for each use. O2.5
    nondeterminism
    The same input can take different routes or give different results on different runs. O1.3
    p95
    The 95th percentile: the value that 95% of requests come in at or under. A p95 latency limit means 95% of requests must finish within the limit. O1.3
    p95
    The response time that 95 out of every 100 requests meet or beat. It describes the slow end of the distribution, so a commitment written against it is a commitment about the tail. O1.6
    parallel fan-out
    The coordinator dispatches independent subtasks together and aggregates their results, so the wall-clock time is that of the longest branch. O1.4
    performance SLAs
    Service-level agreement: a stated commitment on a measure such as response time, availability or accuracy. O1.6
    privilege separation
    Giving each role only the tools it needs, set in its configuration, such as a drafter with no write access or a verifier with no search access. O1.4
    programmatic precondition
    A check in code that blocks a step until a required earlier step has returned, so the order holds every time instead of most of the time. O1.2
    Prompt caching
    Reuse of an unchanged beginning of the prompt across requests, so the model does not process it from scratch each time. It reuses the input prefix and never stores a reply. O2.5
    prompt chaining
    A workflow pattern in which a fixed sequence of steps runs in order and each step's output feeds the next. O1.3
    proxy signal
    A fast measure that stands in for a slow one, such as the rate at which underwriters override the model's output instead of a loss ratio that arrives after 12 months. O1.1
    RAG
    Retrieval-augmented generation: at request time, fetch the relevant pieces of your own documents and place them in the model's context, so it answers from them. O3.5
    request path
    The steps that run while the user waits for an answer. O1.6
    reranker
    A second, slower and more accurate model that rescores the candidates and reorders them, so the best few can be passed on. O3.6
    risk-tier split
    A split by how much damage a wrong action can do and whether it can be undone: reversible actions run on their own and irreversible ones wait at a gate. It is the main governance lever. O1.5
    routing
    A workflow pattern in which a request is classified and then dispatched to one of several specialised handlers. The branches are listed in advance, so the model chooses from a fixed menu. O1.3
    scratchpad
    A short, fixed space in the answer where the model writes brief working before it commits to a result. O2.3
    seam
    The boundary between two units of work, where a validation, an approval or a cost control can attach. O1.5
    sequential chaining
    Running subagents one after another because each one's input depends on the previous one's output, such as a step that needs an entity extracted by the step before it. O1.4
    Skill
    A packaged set of instructions, and optionally files and scripts, that Claude loads when a task calls for it. O2.5
    SLA
    Service-level agreement: a stated commitment about how a service performs, such as how fast it responds. O1.3
    stateless
    Each call is independent and the server keeps no memory of earlier calls. Anything the model should know must travel in the request. O2.4
    Streaming
    Sending the response to the consumer in pieces as the model produces them, instead of all at once when it is complete. O3.3
    structured error propagation
    Returning a failure to the coordinator as data it can act on, such as the type of failure, what was attempted and any partial results, instead of a bare error string. O1.4
    structured summary
    A compact record of one unit's findings in named fields, such as issues found, symbols changed and dependencies touched, passed to the next unit instead of the raw input. O1.5
    subagents
    A specialist agent that the coordinator starts for one narrow part of the task. Its context is isolated, so it knows only what the coordinator passed it. O1.4
    sufficiency criteria
    The conditions a coordinator checks the synthesis against to decide that the work is finished, for example that every subtopic in the brief has two sources. O1.4
    synthesis agent
    The subagent that writes the final report from the findings the other subagents returned. O1.4
    system prompt
    The instruction block a developer sets before the user speaks. It frames every turn of the conversation. O2.2
    tail
    The slowest and costliest few percent of requests, the ones far out on the long side of the distribution. O1.3
    trace
    The record of one request's path through the system: each tool call with arguments and results, the context retrieved, the decision points, all tied to one identifier. O3.4
    validation gate
    A check inside a workflow that tests an intermediate result and sends failures down a different route. O1.3
    value unit
    The business unit in which value is stated, such as minutes per item, FTE-hours per 1,000 items, dollars per transaction or days of turnaround. O1.1
    wall-clock time
    Elapsed time from request to result, as the person waiting experiences it. With parallel branches it equals the longest branch. O1.4
    workflow
    A design in which fixed steps run in code and the code, not the model, sets the path. A workflow can branch, because the branches are written down in advance. O1.3
    wrong-stance signals
    Five properties of a step that show handing the decision itself to the model is the wrong stance: irreversible and rare, a regulation requiring a human decision-maker, novel creative output of low repeatability, the human relationship as the product, and a human gating every iteration. O1.1
    zero-shot
    A prompt that gives instructions and no worked examples. O2.3

    Sources and version

    What every claim in this course rests on, in order of authority, and what it deliberately does not rest on.

    Order of authority

    1. The official exam guide, version 1.0, effective July 2026. The 38 objectives and the seven domain weights are copied from the PDF by script, not typed. The PDF is the file that Anthropic's public Partner Academy certifications page links. It is 358,335 bytes, and its SHA-256 begins 19a111ae61a07066.

    2. Pearson VUE's Anthropic program page and the Partner Academy FAQ, for logistics: scoring, retakes, the 48-hour cancellation rule and the 7 December content change. Read 2026-10-22.

    3. The course corpus: 78 sections and 372 testable decisions, called facets, that this project derived from the guide and reviewed. Every decision rule in a chapter comes from it.

    4. Anthropic's live documentation and engineering posts, checked for any product fact a chapter adds beyond the corpus. Checks made: "Introducing Contextual Retrieval" (read 2026-10-24); the model overview, prompting guidance, extended thinking, prompt caching, context windows and Agent Skills pages (2026-10-25); "Building effective agents", the multi-agent research post, and the Agent SDK subagent and agent-loop pages (2026-10-25); the tool definition, tool search, MCP architecture and Claude Code MCP pages (2026-10-26); and the Claude Code memory, skills, hooks and CLI pages (2026-10-27). Each chapter cites the pages it used with the date.

    Labels

    Knownstated in the guide or another Anthropic source. Inferencereasoned from known facts and marked as such. Uncertainnot settled by any source. Recommendedmy advice, not a fact about the exam. Design shapea further scenario from this project's own set, summarised without its full option list. The wrong-answer family labels such as HALF-MOVE are defined on the Trap families page.

    How the chapters were checked

    Each chapter was checked by script against the guide and the corpus, then read once by an independent auditor and an independent cold reader. Study notes, called the corpus, state each decision the exam can test as a situation, an answer and a reason, and name for each section a discriminator, the one fact that separates the right answer from the tempting one. The tag on each block, such as §3.9, names the corpus section it teaches.

    Not used as sources

    Community certification guides, which have contradicted Anthropic's own pages before, and the 2026-10-22 revalidation notes written by Antigravity, which are audit notes with corrections attached.

    Version

    This course is pinned to guide v1.0. Anthropic publishes updated guides on 17 November 2026. A sitting on or after 7 December 2026 is governed by the updated guide, and every sheet would need rechecking against it, objective by objective.
